lessons.title: How to take the pulse. Endoscopy
objectives: Explain twelve terms related to pulse assessment and endoscopy.
Give a clear, sequenced explanation and ask permission before a routine observation.
Distinguish a pulse finding from a diagnosis and explain the purpose of upper gastrointestinal endoscopy.
Clarify preparation instructions and check the patient’s understanding without inventing clinical directions.

stages.label: WARM-UP
stages.detail: Show the pulse and informed-consent cards. Ask: What would you explain before checking a patient’s pulse? What might a patient ask before an endoscopy? Pairs agree on one permission question and one clarification question.

stages.label: VISUAL VOCABULARY CARDS
stages.detail: Use Handout 1. Pupils scan all twelve terms, practise pronunciation, and explain four terms to a partner. Each pupil writes two original sentences; the other sentence spaces are for later practice.

stages.label: LANGUAGE DISCOVERY
stages.detail: Use Handout 2: sequencing an explanation and asking permission. Pupils compare the examples, explain the patterns, complete Practice A, and justify two answers with a partner.

stages.label: READING
stages.detail: Use Handout 3, “Two Explanations before a Procedure”. Read for the main message, then answer five questions. Partners support their answers with the relevant part of the text.

stages.label: LISTENING
stages.detail: Use Handout 4, “Checking What the Patient Has Understood”. Allow one minute to preview the questions. Read the teacher script twice, with a pause between readings; pupils answer, compare, and check.

stages.label: SPEAKING AND CULTURE EXCHANGE
stages.detail: Use Handout 5. Allow three minutes to prepare, four minutes for the first role-play, four minutes with roles changed, two minutes for the culture exchange, and two minutes for partner feedback.

stages.label: MINI-QUIZ AND HOMEWORK
stages.detail: Pupils answer the six questions independently. Check briefly with the teacher key, identify one recurring error, and assign the written homework in Handout 6.

vocabulary.definition: the rhythmic expansion of an artery as blood is pumped by the heart.
the artery on the thumb side of the wrist where a pulse can be felt.
the number of pulse beats counted in one minute.
the pattern and regularity of repeated heartbeats.
examination by feeling a body area with the hands or fingers.
an initial or usual measurement used for later comparison.
examination inside the body using an instrument with a light and camera.
a lighted instrument used to view the inside of the body.
the connected organs through which food passes during digestion.
removal of a small tissue sample for examination.
use of medicine to reduce alertness and help a patient relax during a procedure.
voluntary agreement after the relevant information has been understood.

grammar.title: Sequencing an explanation and asking permission
notes: • Use first, next, and finally to order an explanation. Use before or after + -ing when the same person performs both actions.
• Use May I …? to ask permission and Could you …? to make a polite request. A question is followed by listening to the answer.
• Use may or can for possible actions during a procedure. Do not turn a possible biopsy or sedation into a certainty.

formula.label: Permission
formula.text: “May I check your pulse at your wrist?” — Ask before beginning.

formula.label: Sequence
formula.text: “After explaining the observation, check that the patient agrees.” — after + -ing form

formula.label: Possibility
formula.text: “The clinician may take a small tissue sample.” — may + base verb, not a promise.

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: May I __________ your pulse? (check / checking)
2. Complete: Before __________, explain what you will do. (starting / start)
3. Complete: The clinician may __________ a biopsy. (take / takes)
4. Rewrite politely: “Show me your preparation instructions.” Begin “Could you …”.

reading.title: Reading: Two Explanations before a Procedure
body: Pulse assessment and endoscopy provide different information. A pulse can be felt at the wrist and counted to describe its rate. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy uses a lighted camera to examine the oesophagus, stomach, and duodenum; a clinician may also collect a biopsy (MedlinePlus, 2025; NIDDK, n.d.).

In this fictional case, Mr Aziz arrives for an endoscopy appointment. The nurse explains a routine pulse observation and asks permission. She describes placing two fingertips gently at the wrist and counting for a full minute. The simulated finding is 76 beats per minute with a regular rhythm. She records the finding without treating one measurement as a diagnosis.

Mr Aziz asks whether he should stop a medicine. The nurse checks his written instructions and refers the question to the responsible clinician rather than guessing. She explains that preparation depends on the planned procedure and individual needs. Before finishing, she asks him to describe which instruction needs clarification. The conversation supports understanding; it does not replace the formal consent discussion.
questions: 1. What does upper gastrointestinal endoscopy examine?
2. What does the nurse do before the pulse observation?
3. What rate and rhythm are recorded in the simulated case?
4. How does the nurse respond to the medicine question?
5. How does she check Mr Aziz’s understanding?

listening.title: Listening: Checking What the Patient Has Understood
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The nurse asks to check the pulse at the __________.
2. The count lasts one full __________.
3. The simulated pulse rate is __________ beats per minute.
4. The appointment is in the __________ unit.
5. The nurse will check the question with the responsible __________.
script: Nurse: Good morning, Mr Aziz. May I check your pulse at your wrist before we discuss your appointment?
Patient: Yes. Will you explain what you are doing?
Nurse: Certainly. I will place two fingertips gently at your wrist and count for one full minute. This is a routine observation.
Patient: Thank you. What is the result?
Nurse: The rate is 76 beats per minute, with a regular rhythm. I will record both findings.
Patient: My appointment is in the endoscopy unit. I have brought the preparation instructions, but I am unsure about one medicine.
Nurse: Let us check the written instructions. I will confirm that question with the responsible clinician; I will not guess.
Patient: So I should show you the instructions and explain which medicine I am asking about.
Nurse: Yes. That will help us clarify the information you need.

speaking.outcome: Agree on a three-step explanation: permission, a factual pulse report, and a clarification request. Use three glossary terms and two sequence markers.
speaking.roleA: You are a nurse in a simulated endoscopy unit. Ask permission to explain a pulse observation. Your training record says 80 beats per minute, regular rhythm. Describe the finding, ask for the preparation leaflet, and identify one question for the clinician. Do not change medicines or invent fasting instructions.
speaking.roleB: You are a patient attending an endoscopy appointment. You agree to a routine pulse observation but want a clear explanation. Your leaflet is available, yet you are unsure about a medicine instruction. Ask what endoscopy means and how your question will be clarified.
prompts: Agree on a three-step explanation: permission, a factual pulse report, and a clarification request. Use three glossary terms and two sequence markers.
Change roles. For an information-gap task, cover your partner’s card while exchanging information. In feedback, name one effective phrase and one phrase to improve.

culture.title: The history and development of traditional medicine
notes: In groups of four, prepare a brief response during the speaking stage. Choose a spokesperson and keep the exchange within the two minutes allocated.

Use the syllabus label as a historical enquiry. Prepare one question about how observations were described in the past and one about how evidence is checked today. The syllabus supplies no historical passage, so do not invent dates, discoveries, or treatment claims.
Useful language: “The syllabus names …”; “An individual may prefer …”; “Could you tell me …?”; “A cultural belief and evidence of a treatment effect are different questions.”

homework: Write 100–120 words describing a fictional pre-endoscopy conversation. Include five glossary terms, a permission question, two sequence markers, a simulated pulse finding, and one question referred for clarification. Do not invent preparation or medicine instructions.
Check your work: clear meaning; accurate vocabulary; required language structures; no unsupported medical claims.

practice a: 1. check 2. starting 3. take 4. Could you show me your preparation instructions? 5. After explaining the observation, ask whether the patient agrees.
reading: 1. The oesophagus, stomach, and duodenum. 2. She explains the observation and asks permission. 3. 76 beats per minute; a regular rhythm. 4. She checks the written instructions and refers the question to the responsible clinician. 5. She asks him to describe which instruction needs clarification.
mini-quiz: 1. radial artery 2. explain 3. B 4. biopsy 5. The responsible clinician or appropriate qualified professional. 6. For example: Could you explain which instruction you need us to clarify?

vocabulary.definition: pain that persists or recurs for longer than three months.
the severity of pain as experienced and described by the person.
the body area in which a person experiences pain.
the time or manner in which a symptom begins.
a temporary increase in symptoms compared with the person’s usual state.
pain caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system.
pain triggered when receptors respond to actual or threatened damage in tissues other than nerves.
the effect of pain on activities, sleep, mood, or relationships.
planning manageable activity and rest to support consistent participation.
a specific daily activity a person hopes to improve or regain.
a record of pain, relevant activities, and changes over time.
actions a person takes, with suitable support, to manage a long-term condition.

grammar.title: Describing duration and a symptom timeline
notes: • Use present perfect for an experience continuing to now: “I have had pain for six months.”
• Use for + a duration and since + a starting point. Ask “How long have you …?” to establish duration.
• Use past simple for a finished event: “The pain interrupted my sleep last night.” Do not change a patient report into an observed fact.

formula.label: Continuing experience
formula.text: “She has had knee pain for six months.” — has + past participle; for + duration.

formula.label: Starting point
formula.text: “He has kept a diary since Monday.” — since + a starting point.

formula.label: Finished event
formula.text: “She missed the meeting yesterday.” — Past simple with a finished time.

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: She __________ had pain for four months. (has / have)
2. Complete: He has used a diary __________ Monday. (since / for)
3. Complete: I have noticed this change __________ two weeks. (for / since)
4. Complete: The patient __________ the appointment yesterday. (attended / has attended)

reading.title: Reading: Listening beyond a Pain Score
body: Chronic pain lasts longer than three months and can affect daily activities, sleep, and emotional wellbeing. A conversation about pain therefore needs more than a single score. Support can include manageable activity, pacing, and attention to the person’s goals (NHS inform, 2026a, 2026b).

In this fictional case, Leila reports knee pain for six months. It usually feels like an ache, but standing while preparing meals is difficult. She has kept a pain diary since Monday. Yesterday, she stopped cooking halfway through a meal. The nurse records Leila’s description rather than calling her unwilling to work. She asks what a successful day would look like.

Leila would like to prepare a simple lunch with fewer interruptions. The nurse summarises this functional goal and asks which activities and rest periods are already manageable. They agree to bring the diary to a clinical review. The nurse does not promise that pacing will remove the pain or assume that its duration proves a particular cause. Leila confirms that the summary reflects her experience.
questions: 1. How long has Leila had knee pain?
2. Which activity is difficult for her?
3. When did she begin keeping a pain diary?
4. What functional goal does she identify?
5. Which two assumptions does the nurse avoid?

listening.title: Listening: A Pain-history Interview
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The patient has had shoulder pain for __________ months.
2. He has kept a diary since __________.
3. The pain interrupted his __________ last night.
4. His functional goal is to get __________ with less help.
5. He will bring his diary to the clinical __________.
script: Nurse: How long have you had the shoulder pain, Mr Karim?
Patient: I have had it for five months. I have kept a diary since Tuesday.
Nurse: How has the pain affected you recently?
Patient: It interrupted my sleep last night. Getting dressed is also difficult.
Nurse: Which activity would you most like to make more manageable?
Patient: I would like to get dressed with less help. I do not expect everything to change immediately.
Nurse: I will record that functional goal. Please bring your diary to the clinical review so the team can discuss the pattern with you.
Patient: So the diary is a way to explain what happens, not proof of a particular diagnosis.
Nurse: Exactly. Your description, the assessment, and the review all matter.

speaking.outcome: Produce a four-sentence summary including duration, a timed event, pain interference, and one functional goal. Use three glossary terms and ask the patient to confirm the meaning.
speaking.roleA: You are a nurse interviewing a patient about long-standing pain. Establish location, duration, a recent difficult activity, and a functional goal. Summarise the patient’s report using present perfect and a past-simple example. Ask the patient to check your summary.
speaking.roleB: Your fictional facts: lower-back pain for eight months; a diary since Friday; yesterday you stopped gardening after ten minutes. Your goal is to spend a manageable amount of time in the garden. You want your report taken seriously without receiving a promise of a cure.
prompts: Produce a four-sentence summary including duration, a timed event, pain interference, and one functional goal. Use three glossary terms and ask the patient to confirm the meaning.
Change roles. For an information-gap task, cover your partner’s card while exchanging information. In feedback, name one effective phrase and one phrase to improve.

culture.title: Traditional European medicine
notes: In groups of four, prepare a brief response during the speaking stage. Choose a spokesperson and keep the exchange within the two minutes allocated.

For “Traditional European medicine”, practise asking about an individual’s past experiences of pain care. Do not assume that all European communities share one practice. Agree on a respectful question and explain why a patient’s experience is different from evidence that a treatment works.
Useful language: “The syllabus names …”; “An individual may prefer …”; “Could you tell me …?”; “A cultural belief and evidence of a treatment effect are different questions.”

homework: Write a 100–120-word fictional pain-history summary. Use five glossary terms, present perfect with since and for, one past-simple event, and one functional goal. Distinguish what the patient reports from what has been observed.
Check your work: clear meaning; accurate vocabulary; required language structures; no unsupported medical claims.

lessons.title: Chronic pain. Nutrition and obesity
objectives: Explain twelve terms used in nutrition and weight-related discussions.

vocabulary.definition: the intake and use of food substances needed for health and body function.
a complex chronic disease involving excess body fat that can impair health.
a screening measure calculated from weight in relation to height squared.
a substance in food that the body needs for growth, repair, or function.
plant-food components that are not fully digested in the small intestine.
a nutrient used to build and maintain tissues and many body molecules.
the amount of energy obtained from food and drink.
the amount of a food served or eaten at one time.
the feeling of fullness after eating.
a harmful lack, excess, or imbalance of energy or nutrients.
a qualified professional who assesses and supports nutritional needs.
care planned around an individual’s needs, values, and preferences.

grammar.title: Quantities and non-judgemental questions
notes: • Use many or fewer with countable plurals: meals, snacks, and portions. Use much or less with uncountable nouns: sugar, fibre, and time.
• Use a lot of with either type: a lot of vegetables; a lot of information. Information and advice do not normally take a plural -s.
• Ask permission before sensitive discussion: “Would you be comfortable talking about …?” Describe a reported habit rather than label the person.

formula.label: Countable noun
formula.text: “How many meals did you prepare yesterday?” — many + countable plural

formula.label: Uncountable noun
formula.text: “How much time can you comfortably spend cooking?” — much + uncountable noun

formula.label: Comparison
formula.text: “She reports fewer snacks and less added sugar.” — fewer + plural; less + uncountable

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: How __________ meals do you prepare at home? (much / many)
2. Complete: The patient has __________ time for shopping. (less / fewer)
3. Complete: She reports __________ sugary drinks this week. (less / fewer)
4. Complete: How __________ fibre is listed on the label? (much / many)

reading.title: Reading: A Meal Plan That Fits Real Life
body: Obesity has biological, behavioural, environmental, and social influences; it should not be reduced to willpower. A healthy diet depends on variety, suitable amounts, and individual circumstances. Nutritional needs cannot be understood from appearance alone (WHO, 2025, 2026).

In this fictional case, Nadia lives with chronic pain and wants help with meal preparation. The nurse asks permission to discuss her routine. Nadia explains that carrying shopping bags and standing at the cooker are difficult. She sometimes misses lunch because preparing food takes too much effort. Her main concern is a manageable routine, not a demand for a rapid change in body weight.

The nurse asks how many meals Nadia usually prepares and how much help is available. Together they identify a question for the dietitian about convenient, balanced options. They do not set a calorie target or promise that a particular food will cure pain. Nadia agrees to bring a short record of meals and practical difficulties to the review. The record will support an individual discussion, not a judgement about her character.
questions: 1. Why should obesity not be reduced to willpower?
2. Which two physical tasks are difficult for Nadia?
3. Why does she sometimes miss lunch?
4. What question will be discussed with the dietitian?
5. Which two things do the nurse and Nadia avoid setting or promising?

listening.title: Listening: Preparing for a Nutrition Review
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The patient finds carrying shopping __________ difficult.
2. Standing while __________ also increases the difficulty.
3. The nurse asks how __________ meals the patient prepares.
4. The patient will bring a record covering __________ days.
5. They will discuss the record with a __________.
script: Nurse: Would you be comfortable discussing how meals fit into your day?
Patient: Yes. My pain makes carrying shopping bags difficult. Standing while cooking is also hard.
Nurse: How many meals do you usually prepare yourself?
Patient: Usually one main meal. I have less time and energy for preparation than before.
Nurse: What would you most like help with?
Patient: Convenient meals that suit my needs. I do not want a strict plan that I cannot manage.
Nurse: Please bring a record covering three days to the nutrition review. We can discuss your questions with a dietitian.
Patient: I will write down the meals and the practical difficulties, not just the amount I eat.
Nurse: That information will help explain your circumstances and priorities.

speaking.outcome: Record one practical barrier, one available source of support, and one agreed nutrition question. Use three glossary terms and both quantity question forms.
speaking.roleA: You are a nurse. Ask permission to discuss meals, then ask about meal frequency, cooking time, and available support. Use how many and how much. Agree on one question for the dietitian. Do not assume the patient’s weight or prescribe a restrictive diet.
speaking.roleB: Your fictional facts: pain makes standing difficult; you cook one main meal daily; a relative can help with shopping; you want convenient meals and clear information. Ask whether a single food can cure pain, and check that the nurse avoids making that promise.
prompts: Record one practical barrier, one available source of support, and one agreed nutrition question. Use three glossary terms and both quantity question forms.
Change roles. For an information-gap task, cover your partner’s card while exchanging information. In feedback, name one effective phrase and one phrase to improve.

culture.title: Traditional medicine
notes: In groups of four, prepare a brief response during the speaking stage. Choose a spokesperson and keep the exchange within the two minutes allocated.

For “Traditional medicine”, ask how a patient’s food traditions and preferences could be included in a conversation. Do not classify a whole culture’s diet as healthy or unhealthy. Practise a question that combines respect for preferences with discussion of individual nutritional needs.
Useful language: “The syllabus names …”; “An individual may prefer …”; “Could you tell me …?”; “A cultural belief and evidence of a treatment effect are different questions.”

homework: Write 100–120 words about a fictional nutrition conversation with a person living with chronic pain. Include five glossary terms, how much, how many, less, and fewer. Identify a practical barrier and a question for the dietitian without giving a calorie target or promising pain relief.
Check your work: clear meaning; accurate vocabulary; required language structures; no unsupported medical claims.

vocabulary.definition: a serious infection caused by the bacterium Salmonella Typhi.
the bacterial serotype that causes typhoid fever.
having no noticeable symptoms of a condition.
a person who harbours an infectious agent and may transmit it without symptoms.
the spread of an infectious agent from a source to another person.
spread when organisms from faeces are swallowed, often in contaminated food or water.
the presence of unwanted microorganisms or other harmful material.
more cases of a disease than expected in a place and period.
a systematic enquiry into disease patterns, sources, and spread.
a sample of faeces collected for laboratory examination.

grammar.title: Reporting events without adding blame
notes: • Use past simple for a completed historical event: “The investigator examined the records.”
• Use past passive when the event or evidence is the focus: “The samples were examined.” Keep the agent when it is important and known.
• Distinguish sourced facts from classroom interpretations. Words such as therefore do not justify a conclusion that the evidence does not support.

formula.label: Past simple
formula.text: “Mary Mallon worked as a cook.” — A completed historical statement.

formula.label: Past passive
formula.text: “The laboratory samples were examined.” — were + past participle

formula.label: Attribution
formula.text: “The student said that the two cases were different.” — A classroom statement, not a historical fact.

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: Mary Mallon __________ as a cook. (worked / has worked)
2. Complete: The samples __________ examined. (was / were)
3. Complete: The investigator __________ the records. (reviewed / has review)
4. Change to passive: “The laboratory examined the specimen.”

reading.title: Reading: Symptoms, Evidence, and a Historical Name
body: Chronic pain and asymptomatic infection carriage raise different questions. Pain is an experience a patient reports. A carrier may harbour an infectious agent without noticeable symptoms. The two syllabus topics are studied together here to practise avoiding assumptions based on appearance, not to suggest that one causes the other.

Mary Mallon, remembered by the historical label “Typhoid Mary”, worked as a cook in New York. Public-health investigations linked typhoid cases to her, and laboratory testing identified her as a carrier of Salmonella Typhi. The National Museum of Health and Medicine discusses her case as a complex history of infection, evidence, and public response (NMHM, 2020). Typhoid can spread through food or water contaminated with the bacteria (CDC, 2024).

In a fictional seminar, students compare two poor conclusions: “No visible injury means no pain” and “No symptoms means no infection.” They replace each with a question about the information needed. Their final summary separates the historical account from their discussion. They use Mary Mallon’s name and neutral clinical terms rather than turn her nickname into an insult.
questions: 1. Why are the two syllabus topics discussed together?
2. What work did Mary Mallon do?
3. What did laboratory testing identify?
4. Which route of spread is mentioned?
5. Which two unsupported conclusions do the students challenge?

listening.title: Listening: A Seminar on Careful Conclusions
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The two topics are different __________.
2. Mary Mallon worked as a __________.
3. Her carrier status was investigated using laboratory __________.
4. The first fictional patient reports pain for __________ months.
5. The group should avoid a __________ nickname in its summary.
script: Tutor: Why have we placed these two topics in today’s discussion?
Student: They are different conditions, but both remind us not to judge only by appearance. We are not claiming that chronic pain causes typhoid.
Tutor: Which historical facts will you include?
Student: Mary Mallon worked as a cook. Her carrier status was investigated using laboratory testing. We will distinguish that history from our fictional examples.
Tutor: What does the first fictional patient report?
Student: Pain for seven months. We should ask about that experience rather than dismiss it because no injury is visible.
Tutor: And what does asymptomatic mean in the infection discussion?
Student: Having no noticeable symptoms. It does not establish that there is no infection.
Tutor: Good. Use neutral language and avoid a blaming nickname in your summary.

speaking.outcome: Create two separate two-sentence summaries: one patient report and one historical account. Use three glossary terms, one past-simple sentence, and one past passive. Add no causal link between the cases.
speaking.roleA: You are a nursing student with Card A: a fictional person reports pain for four months; the cause has not been established. Explain why appearance alone is insufficient. Ask your partner for the historical facts on Card B and keep the cases separate.
speaking.roleB: You are a nursing student with Card B: Mary Mallon worked as a cook; an investigation linked typhoid cases to her; testing identified carrier status. Share the facts in neutral language. Ask how this differs from the pain case and challenge any implied causal link.
prompts: Create two separate two-sentence summaries: one patient report and one historical account. Use three glossary terms, one past-simple sentence, and one past passive. Add no causal link between the cases.
Change roles. For an information-gap task, cover your partner’s card while exchanging information. In feedback, name one effective phrase and one phrase to improve.

culture.title: Traditional medicine
notes: In groups of four, prepare a brief response during the speaking stage. Choose a spokesperson and keep the exchange within the two minutes allocated.

For “Traditional medicine”, discuss how an unfamiliar health explanation could be explored without ridicule. Ask for the source of a claim and distinguish a historical belief from present evidence. Do not invent a traditional treatment for typhoid or recommend one.
Useful language: “The syllabus names …”; “An individual may prefer …”; “Could you tell me …?”; “A cultural belief and evidence of a treatment effect are different questions.”

homework: Write 100–120 words comparing how evidence is described in a fictional chronic-pain conversation and the historical Mary Mallon case. Use five glossary terms, two past-simple verbs, and two past passives. Keep the cases separate and cite the historical source named in the reading.
Check your work: clear meaning; accurate vocabulary; required language structures; no unsupported medical claims.

vocabulary.definition: maintaining abilities and supportive conditions that enable wellbeing in later life.
the length or long duration of a person’s life.
the average years of life expected in a population under specified mortality conditions.
a person’s experience of wellbeing and satisfaction in their circumstances.
the capacity, supported by the environment, to do things a person values.
care intended to prevent illness or detect health problems early.

relationships and contact that link a person with others.

grammar.title: Discussing possible benefits and patient-chosen goals
notes: • Use may or can + a base verb to describe a possible benefit, not a guarantee: “An adapted routine may support participation.”
• Use could to offer an option and to + a base verb to explain its purpose: “We could arrange a review to discuss your goal.”
• Ask an open question before offering an option. A person’s age alone does not tell you which activities or changes are suitable.

formula.label: Possible benefit
formula.text: “A supportive environment may improve participation.” — may + base verb

formula.label: Option
formula.text: “We could discuss ways to make the visit manageable.” — An offer, not a command.

formula.label: Purpose
formula.text: “The review is arranged to discuss your priorities.” — to + base verb

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: A realistic routine may __________ participation. (support / supports)
2. Complete: We could __________ your priorities together. (review / reviewed)
3. Complete: The meeting is arranged __________ discuss your goal. (to / for)
4. Rewrite carefully: “This habit guarantees a longer life.” Use may.

reading.title: Reading: More Than a Number of Years
body: Healthy ageing is not defined only by the absence of disease. The World Health Organization emphasises the ability to do what a person values and the environments that support that ability. Relationships, mobility, and participation can matter alongside the management of health conditions (WHO, 2020).

In this fictional review, Mr Rahim is 68 and wants to attend a weekly reading group. The nurse does not assume that every person of his age needs the same plan. She asks what makes attendance difficult. He explains that transport and tiredness are the main barriers. He would like to discuss a manageable routine and the support available locally.

The nurse summarises his priority and arranges a discussion with the appropriate team member. They will review the transport options and his concern about tiredness. He chooses one next step: ask his neighbour about travelling together. No one promises that this will extend his life. The plan is judged by whether it addresses his own goal and can be maintained, not by a slogan about a perfect lifestyle.
questions: 1. Does healthy ageing require complete freedom from disease?
2. What does Mr Rahim want to attend?
3. Which two barriers does he describe?
4. What next step does he choose?
5. How should the plan be judged in the final paragraph?

listening.title: Listening: Choosing One Realistic Step
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The patient wants to attend a weekly __________ group.
2. The two barriers are transport and __________.
3. The patient will ask a __________ about travelling together.
4. The team will discuss the concern at a __________.
5. The nurse says the plan does not guarantee a __________ life.
script: Nurse: Which activity would you most like to make easier, Mr Rahim?
Patient: Attending the weekly reading group. Transport and tiredness have made it difficult.
Nurse: We could review those barriers rather than give you a long list of changes. What support is available?
Patient: My neighbour attends the group. I could ask whether we can travel together.
Nurse: That is a step you have chosen. We can also discuss your tiredness at a review with the team.
Patient: Does this mean that joining the group will make me live longer?
Nurse: No plan guarantees a longer life. The aim here is to support a meaningful activity and understand your concerns.
Patient: I will ask my neighbour about transport and bring my questions to the review.
Nurse: That matches your priorities. We can check later whether the arrangement is manageable.

speaking.outcome: Agree on one meaningful goal, one practical barrier, and one patient-chosen next step. Use three glossary terms, could, and one purpose sentence.
speaking.roleA: You are a nurse. Ask what a fictional older adult values, what makes participation difficult, and what support is available. Offer two options with could, explain their purpose, and let the patient choose one step. Do not prescribe a standard plan based only on age.
speaking.roleB: You are 70 and would like to visit a friend regularly. Transport is difficult, but a relative may be able to help. You want one manageable step, not a list of “secrets”. Ask whether the suggested action guarantees a longer life and listen for a careful answer.
prompts: Agree on one meaningful goal, one practical barrier, and one patient-chosen next step. Use three glossary terms, could, and one purpose sentence.
Change roles. For an information-gap task, cover your partner’s card while exchanging information. In feedback, name one effective phrase and one phrase to improve.

vocabulary.definition: a long duration of life.
the average years of life expected in a population under specified mortality conditions.
care intended to prevent illness or detect health problems early.
a varied pattern of eating that provides suitable amounts of energy and nutrients.
the body’s state of having the fluid needed for normal function.
body movement that uses energy.
the force of circulating blood against artery walls.

a traditional medical system named here as a cultural study topic.

grammar.title: Comparatives, superlatives, and careful advice
notes: • Use a comparative with than and a superlative with the: easier than; more balanced than; one of the most manageable options.
• Use parallel comparatives to relate changes: “The more regular the routine is, the easier it may be to follow.” A grammatical pattern does not establish a medical law.
• Use because for a reason and therefore or as a result for a consequence. Retain may, can, or could when a benefit is possible rather than guaranteed.

formula.label: Comparative
formula.text: “A manageable routine may be easier to maintain than an extreme plan.” — Comparison with than.

formula.label: Superlative
formula.text: “This may be one of the most useful changes for this patient.” — one of the + superlative + plural noun

formula.label: Parallel comparative
formula.text: “The clearer the explanation is, the easier it may be to follow.” — the + comparative in both clauses

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: A balanced diet is usually __________ than an extreme diet. (safe)
2. Complete: The __________ the routine is, the easier it may be to follow. (regular)
3. Complete: Preventive care can help clinicians find some problems __________. (early)
4. Complete: For this patient, the agreed option is one of the __________ changes. (manageable)

reading.title: Reading: Advice That Sounds Professional
body: A healthcare worker should explain lifestyle options clearly and carefully. Healthy-ageing guidance discusses activity, eating patterns, sleep, and other aspects of wellbeing; it does not offer a guarantee that one habit prevents every disease (NIA, 2022). In this language lesson, the examples are fictional and must be adapted to the person’s needs.

Comparatives show realistic choices: “A routine you can maintain may be easier than an extreme plan.” Superlatives can help discuss priorities: “The most useful first step is the one we have agreed is manageable for you.” A parallel comparative can improve clarity: “The clearer the explanation is, the easier it may be to follow.” These structures compare options; they do not prove a health outcome.

Because the patient reports tiredness, the nurse offers to discuss the sleep routine at a review. The patient asks for one explanation at a time; therefore, the nurse pauses and checks understanding. In the culture project, Traditional Unani medicine remains a study topic rather than a treatment recommendation. Pupils practise respectful questions about beliefs without presenting traditional methods as a replacement for appropriate care.
questions: 1. Find one comparative structure in the text.
2. Find one superlative structure in the text.
3. Why is “This habit prevents every disease” an unsuitable claim?
4. What is the purpose of the culture project?
5. Rewrite carefully: “This diet is the only way to live longer.”

listening.title: Listening: Wellness Appointment
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. A routine you can continue is often __________ than a difficult plan.
2. The more manageable the routine is, the __________ it may be to follow.
3. Preventive care can help identify some problems __________.
4. For this patient, the __________ important first step is discussing sleep.
5. We will discuss one point at a time; __________, there is no need to remember a long list today.
script: Nurse: Good morning, Mr Hasanov. We are not looking for one magic secret. We are comparing small steps that are realistic for you.
Patient: I would prefer one manageable change, not a difficult plan.
Nurse: A routine you can continue is often better than a difficult plan. The more manageable the routine is, the easier it may be to follow.
Patient: What about preventive care?
Nurse: Preventive care can help identify some problems earlier. What would you like us to discuss first?
Patient: My sleep. Tiredness makes other activities harder.
Nurse: For you, the most important first step is discussing sleep at your review. We will not promise that one change solves every problem.
Patient: Please give me time to understand each point.
Nurse: Certainly. We will discuss one point at a time; therefore, there is no need to remember a long list today. Could you repeat the agreed next step in your own words?

speaking.outcome: Compare two options and agree on one next discussion or review. Use three glossary terms, two comparatives, one superlative, and a check of understanding.
speaking.roleA: You are a nurse comparing options for a fictional older adult. Ask about sleep, meals, hydration, activity, and preventive care without prescribing a standard target. Compare two manageable choices, invite the patient’s preference, and use teach-back.
speaking.roleB: You are 62. You feel tired and want a simple routine that fits your circumstances. Choose one concern to discuss first and ask questions when a plan sounds difficult. Ask for a comparison rather than a guarantee of a longer life.

vocabulary.definition: a long duration of life.
a plant used or investigated for possible therapeutic effects.
using a substance or behaviour to address illness without professional supervision.
the process through which damaged tissue repairs itself.
a tissue response to injury or infection that may cause swelling and pain.
a substance that affects living cells or biological processes.
a proposed explanation that can be investigated.
research that records events without assigning a treatment.
the ability of an intervention to produce its intended effect under study conditions.
the capacity of a substance to cause harm.
a harmful, unintended response to a medicine or other substance.
a research study that evaluates an intervention in human participants.

grammar.title: Careful claims and contrasting evidence
notes: • Use may or might + a base verb for a possibility, not a proven result.
• Use however to contrast an interesting observation with a limitation.
• Use does not establish or cannot show to explain what evidence does not demonstrate.

formula.label: The plant cures wounds.
formula.text: The observation may justify further research. — Possibility, not a treatment promise.

formula.label: Natural means harmless.
formula.text: A natural substance may still cause harm. — Origin does not establish safety.

formula.label: One animal improved. It works in humans.
formula.text: One observation does not establish human efficacy. — Animal evidence is not a human trial.

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: This observation __________ suggest a useful research question. (may / must)
2. Complete: The wound improved; __________, the report involved only one animal. (however / because)
3. Complete: A single observation does not __________ human safety. (establish / establishes)
4. Rewrite carefully: “Every medicinal plant is safe.” Use may.

reading.title: Reading: An Observation Is Not a Prescription
body: In a published observational report, researchers described a wild Sumatran orangutan applying material from a plant to a facial wound. The wound later closed. The authors discussed self-medication as a possible explanation, rather than presenting a treatment recommendation for humans (Laumer et al., 2024).

In a fictional classroom research meeting, two nursing students examine the difference between observation and inference. “The animal applied plant material” reports an event. “The plant caused recovery” adds a causal claim that this observation alone cannot establish. There was no assigned comparison treatment, and other explanations remain possible.

The students propose a research question about the plant’s bioactive compounds. They also note that investigating human use would require appropriate safety and efficacy studies. Their patient-facing summary is careful: “This is an interesting finding, but it is not a reason to copy the behaviour or apply an unidentified plant to a wound.” The discussion connects curiosity about nature with professional responsibility, not with a promise of longevity.
questions: 1. What event did the researchers observe?
2. Which sentence in the second paragraph adds a causal claim?
3. Give one reason why the observation cannot establish human efficacy.
4. What research question do the students propose?
5. Write one careful sentence for a patient who wants to copy the animal’s behaviour.

listening.title: Listening: The Research Discussion
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The students call the finding an __________, not proof of a cure.
2. There was no assigned-treatment __________ group.
3. The first research concern mentioned is __________.
4. The student would ask for the remedy’s __________.
5. The final summary should contain __________ sentences.
script: Tutor: What is your group’s main finding?
Student: The report describes one animal applying plant material to a wound. We have written “observation”, not “proof of a cure”.
Tutor: Good. What limitation will you mention?
Student: There was no comparison group receiving an assigned treatment. We cannot tell patients that the plant is effective for them.
Tutor: What would you investigate next?
Student: We would first ask about the substance’s safety, including toxicity. We would also examine what evidence exists about efficacy.
Tutor: And what would you say to someone who already uses a plant remedy?
Student: I would ask for its name and tell the healthcare team, without judging the person.
Tutor: Your final summary should be three sentences long and include the word “may”.

speaking.outcome: Agree on a two-sentence explanation that separates an observation from a recommendation. Use three glossary terms and two cautious structures.
speaking.roleA: You are a nurse. A patient has read about animals using plants and asks whether the same approach can support a longer life. Ask what product or plant they mean. Explain the limits of the evidence and suggest a discussion with a qualified professional.
speaking.roleB: You are a patient. An online story impressed you, but you do not know the plant’s name or ingredients. You have not used it. Ask whether “natural” means safe and what you should check before considering it.
prompts: Agree on a two-sentence explanation that separates an observation from a recommendation. Use three glossary terms and two cautious structures.
Change roles. For an information-gap task, cover your partner’s card while exchanging information. In feedback, name one effective phrase and one phrase to improve.

culture.title: Traditional African medicine
notes: In groups of four, prepare a brief response during the speaking stage. Choose a spokesperson and keep the exchange within the two minutes allocated.

Discuss the syllabus label “Traditional African medicine” as a cultural enquiry, not one uniform set of practices. Prepare two respectful questions about a person’s own remedy use and one question about evidence. Do not attribute a practice to everyone in a country or region.
Useful language: “The syllabus names …”; “An individual may prefer …”; “Could you tell me …?”; “A cultural belief and evidence of a treatment effect are different questions.”

homework: Write 100–120 words: “Why an interesting treatment claim needs careful evidence.” Use five glossary terms, may or might, and however. Separate the reported animal observation from your own interpretation.
Check your work: clear meaning; accurate vocabulary; required language structures; no unsupported medical claims.

vocabulary.definition: a mental health condition that can affect perception, thinking, and daily functioning.
a state in which a person has difficulty distinguishing some experiences from external reality.
medicine used to reduce psychotic symptoms.
structured psychological treatment through work with a trained professional.
a therapy that explores links between thoughts, feelings, and behaviour.
clear information that helps people understand a condition and its care.
planned work with a person and their family to improve understanding and support.
help addressing psychological and social needs.
support for regaining or developing skills for daily life.
a collaborative, trusting relationship between a patient and clinician.
a process in which the patient and clinician consider options together.
a personal process of improving wellbeing and meaningful daily functioning.

grammar.title: Explaining purpose without promising a cure
notes: • Use to + a base verb to explain purpose: “The meeting is arranged to discuss your goals.”
• Use can help or may support for possible benefits, not guaranteed outcomes.
• Use an open question before advice: “What would you most like help with?”

formula.label: Purpose
formula.text: Psychoeducation is offered to improve understanding. — to + base verb

formula.label: Possible benefit
formula.text: Family work may support communication. — may + base verb

formula.label: Shared decision
formula.text: Which option would you like to discuss first? — An open, non-directive question

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: The session is arranged __________ discuss your concerns. (to / for)
2. Complete: Psychological support may __________ daily coping. (improve / improves)
3. Complete: Rehabilitation can help people __________ everyday skills. (develop / developing)
4. Rewrite: “This therapy will solve every problem.” Use may.

reading.title: Reading: A Care Plan Built around a Person
body: Care for schizophrenia can include antipsychotic medication, psychological treatment, and practical or family support. Different interventions have different purposes, and the person’s goals matter when options are discussed (NIMH, n.d.; NHS, n.d.).

In this fictional case, Samir wants to return to a training course. He tells the nurse that morning tiredness is making attendance difficult. Rather than describing him as unmotivated, the nurse asks when the tiredness occurs and arranges a discussion with the prescribing clinician. She does not change the medication herself.

Samir also wants help explaining his difficulties to his sister. With his agreement, the team offers a family meeting. The nurse explains that psychoeducation can help people understand the condition and available support. A rehabilitation worker will discuss a manageable study routine with him.

The plan records Samir’s priority, the support offered, and the next review. It does not promise that one intervention will remove every difficulty. At the end, the nurse asks Samir to explain the agreed next steps in his own words.
questions: 1. What is Samir’s main goal?
2. Why does the nurse ask about morning tiredness?
3. Who will discuss the medication concern with him?
4. What must happen before involving his sister?
5. How does the nurse check understanding at the end?

listening.title: Listening: Choosing the Next Step
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The patient’s priority is his college __________.
2. The nurse suggests a meeting with the __________ worker.
3. The patient asks for __________ option at a time.
4. The review is on __________.
5. The family member he would like to attend is his __________.
script: Nurse: Which concern would you like us to discuss first, Daniel?
Patient: I want to manage my college routine. I understand the medicine is only one part of the plan.
Nurse: We can arrange a meeting with the rehabilitation worker to discuss practical study skills. Would you also like information about psychological support?
Patient: Yes, but please explain one option at a time.
Nurse: Certainly. We can discuss it at your review on Thursday. Would you like a family member to attend?
Patient: My sister, if that is possible.
Nurse: I will record your agreement and ask the team to invite her. What will happen next?
Patient: We will discuss study skills and review the options on Thursday.
Nurse: That matches the plan we have agreed.

speaking.outcome: Agree on one patient priority and two questions for the next review. Use three glossary terms and two purpose structures.
speaking.roleA: You are a nurse explaining support options. Ask about one daily-life goal. Describe two possible forms of support, check whether the person wants family involvement, and explain that medicine concerns need a review with the prescribing clinician.
speaking.roleB: You are a patient who hopes to resume college. You want practical support but feel overwhelmed by too much information. Ask for one explanation at a time and decide whether a relative should join the next meeting.
prompts: Agree on one patient priority and two questions for the next review. Use three glossary terms and two purpose structures.
Change roles. For an information-gap task, cover your partner’s card while exchanging information. In feedback, name one effective phrase and one phrase to improve.

culture.title: Traditional Asian medicine
notes: In groups of four, prepare a brief response during the speaking stage. Choose a spokesperson and keep the exchange within the two minutes allocated.

Use “Traditional Asian medicine” as the syllabus’s cultural discussion label. Practise asking about an individual’s beliefs without assuming that all Asian communities use the same approaches. Add one sentence explaining that cultural respect does not replace discussion of treatment evidence and safety.
Useful language: “The syllabus names …”; “An individual may prefer …”; “Could you tell me …?”; “A cultural belief and evidence of a treatment effect are different questions.”

homework: Write 100–120 words describing a fictional care-planning conversation. Include one patient goal, two support options, five glossary terms, and three expressions of purpose or possible benefit. Do not promise a cure.
Check your work: clear meaning; accurate vocabulary; required language structures; no unsupported medical claims.

vocabulary.definition: a sensory experience, such as hearing a voice, without a corresponding external stimulus.
a strongly held false belief that persists despite contrary evidence and is not explained by cultural context.
the usual or initial state used for comparison.
a structured assessment of current appearance, behaviour, thought, perception, and mood.
a person’s awareness and understanding of their condition or difficulties.
the usual timing, duration, and quality of sleep.
a change in symptoms or functioning after an intervention.
an unwanted harmful effect associated with treatment.
a fall in blood pressure on standing that may cause dizziness.
checks of measures such as weight, blood glucose, and blood lipids.
a worsening of health or functioning.

grammar.title: Changes, observations, and patient reports
notes: • Use present perfect for a change linked to now: “Sleep has become shorter.”
• Use past simple with a finished time: “He reported dizziness at 08:00.”
• Attribute information: “The patient reports …” is different from “I observed …”. Do not replace either with an unsupported diagnosis.

formula.label: Current change
formula.text: Her sleep has become more disturbed. — Present perfect

formula.label: Finished event
formula.text: She attended the review yesterday. — Past simple with a finished time

formula.label: Attributed report
formula.text: She reports feeling dizzy when standing. — A report, not a confirmed cause

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: His sleep __________ changed during the past week. (has / have)
2. Complete: The nurse __________ the concern at 09:00 yesterday. (recorded / has recorded)
3. Complete: The patient has felt more tired __________ Monday. (since / for)
4. Rewrite neutrally: “He is lazy.” Fact: he declined a planned walk at 10:00.

reading.title: Reading: A Change from the Baseline
body: Monitoring should consider both mental and physical health. Treatment response, unwanted effects, and relevant physical measurements need review; a diagnosis of schizophrenia does not explain every new physical complaint (NICE, n.d.; NHS, n.d.).

In this fictional handover, the nurse compares today’s information with a documented baseline. Lina usually sleeps for about six hours. Today she reports sleeping for two hours and feeling dizzy when she stands. The nurse records Lina’s words and the time of the report. She does not write that Lina has definitely relapsed or that a medicine has certainly caused the dizziness.

The nurse asks about the onset of the symptoms and informs the responsible clinician according to the local escalation procedure. She also checks which scheduled monitoring results are already available. Her handover separates what Lina reports, what staff have observed, and what still needs assessment.

Lina is included in the discussion. The nurse explains why a review has been requested and asks whether she has any immediate concerns. Accurate reporting supports a clinical decision; it does not replace one.
questions: 1. Which two areas of health should monitoring consider?
2. What change in sleep does Lina report?
3. What physical symptom does she describe?
4. Name one conclusion the nurse should not state as certain.
5. What three kinds of information does the handover separate?

listening.title: Listening: A Brief Monitoring Handover
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. Lina is in room __________.
2. The report of dizziness was made at __________ o’clock.
3. She has slept poorly for __________ nights.
4. Her documented baseline is about __________ hours of sleep.
5. A clinical __________ has been requested.
script: Nurse A: I am handing over a concern about Lina in room four. At nine o’clock, she reported dizziness on standing. She says she has slept poorly for three nights.
Nurse B: What is her usual sleep pattern?
Nurse A: Her documented baseline is about six hours. She reports only two hours last night. I have recorded her words and the time.
Nurse B: Has the responsible clinician been informed?
Nurse A: Yes. A review has been requested. I have not assumed that the symptoms are caused by her medicine.
Nurse B: What information is still needed?
Nurse A: The clinician needs to assess the new symptoms. Please check which scheduled physical monitoring results are available and explain the plan to Lina.

speaking.outcome: Produce a four-sentence handover with baseline, change, attribution, and requested action. Use three glossary terms and two time expressions.
speaking.roleA: You are the outgoing nurse. Your card: patient Alex; usual sleep seven hours; reports three hours last night; reports feeling unusually tired since Monday; declined breakfast at 08:30. A review has been requested. Handover these facts without diagnosing the cause.
speaking.roleB: You are the incoming nurse. You need to know the patient’s baseline, the source of each statement, when the change began, and whether a review has been requested. Ask for missing details rather than accepting labels such as “difficult”.
prompts: Produce a four-sentence handover with baseline, change, attribution, and requested action. Use three glossary terms and two time expressions.
Change roles. For an information-gap task, cover your partner’s card while exchanging information. In feedback, name one effective phrase and one phrase to improve.

culture.title: Islamic medicine
notes: In groups of four, prepare a brief response during the speaking stage. Choose a spokesperson and keep the exchange within the two minutes allocated.

For the syllabus topic “Islamic medicine”, practise asking whether a patient has any personal beliefs or routines they would like the team to consider. Do not infer beliefs from a name or diagnosis. Discuss how to record a preference respectfully while continuing appropriate monitoring.
Useful language: “The syllabus names …”; “An individual may prefer …”; “Could you tell me …?”; “A cultural belief and evidence of a treatment effect are different questions.”

homework: Write a 100–120-word fictional monitoring note. Separate patient reports from observations. Use five glossary terms, present perfect for a current change, past simple for a timed event, and one clear review request.
Check your work: clear meaning; accurate vocabulary; required language structures; no unsupported medical claims.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language — 10 marks
notes: Complete or rewrite. Each item is worth 2 marks.
COURSE 2 | LESSON 10 | STUDENT ASSESSMENT PAPER
practice: 1. Complete: A manageable routine may be __________ than an extreme plan. (easy)
2. Complete: The patient __________ poor sleep at 09:00 yesterday. (reported / has reported)
3. Complete: This observation does not __________ human safety. (establish / establishes)
4. Rewrite carefully: “This habit prevents every illness.” Use may.
5. Write one purpose sentence using: meeting / arranged / discuss / patient’s goals.

reading.title: Reading — 10 marks
body: A Review with Two Different Concerns

This is a fictional assessment case. Amina attends a planned review for long-standing pain. She wants a more manageable daily routine and reports that tiredness makes it difficult to continue an exercise plan. The nurse asks what she can realistically maintain rather than promising that one activity will remove every symptom.

Amina also shows the nurse an online story about an animal using plant material on a wound. She asks whether this proves that a similar product would help her. The nurse explains that an animal observation is not a clinical trial establishing a safe human treatment. She asks for the exact product information and suggests discussing it with the appropriate professional.

Amina has not started the product. The agreed next step is to bring its packaging to her review. The nurse records Amina’s main goal and asks her to explain the plan in her own words. Amina says that she will bring the packaging and continue discussing a manageable routine with the team.
questions: 1. What is Amina’s main daily-life goal?
2. Which reported problem makes the activity plan difficult?
3. Why does the animal story not prove a safe human treatment?
4. Has Amina started the product, and what will she bring to the review?
5. How does the nurse check Amina’s understanding?

listening.title: Listening — 10 marks
directions: The Follow-up Arrangements
Listen twice and answer from the conversation. Each question is worth 2 marks.
questions: 1. On which day is the review?
2. At what time is the review?
3. For how many nights has the patient slept poorly?
4. What should the patient bring?
5. Which relative would the patient like to attend?
script: Nurse: Your follow-up meeting is on Thursday at ten o’clock. What is the first concern you would like to discuss?
Patient: My sleep. I have slept poorly for three nights.
Nurse: Thank you. I will record that. Please also bring the packaging for the product you asked about. Have you started using it?
Patient: No, I wanted to ask the team first.
Nurse: Would you like anyone to attend the meeting with you?
Patient: My sister, please.
Nurse: I will record your agreement to involve her. Could you explain the plan in your own words?
Patient: I will attend on Thursday at ten with my sister, bring the packaging, and discuss my sleep.
Nurse: That matches the arrangements.

Accept equivalent wording that preserves the meaning. For grammar items, award 2 for a correct structure and meaning, 1 for a minor error with the target structure recognisable, and 0 for an incorrect or missing response. Do not penalise an otherwise correct comprehension answer for minor spelling that does not change meaning.
Reading and listening: 2 marks for a complete correct response, 1 for a partly correct response, 0 for an incorrect or missing answer. For Reading 4, award 1 for “not started” and 1 for “packaging”.

vocabulary.definition: a feeling of apprehension or worry that can affect thoughts and the body.
a state of significant emotional discomfort or suffering.
the ability to direct and maintain attention.
mental processes involved in learning, remembering, and understanding.
speech whose connections or structure make it difficult to follow.
reduced motivation to begin or maintain purposeful activity.
reduced participation in social contact or activities.
a period when symptoms have decreased substantially or are absent.
the return or worsening of symptoms after improvement.
a method a person uses to manage a difficulty or stressful experience.
a later meeting to review progress, concerns, or treatment.

grammar.title: Reporting what was said
notes: • With a past reporting verb, a tense can shift back: “I feel anxious” becomes “She said that she felt anxious.” Backshift must not distort what is currently known.
• Reported questions use statement word order: “She asked when the appointment was.”
• Use said that or told + person + that. Keep may as might when reporting a past possibility; never turn it into certainty.

formula.label: “I feel anxious,” she said.
formula.text: She said that she felt anxious. — Statement; pronoun and tense shift.

formula.label: “When is the review?” he asked.
formula.text: He asked when the review was. — No question inversion.

formula.label: “I may need more support,” she said.
formula.text: She said that she might need more support. — Possibility is preserved.

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Report with a past reporting verb: “I feel tired,” Maya said.
2. Report: “I have missed one appointment,” Leo said.
3. Report the question: “When is my review?” Sara asked.
4. Choose: He __________ the nurse that he felt worried. (said / told)

reading.title: Reading: Keeping the Patient’s Meaning
body: A patient’s experience should not be reduced to a label. Schizophrenia can involve changes in perception, thought, motivation, and cognition, but a single sentence in a conversation does not establish a new diagnosis or a relapse (NIMH, n.d.).

In this fictional language exercise, Noah tells the nurse, “I feel worried about returning to class.” The nurse records that he said he felt worried about returning to class. She does not replace this with “He cannot cope with education”, because Noah did not say that.

He then asks, “When is my follow-up appointment?” In the handover, the nurse reports that he asked when his follow-up appointment was. The question becomes a statement after asked; the meaning remains unchanged.

Finally, Noah says, “I may need help planning my journey.” The nurse reports a possibility: he said that he might need help planning his journey. She distinguishes this request from any observed difficulty. Clear reporting allows the next professional to ask useful questions instead of acting on an assumption.
questions: 1. What is Noah worried about?
2. Why is “He cannot cope with education” an unsuitable replacement?
3. How is Noah’s question reported?
4. Which word preserves the uncertainty of may in the reported statement?
5. What does the nurse distinguish from an observed difficulty?

listening.title: Listening: From Conversation to Handover
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. Noah said he felt __________ about returning to class.
2. He did not say that he wanted to __________ his course.
3. The next review is on __________.
4. The nurse used __________ to report a possible support need.
5. The next conversation should clarify which part of the __________ worries him.
script: Nurse A: What did Noah tell you at this morning’s appointment?
Nurse B: He said that he felt worried about returning to class. He did not say that he wanted to leave his course.
Nurse A: Did he ask about follow-up?
Nurse B: Yes. He asked when his next review was. I confirmed that it was on Tuesday.
Nurse A: Was there another concern?
Nurse B: He said that he might need help planning the journey. I recorded that as a possible support need, not as proof that he cannot travel.
Nurse A: What will you pass on?
Nurse B: His concerns and his question. The next conversation should clarify which part of the journey worries him.

culture.title: Traditional Indian medicine
notes: In groups of four, prepare a brief response during the speaking stage. Choose a spokesperson and keep the exchange within the two minutes allocated.

Useful language: “The syllabus names …”; “An individual may prefer …”; “Could you tell me …?”; “A cultural belief and evidence of a treatment effect are different questions.”

vocabulary.definition: care that aims to improve quality of life and relieve suffering in serious illness.
an illness that is expected to lead to death and cannot be cured.
reduction of distress caused by symptoms.
care focused on easing discomfort and supporting wellbeing.
the subjective experience of difficult or uncomfortable breathing.
persistent tiredness or lack of energy.
the worth of a person and their right to respectful treatment.
a person’s ability and right to make informed choices about their own care.
discussion of values and preferences for possible future healthcare.
care that considers physical, psychological, social, and spiritual needs.
a person who provides regular practical or personal support.

grammar.title: Empathy and realistic explanations
notes: • Acknowledge a concern before explaining: “That sounds exhausting.”
• Use can or may to describe support; do not promise that every symptom will disappear.
• Ask what matters to the person instead of assuming a priority.

formula.label: Concern
formula.text: “That sounds difficult. What is troubling you most today?” — Acknowledgement plus an open question.

formula.label: Support
formula.text: “The team can review ways to improve your comfort.” — An achievable process, not a cure promise.

formula.label: Preference
formula.text: “Would you like someone you trust to join us?” — Permission, not an assumption.

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: What __________ most to you today? (matters / matter)
2. Complete: The team can __________ your symptoms. (review / reviews)
3. Complete: Would you like someone to __________ us? (join / joining)
4. Rewrite carefully: “We will remove every symptom.”

reading.title: Reading: Care That Starts with What Matters
body: Palliative care addresses suffering and quality of life for people with serious illness and their families. It can be provided alongside treatment directed at the illness; it is not limited to the final hours of life (WHO, n.d.; NIA, n.d.).

In this fictional case, Mrs Karim tells the nurse that fatigue is making family visits difficult. The nurse asks what matters most to her today. Mrs Karim would like a shorter visit and a quiet period afterwards. The nurse records these preferences and discusses them with the team.

When Mrs Karim mentions uncomfortable breathing, the nurse asks for a clinical review rather than promising that it will disappear. She explains what will happen next in plain language. Mrs Karim agrees that her daughter may join the discussion.

The conversation includes physical comfort, emotional support, and the patient’s choices. It does not assume that every person wants the same visitors, environment, or type of support. The nurse finishes by checking that the agreed plan reflects Mrs Karim’s priorities.
questions: 1. What two broad aims of palliative care are identified?
2. Is palliative care restricted to the final hours of life?
3. What changes does Mrs Karim request for visits?
4. How does the nurse respond to uncomfortable breathing?
5. Why is the daughter’s involvement discussed with Mrs Karim?

listening.title: Listening: A Comfort-focused Conversation
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The patient would like a visit with her __________.
2. The suggested visit lasts __________ minutes.
3. After the visit, she wants __________ time.
4. The symptom needing a review is uncomfortable __________.
5. The nurse will __________ the patient’s preference.
script: Nurse: What would make this afternoon more comfortable for you, Mrs Karim?
Patient: I would like a short visit with my daughter, but I become tired quickly.
Nurse: Would a twenty-minute visit followed by some quiet time suit you?
Patient: Yes. Please keep the room quiet afterwards.
Nurse: I will record that preference. Is anything else troubling you?
Patient: My breathing feels uncomfortable.
Nurse: Thank you for telling me. I will request a clinical review now and explain the plan as soon as it is agreed. Would you like your daughter to be present?
Patient: Yes, I would.
Nurse: To check that I have understood: a short visit, quiet time afterwards, and a review of your breathing. Is that correct?
Patient: Yes.

speaking.outcome: Agree on two care preferences and one review request. Use three glossary terms and one explicit check of understanding.
speaking.roleA: You are a nurse. Ask a fictional patient about comfort, visitors, and one concern they want reviewed. Acknowledge the concern, ask permission before involving a relative, and summarise the agreed next step without promising a cure.
speaking.roleB: You are a patient with a serious illness. You want a quiet room and a short conversation with one relative. You would like the clinical team to review a troubling symptom. Decide what information you are comfortable sharing.

culture.title: Siddha medicine
notes: In groups of four, prepare a brief response during the speaking stage. Choose a spokesperson and keep the exchange within the two minutes allocated.

Treat “Siddha medicine” as the syllabus’s cultural enquiry topic. Ask how a nurse could learn about an individual’s beliefs, preferred routines, or sources of comfort without claiming that a traditional approach cures a terminal illness. Prepare a respectful question and a clear safety boundary.
Useful language: “The syllabus names …”; “An individual may prefer …”; “Could you tell me …?”; “A cultural belief and evidence of a treatment effect are different questions.”

vocabulary.definition: an emotional and personal response to loss.
the experience or state of having lost someone through death.
grief experienced before an expected loss.
recognising another person’s suffering and responding with care.
attentive listening that checks and reflects the speaker’s meaning.
significant psychological discomfort or suffering.
support related to a person’s meaning, values, beliefs, or faith.
protection from unwanted observation or interruption.
temporary care that gives a regular caregiver a break.
help with psychological and social needs.
an expression of sympathy after someone’s death.

grammar.title: Listening, acknowledging, and offering help
notes: • Reflect what the person has said: “It sounds as though you are feeling overwhelmed.”
• Offer choices with would or could rather than instructions about how to grieve.
• Avoid guarantees, fixed timelines, and statements claiming to know exactly how someone feels.

formula.label: Dismissive response
formula.text: Instead of “You will be fine soon”, say “This sounds very difficult.” — Acknowledges the present experience.

formula.label: Offer
formula.text: “Would you prefer a quiet room or some company?” — Gives the person a choice.

formula.label: Follow-up
formula.text: “Could I check with the team about support for you?” — Offers a realistic next step.

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: Would you __________ to speak somewhere private? (prefer / preferred)
2. Complete: It sounds as though you __________ overwhelmed. (feel / feels)
3. Complete: Could I __________ the support team for you? (contact / contacted)
4. Rewrite empathetically: “Do not cry; you must be strong.”

reading.title: Reading: Different Needs in the Same Family
body: Support near the end of life includes emotional, practical, and spiritual needs as well as physical care. Relatives and caregivers may also need support, and their preferences should not be assumed (NIA, n.d.).

In this fictional case, two adult relatives wait outside their father’s room. One wants to talk; the other prefers silence. The nurse does not label one response as better. She asks whether they would like a private space and whether there is someone they would like contacted.

The first relative says that she feels overwhelmed by calls from the wider family. The nurse listens, reflects the concern, and offers to discuss available practical support. The second relative asks for a few quiet minutes. The nurse respects that request.

No one is told to follow a fixed emotional sequence or to recover by a particular date. The nurse explains whom the relatives can contact with questions and offers a later conversation. Her role is to listen and connect them with appropriate support, not to decide how they should feel.
questions: 1. Which non-physical types of support are mentioned?
2. How do the two relatives’ preferences differ?
3. What practical difficulty does the first relative describe?
4. Why would a fixed deadline for grief be inappropriate here?
5. What follow-up does the nurse offer?

listening.title: Listening: A Relative Asks for Support
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The relative feels overwhelmed by other people’s __________.
2. She would like to talk in the __________ room.
3. Her brother prefers to sit __________.
4. She asks about the family-__________ worker.
5. The nurse will return at __________ o’clock.
script: Relative: I am finding it hard to answer everyone’s questions. I do not know what to say.
Nurse: That sounds overwhelming. Would you prefer to talk in the quiet room?
Relative: Yes, please. My brother would rather sit quietly for a few minutes.
Nurse: We can respect both preferences. Is there someone you would like us to contact?
Relative: Not yet. Could I speak to the family-support worker later?
Nurse: I will check their availability. I can return at two o’clock to update you about the arrangements.
Relative: Thank you. I do not need advice about how I should feel.
Nurse: You do not have to explain your feelings in a particular way. We can listen and discuss the support that is useful to you.
