grammar.title: Indirect questions and preferences
notes: • After “Could you tell me …”, use statement order: “where the meeting is”, not “where is the meeting”.
• Use would prefer + to-infinitive, but would rather + base verb.
• Use a conditional offer for a choice: “If you would like more time, we can return later.” Do not turn a preference into an obligation.

formula.label: Direct question
formula.text: “Who would you like to join us?” — “Could you tell me who you would like to join us?”

formula.label: Preference
formula.text: “I would prefer to talk later.” — would prefer + to-infinitive

formula.label: Alternative
formula.text: “I would rather speak in private.” — would rather + base verb

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite

2. Complete: I would prefer __________ with my daughter present. (to talk / talk)

4. Make indirect: “What matters most to you?” Begin “Could you tell me …”.

reading.title: Reading: A Preference Is Not a Promise
body: Serious-illness conversations may include uncertainty, choices about support, and discussion of future care. Clear explanations and attention to individual preferences help the conversation remain centred on the person (NIA, n.d.).

In this fictional grammar exercise, the nurse asks, “Could you tell me who you would like to join the meeting?” The patient replies, “I would prefer to have my daughter present.” The nurse records that preference without assuming permission to contact other relatives.

The patient then says, “I would rather discuss the details tomorrow.” The nurse checks whether any urgent concerns need attention today and explains that non-urgent discussion can be arranged with the team. She does not promise a particular medical outcome.

Before ending, the nurse asks, “Could you explain the arrangements in your own words?” The patient describes the planned meeting and whom she wants present. The nurse corrects one misunderstanding about the time. Grammar makes the questions more considerate, but good communication also requires listening and checking that the details are accurate.
questions: 1. Who would the patient prefer to have present?
2. Does that preference give permission to contact every relative?
3. When would the patient rather discuss the details?
4. What does the nurse check before postponing non-urgent discussion?
5. Which misunderstanding is corrected at the end?

listening.title: Listening: Arranging a Sensitive Discussion
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The patient would prefer to have her __________ present.
2. She does not want other __________ contacted yet.
3. She would rather use the private __________ room.
4. The meeting is at __________ o’clock.
5. The nurse will __________ the contact preference.
script: Nurse: Could you tell me whom you would like at tomorrow’s meeting?
Patient: I would prefer to have my daughter there. Please do not contact other relatives yet.
Nurse: Certainly. Would you rather meet in your room or in the private meeting room?
Patient: I would rather use the meeting room.
Nurse: The team has offered eleven o’clock. Does that time suit you?
Patient: Yes. Will we have time to ask questions?
Nurse: Yes, the meeting is arranged to discuss your questions and preferences. Could you explain the arrangements in your own words?
Patient: Tomorrow at eleven, in the private meeting room, with my daughter.
Nurse: That is correct. I will record your preference about contacting relatives.

grammar.title: Sequencing care and giving respectful reminders
notes: • Use first, before, after, and finally to show the order of actions.
• After before or after, use a noun phrase or -ing form: “after removing gloves”.
• Use a polite reminder without weakening the safety message: “Please clean your hands before continuing.”

formula.label: Sequence
formula.text: “First, explain the task to the patient.” — Introduces the first action.

formula.label: Timing
formula.text: “Clean your hands after removing gloves.” — after + -ing form

formula.label: Reminder
formula.text: “Before you continue, please clean your hands.” — Clear and respectful.

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: Clean your hands after __________ gloves. (removing / remove)
2. Complete: Explain the task __________ you begin. (before / although)
3. Complete: __________, check that the patient has understood. (Finally / Unless)
4. Rewrite politely: “You forgot your hands!”

reading.title: Reading: Gloves Are Not the Whole Plan
body: Hand hygiene helps prevent the spread of microorganisms in healthcare. Gloves do not replace it. Hands should be cleaned at the appropriate moments, including after glove removal; visibly soiled hands require washing with soap and water (CDC, n.d.).

In this fictional observation task, a student watches a nurse finish one care activity and prepare for another. The nurse removes used gloves, cleans her hands, and checks the next task. The student notices that a shared item has not yet been prepared for another patient. Rather than assuming it is clean because it looks clean, she asks about the local cleaning procedure.

The nurse thanks her and explains that patient-care equipment must be handled and cleaned appropriately. They keep clean supplies separate from used items. The student then practises a polite reminder: “Could we check that this item has been prepared before we use it?”
The aim is not to blame a colleague. It is to identify a possible break in infection prevention and communicate clearly enough to address it.
questions: 1. Why do gloves not remove the need for hand hygiene?
2. What should be used when hands are visibly soiled?
3. What does the student notice about the shared item?
4. Why is appearance alone an insufficient basis for assuming an item is ready?
5. What is the purpose of the student’s reminder?

listening.title: Listening: The Ward Walk-through
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The nurse first __________ the task.
2. After removing gloves, she cleaned her __________.
3. The shared item’s cleaning __________ had not been checked.
4. Unused supplies should be __________ from used items.
5. Gloves __________ replace hand hygiene. (do / do not)
script: Tutor: We will review the care sequence, not test anyone’s memory of a product brand. What happened first?
Student: The nurse explained the task to the patient. After the care activity, she removed the gloves and cleaned her hands.
Tutor: What did you notice next?
Student: A shared item was on the trolley, but its cleaning status had not been checked.
Tutor: How did you raise the concern?
Student: I asked, “Could we check that this item is ready before we use it for another patient?”
Tutor: Good. Where should unused supplies be kept?
Student: Separate from used items.
Tutor: And do gloves replace hand hygiene?
Student: No. Both the timing of hand hygiene and appropriate glove use matter.

speaking.roleA: You are observing a care sequence. You know that a staff member has removed used gloves and is about to touch clean supplies without hand hygiene. Give a respectful reminder and explain the concern without blaming the person.
speaking.roleB: You are the staff member. You also notice that the cleaning status of a shared item is unclear. Respond to the reminder, ask your partner what needs checking, and agree on a safe communication step before continuing.

a substance used on living tissue to reduce microorganisms.
a validated process that eliminates all forms of microbial life, including bacterial spores.
a process that removes or reduces contamination to make handling safer.

grammar.title: Passive voice in equipment records
notes: • Present passive: am/is/are + past participle; “The status is checked.”
• Past passive: was/were + past participle; “The tray was cleaned.”
• Modal passive: must/should + be + past participle; “The instructions must be followed.” A passive statement does not prove a process was adequate.

formula.label: Routine
formula.text: “The cleaning status is recorded.” — Present passive.

formula.label: Completed action
formula.text: “The reusable item was processed.” — Past passive; details still matter.

formula.label: Requirement
formula.text: “The manufacturer’s instructions must be followed.” — Modal + be + past participle.

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: The cleaning status __________ recorded on this form. (is / are)
2. Complete: The trays __________ cleaned yesterday. (was / were)
3. Complete: The instructions must __________ followed. (be / been)
4. Change to passive: “Staff check the product label.”

reading.title: Reading: A Clear Instruction Is Specific Enough to Check
body: Cleaning, disinfection, and sterilisation are not interchangeable terms. Equipment processing depends on the item, its intended use, and the relevant instructions. Patient-care equipment should be handled and processed appropriately, and staff should follow the applicable procedure rather than improvise (CDC, n.d.).

In this fictional case, a student reads the note “The item was done.” The statement does not identify the item, the process, or whether it is ready for reuse. The student asks for clarification. A revised note identifies the reusable tray and records that the specified cleaning process was completed.

When asked about a disinfectant’s contact time, the student does not invent a number. She checks the manufacturer’s instructions and the local procedure with the supervisor. She also distinguishes products intended for surfaces from those intended for living tissue.

The passive voice is useful because it places the item and action first. However, a grammatically correct sentence is not enough: the record must also be accurate, complete, and suitable for the clinical task.
questions: 1. Are cleaning, disinfection, and sterilisation interchangeable?
2. What three details are missing from “The item was done”?
3. Where should the student check the required contact time?
4. What distinction is made between a disinfectant and an antiseptic?
5. Why is correct passive grammar alone insufficient?

listening.title: Listening: Clarifying an Equipment Record
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The item discussed is a __________.
2. The process already completed is __________.
3. The instructions are on the __________.
4. The student needs to verify the required contact __________.
5. The supervisor will check the revised __________ before use.
script: Supervisor: Your note says that the tray was prepared. What process was completed?
Student: The cleaning process was completed, but I need to make the wording more specific.
Supervisor: Good. Has the product label been checked?
Student: Yes. The instructions are on the trolley. I have not entered a contact time because I need to verify the required value.
Supervisor: That is better than guessing. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions and our local procedure.
Student: Should I also record the item’s status?
Supervisor: Yes. The record must clearly show whether it is ready for the next intended use.
Student: I will revise the note and ask you to check it before the item is used.

speaking.outcome: Write three accurate passive sentences and one clarification question. Use three glossary terms; do not mark the item ready when that has not been confirmed.
speaking.roleA: You are a supervisor. You receive the incomplete note “Equipment done”. Ask which item was processed, which action was completed, where the instructions are, and whether the item’s status has been confirmed. Do not supply invented product details.
speaking.roleB: You are a student. Your facts: reusable tray; cleaning completed; the next required step and product contact time still need checking; manufacturer’s instructions available. Revise the note in passive forms and request supervision before use.
prompts: Write three accurate passive sentences and one clarification question. Use three glossary terms; do not mark the item ready when that has not been confirmed.

culture.title: Urinotherapy
notes: In groups of four, prepare a brief response during the speaking stage. Choose a spokesperson and keep the exchange within the two minutes allocated.

The syllabus lists “Urinotherapy” but provides no description or evidence. Treat the label only as a discussion of how to respond to an unfamiliar health claim. Do not demonstrate it or describe it as a hygiene method. Practise: “Could you explain what you mean?” and “For this task, the approved infection-prevention procedure must be followed.”
Useful language: “The syllabus names …”; “An individual may prefer …”; “Could you tell me …?”; “A cultural belief and evidence of a treatment effect are different questions.”

homework: Write 100–120 words explaining how an incomplete equipment record should be clarified. Use five glossary terms, two present passives, two past passives, and one modal passive. Do not invent a chemical concentration or contact time.

vocabulary.definition: the substance in a medicine responsible for its intended therapeutic effect.
the standard non-brand name of a medicine or active substance.
the commercial name under which a product is sold.
the physical form of a medicine, such as a tablet or cream.
administration of a medicine by mouth.
application of a medicine to a body surface, commonly the skin.
an authorised instruction for a patient’s medicine or treatment.

grammar.title: Precise descriptions and clarification questions
notes: • Use “by mouth” to explain an oral route and “on the skin” for a skin preparation when that matches its instructions.
• Distinguish form from route: “tablet” names a form; “oral” names a route.
• Ask “Could you clarify …?” when information is missing. A language exercise does not authorise dose selection.

formula.label: Route
formula.text: “The stated route is oral, meaning by mouth.” — Explains an established label detail.

formula.label: Missing information
formula.text: “Could you clarify the individual directions with the pharmacist?” — Does not fill the gap by guessing.

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: Oral means by __________.
2. Complete: A skin preparation is applied __________ the skin when its instructions specify that use. (on / into)
3. Is “tablet” a dosage form or a route?
4. Rewrite safely: “The directions are unclear, so choose a dose yourself.”

reading.title: Reading: Reading the Label before Explaining It
body: Medicine information distinguishes ingredients, intended use, warnings, and directions. A familiar brand name does not remove the need to read the relevant information (FDA, n.d.).

In this fictional classroom case, a student receives a training label. It is not a real medicine and must not be used as a prescription. The label identifies “Training Product A”, an invented active substance, a tablet form, and an oral route. Its directions state: “Use only according to the individual prescription.” No dose is supplied.

The patient role asks whether the tablet should be used in the same way as a different product with a similar-looking box. The student explains that packaging is not enough to establish equivalence. She distinguishes the product name from the active ingredient and asks the supervising professional to clarify the individual directions.

Before finishing, she checks that the patient role understands the difference between form and route. She also identifies the expiry and storage information as details that must be checked on the actual product.
questions: 1. Which four categories of medicine information are named at the start?
2. Is the training label a real prescription?
3. What form and route does the example state?
4. Why can the student not supply a dose from this label?
5. Why is a similar-looking box insufficient to establish equivalent use?

listening.title: Listening: A Label-checking Conversation
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The training product’s dosage form is a __________.
2. Its route is __________.
3. The label does not give a __________.
4. One date to check is the __________ date.
5. A __________ or prescribing clinician can clarify an unclear instruction.
script: Tutor: Please describe the training label without adding information.
Student: The product name is Training Product A. The dosage form is a tablet, and the route is oral.
Tutor: Does the label give a dose?
Student: No. It tells the reader to follow the individual prescription. I must not invent directions.
Tutor: What does “active ingredient” mean?
Student: The substance responsible for the intended therapeutic effect.
Tutor: What else would you check on a real product?
Student: The warnings, expiry date, and storage conditions.
Tutor: Who could clarify an unclear instruction?
Student: The pharmacist or prescribing clinician.
Tutor: Good. Remember that this label is an invented language exercise, not a medicine for use.

speaking.outcome: Explain four label details and identify two missing or unverified details. Use three glossary terms. Do not recommend a medicine, dose, or treatment change.
speaking.roleA: You are a nurse in a simulation. Training label: product name “Training Product A”; invented active substance “Compound X”; form tablet; route oral; directions “See the individual prescription”; dose not supplied. Explain only these details and refer missing directions for clarification.
speaking.roleB: You are a patient role. Ask the difference between the product name, active ingredient, form, and route. Ask whether a similar-looking box means the same directions. Check what needs clarification before any real medicine is used.
prompts: Explain four label details and identify two missing or unverified details. Use three glossary terms. Do not recommend a medicine, dose, or treatment change.
Change roles. For an information-gap task, cover your partner’s card while exchanging information. In feedback, name one effective phrase and one phrase to improve.

Useful language: “The syllabus names …”; “An individual may prefer …”; “Could you tell me …?”; “A cultural belief and evidence of a treatment effect are different questions.”

homework: Write 100–120 words explaining how to discuss a medication label responsibly. Use five glossary terms, distinguish form from route, and include two clarification questions. Do not include a real or invented dose.
Check your work: clear meaning; accurate vocabulary; required language structures; no unsupported medical claims.

vocabulary.definition: the extent to which a person follows a treatment plan agreed with a professional.
a harmful, unintended response to a medicine.
a change in a medicine’s effect caused by another substance.
an immune reaction to a substance that can cause harmful symptoms.
an effect of a medicine other than its intended main effect.
the use of multiple medicines by one person.
a structured assessment of a person’s medicines and related concerns.
the same active substance present in more than one product.
preparing and supplying a medicine according to an authorised request.
explaining medicine use and addressing a person’s questions.
a scheduled dose that was not taken or given.
the detection, assessment, and prevention of medicine-related harm.

grammar.title: Conditional safety messages and teach-back
notes: • Use if to connect a problem with an appropriate next step: “If an instruction is unclear, ask the pharmacist.”
• Avoid one-size-fits-all advice about a missed dose. The correct instruction depends on the medicine and the individual directions.
• Teach-back checks your explanation: ask the person to describe the plan in their own words, not simply to say yes.

formula.label: Uncertainty
formula.text: “If you are unsure, check the medicine-specific instructions with a professional.” — Does not invent a dose rule.

formula.label: New symptom
formula.text: “If a new problem occurs, report it to the healthcare team.” — Describes reporting, not a diagnosis.

formula.label: Understanding
formula.text: “Could you explain what you will check before taking these products together?” — Open teach-back question.

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: If the directions __________ unclear, ask the pharmacist. (are / is)
2. Complete: Please __________ the names of all the products you use. (bring / brings)
3. Complete: Could you explain the plan in your __________ words?
4. Rewrite safely: “Always take twice as much after a missed dose.”

reading.title: Reading: A Complete List Makes the Review More Useful
body: A medication review should consider prescription and non-prescription products. Interactions may involve medicines, supplements, or other substances, and similar ingredients can appear in products with different names (FDA, n.d.; NCCIH, n.d.).

In this fictional case, an older patient brings one prescription list but also mentions two products bought without a prescription. The nurse asks for the packaging rather than assuming what they contain. The patient has not yet taken the two additional products together.

The nurse explains that a pharmacist can check for duplicate ingredients and possible interactions. She also asks whether the patient has noticed unwanted symptoms and records the description without automatically calling every symptom an allergy.

The patient asks what to do after a missed dose. The nurse does not offer a universal rule. She arranges clarification of the medicine-specific instructions. Finally, she asks the patient to explain what information they will bring to the review. The response reveals whether the explanation was clear and which detail needs repeating.
questions: 1. Which kinds of products should be included in the review?
2. Why does the nurse ask for packaging?
3. Have the two additional products already been taken together?
4. Why should the nurse not label every unwanted symptom an allergy?
5. What does the nurse do instead of giving a universal missed-dose rule?

listening.title: Listening: Checking What the Patient Will Bring
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The patient uses __________ products bought from the pharmacy without a prescription.
2. The patient also uses one __________.
3. The nurse asks for the products’ __________.
4. The patient wants to ask about a missed __________.
5. The __________ will check ingredients and possible interactions.
script: Nurse: Please bring an updated list of your prescribed medicines to the review. Do you use anything bought without a prescription?
Patient: Yes, two products from the pharmacy and one supplement. I have not taken the two pharmacy products together.
Nurse: Please bring their packaging as well. The pharmacist can check the ingredients and any possible interactions.
Patient: I also need to ask about a missed dose.
Nurse: We will ask for the instructions for that particular medicine. There is not one rule that fits every product.
Patient: Should I simply take extra?
Nurse: Do not automatically take extra. Let us clarify the appropriate instructions. Could you tell me what you will bring?
Patient: My prescription list and the packaging for the other products.

speaking.outcome: Agree on a complete information list and one question for the pharmacist. Use three glossary terms, one if-clause, and teach-back.
speaking.roleA: You are a nurse preparing for a medication review. Ask about prescription medicines, non-prescription products, supplements, unwanted symptoms, and unclear instructions. Request the exact product information and finish with teach-back. Do not make a dosing decision.
speaking.roleB: You are a patient. You have a prescription list, two products whose ingredients you cannot remember, and a question about a missed dose. You have not combined the additional products. Ask why the packaging matters and repeat the agreed next step.
prompts: Agree on a complete information list and one question for the pharmacist. Use three glossary terms, one if-clause, and teach-back.
Change roles. For an information-gap task, cover your partner’s card while exchanging information. In feedback, name one effective phrase and one phrase to improve.

culture.title: Homeopathy
notes: In groups of four, prepare a brief response during the speaking stage. Choose a spokesperson and keep the exchange within the two minutes allocated.

Discuss the syllabus topic “Homeopathy” without equating the label with proven treatment. NCCIH notes little evidence for effectiveness for specific conditions and possible risks from some products. Practise a respectful question about the exact product and a reminder not to replace prescribed care without a professional discussion.
Useful language: “The syllabus names …”; “An individual may prefer …”; “Could you tell me …?”; “A cultural belief and evidence of a treatment effect are different questions.”

homework: Write 100–120 words about a fictional medication-review conversation. Use five glossary terms, two conditional safety messages, and a teach-back question. Include non-prescription products but no dose recommendations.
Check your work: clear meaning; accurate vocabulary; required language structures; no unsupported medical claims.

An allergy is a particular immune reaction; an unwanted symptom alone does not establish it. 5. She arranges clarification of the medicine-specific instructions.

vocabulary.definition: an upper chamber of the heart that receives blood.
a lower chamber of the heart that pumps blood out.
a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
a blood vessel that carries blood towards the heart.
a very small vessel where exchange occurs between blood and tissues.
blood flow between the heart and lungs.
blood flow between the heart and the rest of the body.
blood containing relatively more oxygen.
blood containing relatively less oxygen, not no oxygen.
a structure that helps maintain one-way blood flow through the heart.
the main artery carrying blood from the left ventricle to the body.
the flow of blood back to the heart through veins.

grammar.title: Explaining a route with sequence and definition
notes: • Use first, then, next, and finally to organise the explanation.
• Use a relative clause to define a structure: “A vein is a vessel that carries blood towards the heart.”
• Use whereas to contrast two routes or functions. Artery and vein describe direction, not oxygen content.

formula.label: Definition
formula.text: “An atrium is a chamber that receives blood.” — that + verb defines the structure.

formula.label: Sequence
formula.text: “Next, blood passes into the right ventricle.” — A sequence marker shows order.

formula.label: Contrast
formula.text: “Pulmonary circulation serves the lungs, whereas systemic circulation serves the rest of the body.” — whereas contrasts the circuits.

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: An artery is a vessel __________ carries blood away from the heart. (that / where)
2. Complete: The right ventricle pumps blood towards the __________.
3. Complete: Blood returns from the lungs to the left __________.
4. Complete: The left ventricle pumps blood into the __________.

reading.title: Reading: Two Connected Circuits
body: The heart connects pulmonary and systemic circulation. Blood returning from the body enters the right atrium and passes into the right ventricle. The right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary arteries towards the lungs. After gas exchange, blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. It then enters the left ventricle, which pumps it into the aorta and onward to the body. Valves help keep the flow moving in the correct direction (NHLBI, n.d.).

A nursing student explains the route to a fictional patient. Instead of saying that arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood, she defines them by direction: they carry blood away from the heart. Pulmonary arteries are a useful example because they carry relatively oxygen-poor blood towards the lungs.

The student uses short stages and asks the patient to explain one section of the route back to her. This reveals a confusion between an atrium and a ventricle, which she then clarifies without overwhelming the patient with additional detail.
questions: 1. Which chamber first receives blood returning from the body?
2. Which ventricle pumps blood towards the lungs?
3. Which vessels return blood from the lungs to the heart?
4. What is the function of cardiac valves?
5. Why are pulmonary arteries useful when correcting a common misconception?

listening.title: Listening: Checking the Route
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. Blood returning from the body first enters the right __________.
2. The right __________ pumps it towards the lungs.
3. Blood returns from the lungs to the __________ atrium.
4. The left ventricle pumps blood into the __________.
5. Veins carry blood __________ the heart.
script: Nurse: Let us follow one part of the circulation. Blood returning from the body first enters the right atrium.
Patient: Does it then go straight to the aorta?
Nurse: No. Next it passes into the right ventricle, which pumps it towards the lungs. After gas exchange, it returns to the left atrium.
Patient: Then it moves into the left ventricle?
Nurse: Exactly. The left ventricle pumps it into the aorta and towards the body.
Patient: So the right side sends blood to the lungs, and the left side sends it to the body.
Nurse: Yes. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, while veins carry it back towards the heart. Could you describe the route to the lungs once more?

culture.title: Mineral therapy
notes: In groups of four, prepare a brief response during the speaking stage. Choose a spokesperson and keep the exchange within the two minutes allocated.

The syllabus label “Mineral therapy” does not specify a substance, dose, or evidence. Discuss why a broad label cannot justify a claim that a product improves circulation. Practise asking which product is meant and referring any proposed supplement use for an individual safety review.
Useful language: “The syllabus names …”; “An individual may prefer …”; “Could you tell me …?”; “A cultural belief and evidence of a treatment effect are different questions.”

grammar.title: A clear handover: situation, background, assessment, request
notes: • State what is happening now, followed by relevant background and the source of the information.
• Distinguish findings from causes: “The patient reports …” does not mean “The patient definitely has …”.
• End with an explicit request. For urgent new symptoms, summon appropriate clinical help promptly rather than delay for a complete interview.

formula.label: Situation
formula.text: “I am calling about new breathlessness.” — Names the immediate concern.

formula.label: Attributed finding
formula.text: “The patient reports chest discomfort that began ten minutes ago.” — Gives symptom and onset without a diagnosis.

formula.label: Request
formula.text: “Please attend for an urgent clinical assessment.” — Makes the required response clear.

practice: Practice A. Complete or rewrite
1. Complete: The patient __________ new breathlessness. (reports / report)
2. Complete: The discomfort __________ ten minutes ago. (began / has begun)
3. Choose the careful statement: A) This proves a clot. B) This requires clinical assessment.
4. Write a handover sentence using: patient / reports / left-leg swelling / since this morning.

reading.title: Reading: A Symptom Report Is Not a Diagnosis
body: New breathlessness and chest pain can signal an urgent problem. When these occur with symptoms suggesting a leg clot, urgent medical assessment is particularly important. Such symptoms cannot be diagnosed safely from a classroom checklist alone (NHS, n.d.).

In this fictional ward scenario, a patient reports new chest discomfort and difficulty breathing. The nurse promptly summons clinical help according to the local emergency procedure. She does not delay while asking every question in a language worksheet.

Her initial handover identifies the patient and the immediate symptoms, states when they began, and makes a clear request for urgent assessment. She distinguishes information supplied by the patient from findings she has personally observed. Further measurements or history can be obtained by the team as appropriate.

After the simulation, the students compare that response with a non-urgent practice case about a previously assessed symptom. They discuss why the purpose of an information-gathering activity must never obscure the need to act promptly when a person is acutely unwell. Their aim is accurate communication, not an unsupported diagnosis.
questions: 1. Which two new symptoms prompt urgent help in the fictional ward case?
2. What does the nurse do before completing a long interview?
3. Name two details included in the initial handover.
4. What sources of information does the nurse keep separate?
5. Why should the worksheet not be followed mechanically in an urgent situation?

listening.title: Listening: Requesting Urgent Assessment
directions: Listen twice. Complete each answer from the conversation. The teacher’s full script is in the teacher copy at the end of the lesson.
After listening, compare answers and identify the phrase that helped you choose one answer.
questions: 1. The nurse is calling from room __________.
2. The chest symptoms began __________ minutes ago.
3. The patient reports swelling in his __________ leg.
4. The leg swelling has been present since this __________.
5. The nurse requests urgent clinical __________.
script: Nurse: I am calling from room six. Mr Lee reports new chest discomfort and difficulty breathing. He says the symptoms began ten minutes ago. I have activated our local emergency response. Please attend for urgent assessment.
Clinician: I am coming. Has the patient described any other new symptom?
Nurse: He reports swelling in his left leg since this morning. I am reporting his description, not making a diagnosis.
Clinician: Thank you. Stay with the patient and follow the local emergency procedure while the team arrives.

Nurse: Understood. The immediate concerns are chest discomfort and breathlessness, with an onset ten minutes ago. I will pass any additional information to the responding team without delaying their assessment.

speaking.outcome: Deliver a 45–60-second handover with identity, symptoms, onset, and request. Use three glossary terms accurately. Explain afterwards which findings were reported rather than confirmed.
speaking.roleA: You are the nurse in a verbal simulation. Facts: patient Jordan; new chest discomfort and breathlessness; onset five minutes ago; patient reports left-leg swelling since morning; local emergency response already activated. Give a concise handover and request urgent assessment. Do not diagnose a clot.
speaking.roleB: You are the receiving clinician role. Confirm the location and onset, acknowledge the urgent request, and repeat the key symptoms. Keep the exchange short. The exercise is verbal only and does not replace practical emergency training.

For “Sound therapy”, distinguish a person’s preference for a calming environment from a treatment claim about circulation. Practise explaining that any optional comfort activity must not delay assessment of new chest pain, breathlessness, or another urgent concern. Do not claim that sound removes a clot.

reading.title: Reading — 20 marks
body: A Review That Preserves the Patient’s Preferences

This is a fictional assessment case. Mr Karim is receiving care for a serious illness. At a planned review, he says that fatigue has made long family visits difficult. He would prefer shorter visits and would like his daughter to attend the next discussion. He does not give permission to contact other relatives.

The nurse records his preferences and asks whether he has questions about his medicines. He mentions a product bought without a prescription but cannot remember its active ingredient. He has not started taking it. The nurse asks him to bring the packaging and arranges for the pharmacist to clarify possible concerns. She does not assume that every non-prescription product is harmless.

A shared item is brought into the room, but its cleaning status is unclear. Before use, the nurse asks a colleague to confirm that it has been processed according to the appropriate instructions. She also maintains hand hygiene at the required moments.
questions: 1. What visit preference does Mr Karim express, and why?
2. Who may attend the next discussion, and what contact permission has not been given?
3. What medicine-related information is missing, and what does the nurse ask him to bring?
4. What equipment concern is identified, and what happens before use?
5. How does the nurse check understanding, and what misunderstanding is corrected?

listening.title: Listening — 20 marks
directions: Clarifying an Agreed Plan
Listen twice and answer from the conversation. Each question is worth 4 marks: 2 for each requested detail.
questions: 1. State the day and time of the review.
2. Who will attend with the patient, and which room type would the patient prefer?
3. What will the patient bring, and for which professional?
4. Has the patient started the product, and why or why not?
5. Which symptom does the patient mention, and when did it begin?
script: Nurse: Before we finish, could you explain the arrangements for your review?
Patient: It is on Friday at eleven o’clock, and my daughter will come with me.
Nurse: That is correct. What will you bring for the pharmacist?
Patient: The packaging for the product I bought without a prescription. I have not started it because I want the instructions checked first.
Nurse: Thank you. You also mentioned morning tiredness. When did that begin?
Patient: On Monday. Please include that in the questions for the review.
Nurse: I will record your report. Is there anything you would prefer about the meeting?
Patient: I would rather use a private room.
Nurse: I will pass on that preference and confirm the arrangements. Please tell us promptly about any new or urgent symptom rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

Accept equivalent wording that preserves the meaning. For grammar items, award 2 for a correct structure and meaning, 1 for a minor error with the target structure recognisable, and 0 for an incorrect or missing response. Do not penalise an otherwise correct comprehension answer for minor spelling that does not change meaning.
Reading and listening: each question asks for two details. Award 2 per correct detail, 1 if the detail is partly correct, and 0 if missing or wrong. Total per question: 4 marks.

vocabulary.definition: A structured enquiry into a person’s pain and its effects.
The time or circumstances in which a symptom begins.
The part of the body where a symptom is experienced.
How intense or serious a symptom is.
The spread of pain from one area to another.
The length of time a symptom has been present.

Something that makes a symptom worse.
Something that makes a symptom less troublesome.
A medicine used to relieve pain.
The effect of a condition on everyday activities.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Open questions; past simple and present perfect

Use the past simple for a completed onset event: “It began yesterday.” Use the present perfect for a symptom continuing now: “It has lasted since yesterday.” Use since with a starting point and for with a period. Avoid leading questions.

formula.label: Structure
formula.text: Example — Meaning / use

formula.label: Past simple
formula.text: When did the pain begin? — Ask about a completed starting event.

formula.label: Present perfect + since
formula.text: It has hurt since Monday. — Connect a starting point with the present.

formula.label: Open question
formula.text: How has it affected your sleep? — Explore the patient’s experience.

practice: Practice A. Complete, choose or rewrite
1. Complete: When ___ the pain begin yesterday? (did / has)
2. Complete: It has lasted ___ two days. (for / since)
3. Complete: I have felt discomfort ___ Monday. (for / since)
4. Correct: “Where the pain is?”

reading.title: Reading
body: A Pain History, Not a Diagnosis
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

During a simulated clinic visit, Mr Karimov describes an ache in his right shoulder. It began on Monday after he carried a heavy bag. He has had discomfort for two days, and it becomes worse when he reaches upwards. He rates it as six out of ten. The student feldsher asks whether the pain spreads elsewhere rather than assuming that it remains in one place. Mr Karimov says that it does not spread and that he slept poorly last night.

The student records the patient’s own description, the onset, the severity and the effect on sleep. She also asks what he has already tried, but does not select a medicine independently. Her supervisor will assess the problem and decide what further care is needed. Pain assessment should consider the person’s experience and daily functioning, not only a number on a scale. [R1]
questions: 1. Where is the reported pain?
2. What happened before the pain began?
3. Which everyday activity has been affected?
4. Find a present-perfect structure in the text.
5. Why is “The cause has not yet been established” useful?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The pain is in the left ___.
2. It began after a long ___.
3. It has lasted for about ___ hours.
4. The current rating is ___ out of ten.
5. The activity that makes it worse is ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Feldsher: Could you tell me where the pain is? Patient: It is in my left knee. Feldsher: When did it begin? Patient: It began yesterday, after a long journey. It has lasted for about twenty hours. Feldsher: Does it spread anywhere? Patient: No. It stays in my knee. Walking makes it worse. Feldsher: How severe is it now? Patient: Five out of ten. I also slept badly. Feldsher: Thank you. I will record your description and ask my supervisor to assess you. Could you confirm that walking makes it worse? Patient: Yes, that is correct.

speaking.outcome: Communication outcome: Produce a four-sentence pain handover containing one past-simple and one present-perfect structure.
speaking.roleA: Ask about site, onset, duration, severity, spread and daily functioning. You have no diagnosis. Summarise what the patient reports and identify one question for your supervisor.
speaking.roleB: Your lower back began aching two days ago after a long bus journey. You rate it four out of ten; sitting for a long time makes it worse. It does not spread. You want to know why the cause is still uncertain.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Descriptive language; there is / there are; may and might

Use there is with one countable finding and there are with plural findings. Use precise location phrases, such as on the lateral border. May and might express possibility, not confirmation; they do not make an unsupported diagnosis acceptable.

formula.label: Structure
formula.text: Example — Meaning / use

formula.label: There is + singular
formula.text: There is a small patch on the upper surface. — Describe one finding.

formula.label: There are + plural
formula.text: There are two shallow grooves. — Describe more than one finding.

formula.label: May + base verb

reading.title: Reading
body: From Description to Further Assessment
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

A tutor presents a fictional observation card: “One pale patch on the upper surface of the tongue; mild soreness reported for three days.” Students are asked to describe the card, not to diagnose a photograph. One student writes, “There is a patch, and the patient reports soreness.” Another writes, “The tongue proves that the patient has an internal disease.” The class identifies the first statement as a description and the second as an unsupported inference.

A sore or white tongue can have different explanations. Persistent concerns and white patches should be assessed by an appropriate clinician rather than self-diagnosed. [R2] The student therefore asks about duration, discomfort, recent changes and the effect on eating.
questions: 1. How long has soreness been reported?
2. Which statement separates observation from a reported symptom?
3. What makes the internal-disease claim unsuitable?
4. Name two additional details the student asks about.
5. What material replaces a real examination in class?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The red area is on the ___ lateral border.

4. They also need to ask whether ___ is difficult.

Tutor: Please read the fictional oral-assessment card. Student: There is a small red area on the left lateral border of the tongue. The patient reports soreness for four days. Tutor: Is the cause confirmed? Student: No. Several explanations may be possible. Tutor: What information is missing? Student: We need to ask whether the patient has recently bitten the tongue and whether eating is difficult. Tutor: Good. What will you record? Student: The location, the description and the reported duration. I will not write an unconfirmed diagnosis. Tutor: Exactly. Clear description supports the next clinical assessment.

reading.title: Reading
body: A Referral That Preserves the Patient’s Meaning
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

Ms Tursunova attends a fictional follow-up appointment. She says that a sore on the side of her tongue has been present for four weeks. Eating sometimes hurts, and she is worried because it has not healed. The student asks when she first noticed it, whether it has changed and which activities it affects. He does not reassure her that it is “definitely harmless”.

The NHS advises clinical review of a mouth ulcer that lasts longer than three weeks. [R3] In the simulation, the student therefore contacts the supervising clinician to arrange assessment. His referral distinguishes the patient’s account from findings that have not been confirmed: “The patient reports a persistent sore and pain when eating. No diagnosis has been made.”
questions: 1. How long has the sore been present?
2. Which activity sometimes hurts?
3. Why should the concern be reviewed?
4. Which two things does the referral distinguish?
5. Why does the patient repeat the contact plan?

Feldsher: I am calling about a patient who reports a sore on the right side of his tongue. Clinician: How long has it been present? Feldsher: He said that he had noticed it five weeks earlier. He reports pain when eating, but no swallowing difficulty. Clinician: Has a cause been confirmed? Feldsher: No. I have recorded his account and asked for your assessment. Clinician: Please confirm his contact number and explain that the clinic will arrange a review. Feldsher: I will do that and check that he understands the plan.

reading.title: Reading
body: Help That Does Not Take Over
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

In a simulated home visit, Mrs Salimova explains that she can wash and dress independently but finds shopping difficult. She enjoys choosing her own meals and does not want relatives to make every decision. The student initially plans to ask her daughter all the questions. His supervisor instead invites him to address Mrs Salimova directly and ask whom she wishes to involve.

The student learns that Mrs Salimova hears more comfortably when people face her and speak clearly. He asks one question at a time and checks whether she wants information written down. Together they identify shopping as the first issue to discuss with the care team. The proposed next step is a review of available support, not an instruction to stop doing activities she values.
questions: 1. Which two activities can Mrs Salimova manage independently?
2. What does she find difficult?
3. Who should be addressed first about her preferences?
4. What communication adjustment does she prefer?
5. What three elements should the final record include?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient can dress and make ___.
2. Carrying ___ is difficult.
3. He agrees that his ___ may join the discussion.
4. He prefers written information in ___ print.
5. He wants to continue visiting the neighbourhood ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Feldsher: Mr Ergashev, which activities can you manage yourself? Patient: I can dress and make breakfast, but carrying groceries is difficult. Feldsher: Would you like your son to join this discussion? Patient: Yes, but please ask me the questions first. Feldsher: Of course. Would written information be helpful? Patient: Large print would be useful. Feldsher: What is your priority today? Patient: I want to keep going to the neighbourhood shop. Feldsher: Let us record that goal and discuss suitable support with the care team. Patient: Thank you for asking what I prefer.

speaking.roleB: You manage personal care independently. You find transport to appointments difficult and want to continue attending a reading group. You prefer written instructions and do not want your nephew to answer for you.
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.

reading.title: Reading
body: Not Simply “Old Age”
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

During a fictional ward handover, a relative says that Mr Ahmedov normally recognises staff and follows conversations. This morning he has become unusually distracted and does not know where he is. The student asks when he was last behaving as usual and whether the change has varied during the day. She records the relative’s account separately from what she has observed.

Dementia is not an inevitable part of ageing. A recent change developing over hours or days, especially with fluctuation, may indicate delirium and needs prompt clinical assessment. [R5, R6] The student does not label the patient as having dementia or decide the cause of the confusion.
questions: 1. What is Mr Ahmedov’s usual functioning according to the relative?
2. When did the new change begin?
3. Which current observation is included in the handover?
4. Why should the student avoid simply writing “old age”?
5. What is the appropriate next step in the case?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.

2. She spoke clearly last ___.
3. The change has been present since this ___.
4. The family history comes from her ___.
5. The student is requesting prompt ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Student: I need to report a new change in Mrs Rasulova’s attention. Supervisor: What is her usual functioning? Student: Her son says that she usually follows a conversation. She spoke clearly last night. Since this morning, she has been distracted and has asked repeatedly where she is. Supervisor: Is this a confirmed diagnosis? Student: No. I am reporting a change from her baseline and requesting prompt assessment. Supervisor: Thank you. Please record when it began and who provided the history. Student: Her son provided the history, and I have also observed difficulty maintaining attention.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Present perfect; neutral descriptions and cautious conclusions

Use the present perfect to ask about recent changes without specifying a finished time. Form questions with have/has + subject + past participle. A laboratory result is a measurement; an interpretation must be attributed to the responsible clinician.

formula.text: This information may help the team plan support. — Avoid claiming more than the information shows.

reading.title: Reading
body: A Nutrition Note with Three Sources of Information
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

Mr Usmonov brings a food diary and a laboratory report to a fictional appointment. He has recently changed his work shifts and now eats his main meal late in the evening. The student asks what food is available during work, how often he eats and what changes he would find manageable. She asks permission before discussing weight.

A balanced dietary pattern depends on individual needs and context. Obesity has interacting biological, behavioural and environmental influences; it should not be reduced to a judgement about character. [R7, R8] The student therefore avoids blaming language and does not promise that a single food will solve the problem.
questions: 1. What recent change has affected Mr Usmonov’s meals?
2. What does the student ask before discussing weight?
3. Which two report details does she check?
4. What three sources are labelled in the note?
5. Why is the laboratory report not treated as a complete explanation?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient has started taking ___ to work.
2. The meal sometimes skipped is ___.
3. The report has not yet been reviewed with the ___.
4. The suggested professional for meal planning is a ___.
5. The patient needs a plan that fits work ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Feldsher: What have you changed in your meals recently? Patient: I have started taking lunch to work, but I still skip breakfast on early shifts. Feldsher: What makes breakfast difficult? Patient: I leave home very early. Feldsher: Have you discussed your laboratory report with the clinician? Patient: Not yet. Feldsher: I will note that the review is pending. Would you like to speak with the dietitian about a practical meal plan? Patient: Yes, especially one that fits my shifts. Feldsher: We can record that preference without making assumptions about the results.

speaking.roleB: You have begun cooking at home twice a week. Late shifts make regular meals difficult. You want affordable options and dislike being judged by your weight. Your laboratory report has not been explained yet.
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Present perfect continuous; although, because and therefore

Use have/has been + -ing for an ongoing activity or experience. Use although for contrast, because for a reason and therefore for a result. Do not use a linker to imply a clinical cause that the case does not establish.

formula.label: Although
formula.text: Although the pain remains, she values the support. — Express contrast without denying the pain.

formula.label: Because / therefore
formula.text: Sleep is a concern; therefore, she will discuss it at review. — Connect a stated concern with an agreed action.

reading.title: Reading
body: Progress Can Include Better Function
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

Ms Yuldasheva has been living with recurring back pain for eight months. She wants to attend her daughter’s school meeting but worries about sitting for a long time. The student asks what matters most to her and how pain has been affecting sleep and activity. Ms Yuldasheva has been keeping a diary and wants the team to consider it at her next review.

Chronic pain lasts or recurs for more than three months. A person-centred assessment considers its effects, priorities and wider circumstances. [R1] In this fictional case, the team will discuss an individual plan rather than promise that one intervention will remove every symptom.
questions: 1. How long has Ms Yuldasheva had recurring pain?
2. What activity matters to her?
3. What has she been keeping?
4. Why is the goal functional rather than a promise of cure?
5. Find one contrast linker.

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The activity the patient has been avoiding is ___.
2. Long periods of ___ are difficult.
3. The diary has been kept for ___ weeks.
4. Another concern is disturbed ___.
5. The patient wants time ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Feldsher: How has the pain been affecting your week? Patient: I have been avoiding the garden because standing for long periods is difficult. Feldsher: What would you like to discuss at your review? Patient: A realistic way to spend some time outside. I have been keeping a diary for three weeks. Feldsher: What else should the team know? Patient: My sleep has been disturbed. Feldsher: I will record both concerns. Although we cannot promise immediate relief, we can make sure your priorities are clear. Patient: Please also mention that gardening is important to me.

speaking.roleA: Ask about a functional goal, a difficult activity and a recent change. Use the diary as patient-reported information. Summarise priorities for a treatment review, not a new prescription.
speaking.roleB: You have had pain for six months and have been missing a weekly craft group. Travel and sitting are difficult. You want to discuss a manageable return, but do not want anyone to promise a cure.
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.
Communication outcome: Agree a patient-defined goal and a two-linker summary for the review.
Peer observation
Culture project: Traditional Asian medicine

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Infinitives of purpose; may, can and could

Use to + base verb to express purpose: “She attends to discuss her concerns.” Use in order to for a more explicit purpose. May and could keep possibilities distinct from guarantees; a grammatical purpose does not prove a health outcome.

reading.title: Reading
body: What Does a Longer Life Mean to the Patient?
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

At a fictional community discussion, Mr Nurmatov says that a long life matters to him because he wants to remain involved with his family. He is less interested in a “secret remedy” than in being able to visit friends and manage everyday activities. The student asks which routine he would like to discuss with his clinician.

Healthy ageing concerns functional ability and well-being, not only the absence of illness. [R9] Physical activity, sleep and social participation are relevant areas for discussion, but individual needs and circumstances vary. [R10] The student does not promise a particular lifespan or recommend the same screening schedule to everyone.
questions: 1. Why does a long life matter to Mr Nurmatov?
2. What does healthy ageing concern besides illness?
3. How many questions does he prepare?
4. Find an infinitive expressing purpose.
5. Why is one screening schedule not given to everybody?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient wants to stay connected with ___.
2. The suggested meeting frequency is ___.
3. The meeting place should be easy to ___.
4. The patient will write down ___.
5. The purpose of writing is to ___ them.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Feldsher: What would you like to maintain as you grow older? Patient: I want to stay connected with my friends. Feldsher: What could make that easier? Patient: I could plan a weekly meeting at a place I can reach. Feldsher: Would you like to discuss activity and preventive care at your next appointment? Patient: Yes. I will write down my questions to remember them. Feldsher: Good. The aim is a realistic plan, not a promise about how long anyone will live. Patient: My first goal is to keep seeing my friends regularly.

speaking.roleA: Ask what the person values, what makes participation difficult and which question should go to the clinician. Explain purposes with to + infinitive. Do not promise lifespan extension.
speaking.roleB: You are 64 and want to remain active in your community. Transport is difficult, and you prefer a small realistic change to a strict lifestyle programme. Ask which question to raise at your next appointment.
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.
Communication outcome: Create a three-sentence goal statement with two purpose infinitives and one cautious modal.

vocabulary.definition: A routine that a person can continue over time.
A change in a person’s usual actions or routines.
The extent to which an agreed care plan is followed.
Confidence in one’s ability to carry out an action.
Something that makes an action more difficult.
Something that helps an action become possible or easier.
Waking behaviour involving very little energy use while sitting or reclining.

A collaborative approach to exploring motivation and change.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Comparatives, superlatives and first conditionals

Use -er or more + adjective to compare two options and the + superlative to prioritise within a stated context. In a first conditional, use if + present simple, then will/can + base verb. Keep conclusions individual rather than universal.

formula.label: Structure
formula.text: Example — Meaning / use

formula.label: Comparative
formula.text: A flexible plan may be easier than a rigid one. — Compare two options cautiously.

formula.label: Superlative
formula.text: The most useful goal is the one we agree together. — Prioritise within this discussion.

formula.label: First conditional
formula.text: If the shift changes, we will review the plan. — Link a possible future event and response.

practice: Practice A. Complete, choose or rewrite
1. Complete: This plan is ___ to follow. (easy; comparative)
2. Complete: It is the ___ manageable option for this patient. (most / more)
3. Complete: If the shift changes, we ___ review the plan. (will / would)
4. Correct: “If she will need help, she will call.”

reading.title: Reading
body: A Setback Becomes Information
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

At a fictional review, Ms Qodirova says that her new routine worked during the first week but became difficult after her shifts changed. She feels that she has failed. The student asks which part was manageable and which part no longer fits her day. Ms Qodirova explains that meeting a friend once a week is easier than attending an activity every evening.

The discussion focuses on a sustainable habit rather than a perfect record. The student says, “If your schedule changes again, we will discuss an alternative.” They compare two plans and agree to record participation, not to use the plan as proof of disease prevention or longer life.
questions: 1. What made the routine difficult?
2. Which option is easier for Ms Qodirova?
3. What will happen if the schedule changes again?
4. What will they record?
5. Why is “failure” not the most useful label here?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The easier option was the ___ meeting.
2. The main barrier was a changed work ___.
3. The patient wants an alternative ___.
4. The next review is in ___ weeks.
5. The patient will note what ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Feldsher: Which part of the plan was easiest to continue? Patient: The weekly meeting was easier than the daily activity. Feldsher: What was the biggest barrier? Patient: My work schedule changed. Feldsher: If that happens again, we will review the timing. What would make the plan more manageable? Patient: Having an alternative day. Feldsher: Let us record that. We will discuss your experience again in two weeks. Patient: I will note what helps rather than just count missed days. Feldsher: That will give us useful information for the next discussion.

speaking.outcome: Communication outcome: Agree a preferred option, one alternative and a review condition.
speaking.roleA: Compare two patient-suggested plans. Ask for one barrier and one facilitator. Use a first conditional to agree how the plan will be reviewed if circumstances change.
speaking.roleB: You prefer a weekly social activity to a daily commitment. Caring for a relative sometimes changes your schedule. You would like an alternative time and a plan that does not treat a missed session as failure.
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.
Communication outcome: Agree a preferred option, one alternative and a review condition.
Peer observation

reading.title: Reading — 5 marks
body: Mary Mallon: Infection, Communication and Public Trust
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

Mary Mallon, often called “Typhoid Mary”, worked as a cook in the New York City area in the early twentieth century. She carried Salmonella Typhi without showing the symptoms that people commonly associated with illness. Her history became an important example in discussions of asymptomatic carriage and disease investigation. [R13]

Typhoid can spread through food or water contaminated with the bacteria. Feeling well does not establish that a person cannot transmit an infection. Handwashing and safe food and water practices are important preventive measures. [R11, R12]
questions: 1. What was Mary Mallon’s occupation?
2. Which bacterium did she carry?
3. What does asymptomatic carriage mean in the text?

5. What should students avoid inventing?

script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Health educator: Today we are discussing how someone can carry an infection without feeling ill. Resident: Does feeling well prove that a person cannot spread it? Health educator: No. In typhoid, bacteria can reach food or water and then another person. Resident: What information should the community receive? Health educator: A clear explanation of the concern, advice about handwashing and food safety, and directions to the responsible health service. Resident: Should we call people by insulting labels? Health educator: No. Respectful communication helps people ask questions. Please repeat the difference between having no symptoms and having no possible risk.

notes: Defining relative clauses; infinitives of purpose

Use who for a person and which or that for a thing or service. A defining relative clause identifies the noun and normally has no commas. Use an infinitive to explain purpose: “a plan to support participation”.

reading.title: Reading
body: One Patient, Different Questions
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

In a fictional rehabilitation meeting, Mr Safarov brings three questions. He wants to understand support for walking, for dressing independently and for communicating more clearly. The student explains that different professionals may contribute to a coordinated plan. A physiotherapist focuses on movement and physical functioning; an occupational therapist helps with everyday activities; a speech and language therapist addresses relevant communication needs. Rehabilitation is organised around the person’s goals and preferences. [R14]

The student does not promise which therapy will produce a particular result or assign a treatment programme herself. Instead, she helps Mr Safarov prepare the right questions for the team. “Which professional can discuss dressing with me?” is more useful than “Which therapy is best for everyone?”

2. Which therapist can discuss everyday activities such as dressing?
3. What should organise the rehabilitation plan?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.

script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Student: Which question would you like the rehabilitation team to answer first? Patient: I want help with activities at home, especially dressing. Student: An occupational therapist is a professional who can discuss daily activities with you. Patient: Who can explain my movement goals? Student: The physiotherapist can clarify that part of the plan. Patient: Will one appointment solve everything? Student: I cannot promise that. The team will discuss your goals and review progress. Patient: Please write down my dressing question so that I remember to ask it. Student: Certainly. We will keep that as your first priority.

reading.title: Reading
body: An Option Is Not a Promise
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

A fictional patient tells the student that she has seen an advertisement for an approach described as “natural” and therefore “certain to be safe”. She wants to know whether she should replace her existing care. The student does not make that decision. She asks what the patient hopes to achieve and helps her prepare questions for the responsible clinician.

A non-mainstream approach used alongside conventional care is described as complementary; use instead of conventional care is described as alternative. These labels describe how an approach is used, not proof that it is effective or harmless. [R15]
questions: 1. What unsupported claim appears in the advertisement?
2. What is the difference between complementary and alternative use?
3. Do these labels prove effectiveness?
4. What practical burden does the patient identify?
5. What next step does she repeat?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient hopes daily activities will become ___.
2. Questions should include benefits and unwanted ___.
3. The patient also asks about the number of ___.
4. The next discussion is with the responsible ___.
5. The student will record preferences and unanswered ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Patient: I have read about a new approach and want to know whether to add it to my care. Feldsher: What do you hope it will help with? Patient: I hope it will make daily activities easier. Feldsher: Let us list questions about benefits, unwanted effects and possible interactions with your current care. Patient: I also need to ask about the number of appointments. Feldsher: Good. Could you explain our next step in your own words? Patient: I will discuss these questions with the responsible clinician before making changes. Feldsher: Exactly. I will record your preferences and the questions that remain unanswered.

notes: Present simple; relative clauses for structure and function

reading.title: Reading
body: Explaining a Familiar Word Precisely
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

A student is preparing a fictional patient-information display about blood. Her first draft says only, “Blood keeps us alive.” The tutor asks her to explain the components more precisely. She writes that red blood cells carry oxygen with haemoglobin, white blood cells contribute to immune defence, platelets help clot formation and plasma carries cells and dissolved substances. [R16, R29]

The student then checks the language. “Plasma carry” becomes “plasma carries”, while “red cells carries” becomes “red cells carry”. She also decides to introduce “erythrocytes” only after giving the familiar phrase “red blood cells”.
questions: 1. Which protein helps red blood cells carry oxygen?
2. Which component contributes to immune defence?
3. Which component contributes to clot formation?
4. Why does the student give “red blood cells” before “erythrocytes”?
5. Does knowing the functions authorise independent diagnosis from a test?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. Another name for red blood cells is ___.
2. Their oxygen-carrying protein is ___.
3. White cells contribute to immune ___.
4. Platelets help form ___.
5. The liquid part of blood is ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Student: Red blood cells are also called erythrocytes. They carry oxygen using haemoglobin. Patient: And what do white cells do? Student: They contribute to immune defence. Platelets are cell fragments that help blood form clots. Patient: What is plasma? Student: It is the liquid part that carries blood cells and dissolved substances. Patient: Does that explain my blood-test result? Student: It explains the basic terms, but the clinician needs to interpret your particular result. Patient: So this is an explanation of functions, not my diagnosis. Student: Exactly.

speaking.outcome: Communication outcome: Complete a four-component explanation and make the distinction between background knowledge and an individual result.
speaking.roleA: Explain the four major components of blood. Use a plain term before each academic term where appropriate. Ask the patient to match a component to a function and correct any misunderstanding.
speaking.roleB: You have heard “erythrocytes” and “platelets” but do not know what they mean. Ask whether plasma is a cell and whether this explanation by itself tells you what your personal test result means.
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.
Communication outcome: Complete a four-component explanation and make the distinction between background knowledge and an individual result.
Peer observation
Culture project: Non-traditional methods of treatment

practice a: 1. carry 2. carries 3. that 4. White blood cells help defend the body. 5. Red blood cells carry oxygen.
reading 1–5: 1. Haemoglobin. 2. White blood cells / leucocytes. 3. Platelets. 4. To make the explanation understandable before adding the academic term. 5. No.
mini-quiz 1–6: 1. Red blood cell. 2. Haemoglobin. 3. is 4. White blood cells / leucocytes. 5. Platelets help clot formation. 6. No.
speaking: model: “Red blood cells, or erythrocytes, carry oxygen using haemoglobin. White cells contribute to defence. Platelets help clotting, while plasma is the liquid part. Your clinician will explain how your own results fit your health situation.”
culture / revision: “Which measurable effect is claimed?” “What evidence supports that effect and its safety?” A vague phrase such as “cleans the blood” is not a precise clinical explanation.

Use be + past participle to describe a process: “The report is checked.” Use has/have been + past participle for a completed action relevant now. Keep “reported”, “confirmed” and “pending” distinct; do not invent a missing result.
