reading.title: Reading
body: Before Explaining the Number
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

A fictional patient brings a printed blood report to an appointment. The student notices that one identifier on the report differs from the appointment record. She does not assume that the report belongs to the patient and does not discuss its values as if they were confirmed. She records the discrepancy and asks her supervisor to verify the information.

The patient also asks whether a result outside the printed comparison range always proves disease. A complete blood count measures several features of blood cells, and results must be considered with other clinical information. An out-of-range result does not by itself provide a complete diagnosis. [R17]
questions: 1. What mismatch does the student notice?
2. What does she do before discussing values?
3. What does a complete blood count measure?
4. Does one out-of-range result provide a complete diagnosis?
5. Name one action the case does not authorise.

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The discrepancy concerns the patient ___.
2. The concern has been ___.
3. The details must be ___ first.
4. The result will be interpreted in ___.
5. No ___ has been made about the patient’s condition.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Student: I have found a difference between the identifier on this report and the appointment record. Supervisor: Has it been checked? Student: Not yet. The discrepancy has been recorded, but the report has not been discussed as a confirmed result. Supervisor: Good. We must verify the details first. Patient: Does that mean the number proves something is wrong with me? Student: No conclusion has been made. First, the report details must be confirmed; then the clinician can interpret the result in context. Patient: I understand why you are checking before explaining the numbers.

No; report the discrepancy through the appropriate process. 5. The report is reviewed. 6. The result has not yet been interpreted, so no diagnosis is being stated.

culture / revision: “A platelet is a blood component; a platelet count is a measurement; explaining the result for a particular patient is clinical interpretation.”

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Empathetic language; would like, could and open questions

Use would like to invite preferences and could to offer possibilities. Empathetic statements acknowledge feelings without claiming to know exactly how someone feels. An open question is often more useful than false reassurance.

reading.title: Reading
body: Care Continues When Priorities Change
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

In a fictional conversation, Mr Sobirov asks whether palliative care means that the team has stopped caring for him. The student explains that its purpose is to relieve suffering and support quality of life. Palliative care can address physical, psychological, social and spiritual concerns; it is not limited to the final hours of life. [R18]

Mr Sobirov says that his main worries are discomfort and not knowing whom to ask for information. He would like his sister to attend the next discussion, but he wants questions addressed to him first. The student records these preferences and asks the supervising clinician to explain the current care plan.
questions: 1. What misconception does Mr Sobirov express?
2. What is the main purpose of palliative care in the text?
3. Whom would he like to involve?
4. What does he want concerning how questions are asked?
5. How does the student respond to a request for an exact prognosis?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient is worried about ___.
2. He wants his ___ to understand the plan.
3. He asks staff to speak to him ___.
4. The student will ask the ___ to explain the plan.
5. The student avoids presenting uncertainty as something ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Patient: Does this change mean there is nothing more you can do for me? Feldsher: Your care continues. I would like to understand what matters most to you today. Patient: I am worried about discomfort and about my wife not understanding the plan. Feldsher: Would you like her to join the next discussion? Patient: Yes, but please speak to me directly too. Feldsher: Of course. I will ask the clinician to explain the plan and your questions about comfort. Patient: Can you tell me exactly what will happen? Feldsher: I do not want to give you an uncertain answer as if it were definite. Let us bring that question to the clinician.

speaking.roleA: Student A: Student feldsher
speaking.roleB: Student B: Patient or professional observer
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.

practice a: 1. involve 2. Could I ask the clinician? 3. Who would you like to involve in the discussion? 4. I can hear that you are worried. What concerns you most? 5. What would help you feel more comfortable right now?

culture / revision: “What reliable evidence supports the claimed benefit and safety?” The label alone is insufficient to recommend a practice or replace the agreed care plan.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Reported requests; could, would prefer and respectful clarification

Use asked for + noun to report a request and asked whether + clause to report a question. Would prefer expresses a choice without pressure. In a handover, attribute requests accurately and share only relevant information through the appropriate care process.

reading.title: Reading
body: Listening Without a Timetable
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

A fictional relative, Ms Akbarova, has just attended a meeting after her father’s death. She asks for a quiet place and says that she cannot remember all the information she has been given. The student offers a short written summary and asks whether she would like a support person contacted. Ms Akbarova prefers to telephone her cousin herself.

Grief can involve different feelings and does not require everyone to react in the same way or at the same pace. [R25] The student therefore does not tell her how she ought to feel. He uses a simple condolence, allows a pause and checks which practical question matters first.
questions: 1. What two forms of support does Ms Akbarova request or accept?
2. Whom does she want to contact herself?
3. Why should the student avoid saying how she ought to feel?
4. What information belongs in the handover?
5. Why should service availability be checked before a promise is made?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The relative would like a written ___.
2. She would prefer a ___ place.
3. She wants to call her ___ herself.
4. The student will check the appropriate ___.
5. They will first focus on the chosen ___ question.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Relative: I cannot remember everything that was explained. Feldsher: I am sorry for your loss. Would a short written summary help? Relative: Yes, and I would prefer a quiet place while I read it. Feldsher: Would you like someone contacted? Relative: I will call my sister myself. Could you tell me whom to ask if I have another question? Feldsher: I will check the appropriate contact and write it down for you. Relative: Thank you. I do not feel ready to discuss everything now. Feldsher: That is all right. We can focus on the practical question you have chosen.

speaking.roleB: Student B: Relative or professional observer

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Zero and first conditionals; obligation and prohibition

Use the zero conditional for general relationships: if + present, present. Use the first conditional for a possible future situation: if + present, will + base verb. Must expresses an obligation in the given procedure; must not expresses a prohibition.

formula.label: Structure
formula.text: Example — Meaning / use

formula.label: Zero conditional

formula.label: First conditional
formula.text: If supplies are missing, I will report the problem. — Agree a future response.

formula.label: Obligation
formula.text: Staff must follow the relevant hand-hygiene procedure. — State an agreed requirement.

practice: Practice A. Complete, choose or rewrite
1. Complete: If supplies are missing, I ___ report it. (will / would)
2. Complete: If contaminated hands touch a surface, microorganisms can ___. (spread / spreads)

4. Choose: Gloves ___ replace hand hygiene. (do not / always)

reading.title: Reading
body: A Glove Is Not a Complete Hygiene Plan
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

In a fictional ward sequence, a student removes gloves after a care task and immediately reaches for a shared computer keyboard. Her partner pauses the exercise and asks which step has been missed. They identify hand hygiene after glove removal as the missing action.

Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. Healthcare workers should clean their hands after removing gloves; soap and water are needed when hands are visibly soiled, and the appropriate method also depends on the clinical situation and local precautions. [R20] The class does not reduce every hygiene decision to a single product.
questions: 1. What action is missing after glove removal?
2. Which shared item does the student reach for?
3. Do gloves replace hand hygiene?
4. Which method is needed when hands are visibly soiled?
5. How do the pupils propose responding to an empty dispenser?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. Before touching shared notes, the student must clean the ___.
2. An empty dispenser is a missing ___.
3. The student will follow the approved local ___.
4. Visible soiling requires soap and ___.
5. Feedback should refer to the ___ rather than criticise the person.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Observer: In this scenario, you have removed the gloves. What happens before you touch the shared notes? Student: I need to clean my hands. Observer: What if the dispenser is empty? Student: I will report the missing supply and follow the approved local process for obtaining the appropriate hand-hygiene materials. Observer: Do gloves replace hand hygiene? Student: No. If hands are visibly soiled, soap and water are needed. Observer: How will you mention the lapse to a colleague? Student: I will identify the missing step respectfully and refer to the procedure, rather than criticise the person.

speaking.outcome: Communication outcome: Produce a corrected sequence and a non-blaming incident-prevention message.
speaking.roleA: Review your partner’s fictional task sequence. Identify one hand-hygiene lapse and one missing-supply issue. Give a respectful correction and agree a first-conditional response.
speaking.roleB: Your scenario has two gaps: moving from glove removal to shared paperwork, and an empty dispenser. Ask why gloves are not enough and how to report the supply problem without concealing the lapse.
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.
Communication outcome: Produce a corrected sequence and a non-blaming incident-prevention message.
Peer observation
Culture project: Homeopathy

practice a: 1. will 2. spread 3. If gloves are removed, I will clean my hands. 4. do not 5. If the dispenser is empty, I will report it.
reading 1–5: 1. Hand hygiene. 2. A computer keyboard. 3. No. 4. Soap and water, following the relevant procedure. 5. Report it to the responsible staff member and record the issue as appropriate.

culture / revision: Hand hygiene remains part of infection prevention. Interest in homeopathy does not justify omitting it, and claims about clinical benefit need reliable evidence.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Passive voice; sequencing and must / must not

Use sequencing words to explain an authorised process, not to invent one. Passive voice highlights the item: “The status is checked.” Must not expresses a prohibited action in the simulation. Exact products, times and methods must come from the applicable instructions.

formula.text: Example — Meaning / use

formula.label: Sequence
formula.text: First, the instructions are consulted; then the status is verified. — Order communication checks.

formula.label: Prohibition
formula.text: An uncertain device must not be assumed ready for use. — Prevent an unsupported assumption.

reading.title: Reading
body: The Status Label Matters
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

During a fictional equipment handover, a student sees an endoscope with an unclear processing label. Another student suggests that a quick wipe should be enough because the device looks clean. The group pauses the scenario. They distinguish visible cleanliness from confirmation that the required processing has been completed.

Cleaning and disinfection are different processes. Reusable endoscopes require appropriate reprocessing by trained staff using the applicable device instructions and approved procedures; an improvised wipe does not establish readiness. [R21] The language task does not teach chemical preparation or endoscope reprocessing.
questions: 1. What is unclear in the case?
2. Why is a quick wipe not enough to establish readiness?
3. Who should perform the approved reprocessing?
4. What three facts are reported?
5. What should the students not choose independently?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The device in the handover is an ___.
2. The processing ___ is unclear.
3. Its readiness has not been ___.
4. The processing ___ needs checking.
5. Contact time must come from the applicable ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Student: The endoscope is here, but the processing label is unclear. Supervisor: Has its status been confirmed? Student: No. I have not assumed that it is ready because it looks clean. Supervisor: What information should be checked? Student: The relevant instructions and the processing record should be checked by the responsible staff. Supervisor: Will you choose a contact time yourself? Student: No. That must come from the applicable product and device instructions. Supervisor: Good. Record the uncertainty and ask for verification before the equipment is used.

speaking.outcome: Communication outcome: Deliver a device-status handover containing two passives and an explicit request for verification.
speaking.roleA: Student A: Student feldsher
speaking.roleB: Student B: Responsible colleague
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.

Culture project: Sound therapy

The device is present; the label is unclear; its status is unverified. 5. A chemical, contact time or improvised processing method.

culture / revision: A comfort preference concerns the environment. Equipment readiness must be established through the appropriate processing records and instructions, not a claim about sound.

vocabulary.definition: A person’s experience of psychological and emotional functioning.
Emotional discomfort or suffering that a person experiences.
Apprehension or worry, which may occur in many situations.
A state of feeling sad or emotionally low.
Difficulty carrying out everyday activities because of a problem.
An action or approach used to manage a difficult situation.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Open questions; reflective statements and cautious modals

Open questions invite more than yes/no answers. Reflective statements check meaning: “It sounds as though…” does not establish a diagnosis. Use might/could to offer a possibility and ask permission before moving to the next topic.

formula.label: Structure
formula.text: Example — Meaning / use

formula.label: Open question
formula.text: What is worrying you most about the appointment? — Invite a personal account.

formula.label: Reflection
formula.text: It sounds as though not knowing the process is difficult. — Check the meaning you have heard.

formula.label: Offer
formula.text: Would it help to ask the clinician to explain it? — Offer support without making assumptions.

practice: Practice A. Complete, choose or rewrite
1. Correct: “What you are worried about?”
2. Complete: It sounds ___ though the uncertainty is difficult.
3. Complete: Would it help to ___ the procedure? (explain / explaining)
4. Replace the label: “You are a difficult patient.”

reading.title: Reading
body: Anxiety Before a Procedure Is a Concern to Explore
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

A fictional patient waiting for an endoscopy says, “I cannot concentrate because I do not understand what will happen.” The student does not call the patient uncooperative or assume a psychiatric diagnosis. She asks what is most worrying and how long the concern has been affecting daily life.

Mental health includes more than the absence of a diagnosed condition, and support should consider the person’s circumstances and needs. [R22] In this case, the immediate concern is uncertainty about the procedure. The student explains that an endoscope is an instrument with a camera used to look inside the body, then asks the clinical team to clarify the specific procedure and preparation instructions. [R27]
questions: 1. What is the patient’s stated concern?
2. Which label does the student avoid?
3. What is an endoscope described as?
4. Who should clarify the specific procedure and preparation?
5. Does the encounter establish or exclude a mental-health diagnosis?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The main concern is not understanding the ___.
2. The patient has been sleeping ___.
3. The patient wants fewer technical ___.
4. The student will ask the ___ to explain the process.
5. The patient would like to ask some ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Feldsher: What is worrying you most about today’s appointment? Patient: I do not understand the procedure, and I have been sleeping poorly. Feldsher: It sounds as though the uncertainty is difficult. Have I understood correctly? Patient: Yes. I would like someone to explain it without technical words. Feldsher: Would it help if I asked the clinician to discuss the process with you? Patient: Yes, and I would like to ask a few questions. Feldsher: I will record that request. We can also tell the team that your sleep has been affected, so they can discuss any further support you need.

speaking.outcome: Communication outcome: Agree one communication adjustment and a factual request for professional follow-up.
speaking.roleA: Ask about the patient’s concern, its daily impact and the preferred explanation. Use one reflection and an open question. Do not label the patient or explain preparation details you have not been given.
speaking.roleB: You are anxious about an upcoming endoscopy because the leaflet uses unfamiliar words. You want a plain explanation and time to ask questions. You do not want anxiety automatically treated as a psychiatric diagnosis.
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.
Communication outcome: Agree one communication adjustment and a factual request for professional follow-up.
Peer observation
Revision

A structured professional review of mental state, needs and functioning.
A professional evaluation of possible harm and relevant circumstances.
Information suggesting that urgent action may be needed to keep someone safe.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Cumulative review: reported speech, polite requests, modals and conditionals

Review attributed reports, polite requests and conditional action plans. Use must/must not for the stated safety requirements. Confidentiality is important, but the student must not promise secrecy when information needs to be shared with the responsible team to address a safety concern.

formula.text: Example — Meaning / use

formula.label: Polite escalation
formula.text: Could you assess this patient urgently? — Make the requested action explicit.

formula.label: Conditional plan

practice: Practice A. Complete, choose or rewrite — 5 marks
1. Complete: She said ___ she did not feel safe alone.
2. Correct: “Could you to review this concern?”
3. Complete: If the situation changes, I ___ update the clinician. (will / would)
4. Choose: A student ___ promise absolute secrecy about an immediate safety concern. (must not / should always)

reading.title: Reading — 5 marks
body: A Concern That Must Be Passed On
Original teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

In a fictional outpatient encounter, Ms Hamidova says that she has been sleeping poorly and is struggling with a persistent pain problem. While the student listens, she adds, “I do not feel safe on my own today.” The student does not dismiss the statement, promise secrecy or infer a diagnosis from it.

He responds calmly, asks a direct, respectful question about immediate safety, including whether she is thinking of harming herself or ending her life, and contacts the responsible clinician urgently. Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not create such thoughts; listening and helping the person connect with support are important actions. [R23] This classroom exchange is not a full clinical risk assessment.
questions: 1. What statement raises the immediate safety concern?
2. Name one response the student avoids.
3. Whom does the student contact urgently?
4. What three elements are separated in the handover?
5. What must not delay the immediate response?

listening.title: Listening — 5 marks
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The student requests an ___ review.
2. The patient does not feel safe ___.
3. The concern is shared with the responsible ___.

reading.title: Reading
body: Different Roles, One Appointment
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

At a fictional diagnostic centre, Ms Aliyeva arrives for a resting ECG. The receptionist confirms her booking and directs her to the waiting area. A nurse checks what support she needs. The trained practitioner who performs the recording introduces himself and explains his role. An ECG records the heart’s electrical activity; spirometry, offered elsewhere in the centre, assesses lung function through breathing measurements. [R31, R32]

Ms Aliyeva asks whether the appointment means that she has heart disease. The student does not infer a diagnosis from the referral. She explains who will discuss the clinical interpretation and checks the agreed route for communicating results. In this simulated service, the referring clinician will contact the patient after the report has been reviewed.

2. Who confirms the booking?
3. What does an ECG record?
4. Who will contact the patient in this fictional service?
5. Why is the referral alone insufficient to establish a diagnosis?

directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.

Receptionist: Good morning. Your ECG appointment is at ten thirty. I will confirm your booking, then direct you to the waiting area. Patient: Will you explain what the result means? Receptionist: The practitioner will explain the recording process. In this service, the referring clinician will discuss the reviewed result. Patient: So the person who books the test is not necessarily the person who interprets it? Receptionist: That is correct. Student: I will check that the next step is clear and help you find the correct room. Patient: Thank you. I was unsure whom to ask.

reading.title: Reading
body: A Handover That Makes the Next Step Clear
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

During a fictional shift change, a practitioner tells the incoming student that an ECG has been recorded but has not yet been reviewed. The patient has asked when to expect an explanation. A vague handover would say, “The test is finished.” A more useful message separates the completed recording from the pending interpretation.

SBAR organises a message around situation, background, assessment and recommendation or request. A check-back allows the receiver to repeat the message for confirmation. [R34, R35] These communication tools help the class practise structure; they do not authorise a student to supply an independent clinical assessment.

2. Which part remains pending?
3. What does the R in SBAR stand for?

directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.

Practitioner: The recording is complete, but the review is pending. The patient asked when the report would be available. Student: Has anyone promised a time? Practitioner: No. Please contact the supervisor now and confirm the reporting pathway. Student: I will use a check-back: I should contact the supervisor now, explain that the report is pending and ask who will update the patient. Is that correct? Practitioner: Yes. Do not describe the result as normal or abnormal before the appropriate review. Student: Understood. I will record the agreed action, not an assumed result.

notes: Must, must not, should and can; professional boundaries

Use must for a clear obligation, must not for a prohibition, should for advice and can for ability or permitted action. These examples use classroom role boundaries. They do not define the legal nursing scope in Uzbekistan.

reading.title: Reading
body: Knowing When to Ask for Support
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

In a fictional diagnostic department, a student accompanies a nurse during a patient visit. The patient asks the student to explain a complex tracing. The student has learned the vocabulary but has not been trained to interpret the recording. She answers, “I can explain what the appointment involves, but I must ask the qualified practitioner about the result.”

As an international professional example, the UK Nursing and Midwifery Council’s Code emphasises person-centred care, effective practice, safety and professional trust. It also requires professionals to recognise the limits of their competence. [R33] This source illustrates professional language; it is not presented as Uzbek regulation.
questions: 1. What does the patient ask the student to explain?
2. Why does the student seek support?
3. Which professional organisation is used as an international example?
4. What does the student document?
5. Why is a clear professional boundary helpful rather than unhelpful?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The student has not been trained to interpret the ___.
2. She can explain the ___ process.
3. The qualified ___ will discuss the result.
4. The patient’s question should be ___.
5. The student must protect the patient’s ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Nurse: What did the patient ask? Student: He asked me to interpret the tracing, but I have not been trained to do that. Nurse: What can you explain? Student: I can explain the appointment process and help him contact the qualified practitioner. Nurse: Exactly. The practitioner will discuss the result. The patient’s question should also be documented. Student: May I observe that discussion with permission? Nurse: Yes, when the patient agrees and the practitioner can supervise you. Student: I must also protect the patient’s confidentiality. Nurse: Correct. Asking for support is part of responsible learning.

Could you and would you like make requests and offers more respectful. Avoid negative assumptions such as “You understood that, didn’t you?” Teach-back checks the explanation, not the patient’s intelligence. Use a reflective statement before another question.

reading.title: Reading
body: Checking the Explanation, Not Testing the Patient
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

Before a fictional ambulatory ECG appointment, Mr Ergashev says that the leaflet contains too many unfamiliar words. The nurse does not simply read it more loudly. She asks whether he would prefer a slower verbal explanation, written notes or language support. An ambulatory ECG monitor records the heart’s electrical activity over the period specified by the clinical team. [R37]

In this simulated service, the nurse explains the agreed return arrangement and asks the patient to describe the plan in his own words. Teach-back is a way to check whether an explanation has been communicated clearly. [R38] It should not feel like an examination.
questions: 1. What makes the leaflet difficult for Mr Ergashev?
2. Name two communication options the nurse offers.
3. What does an ambulatory ECG monitor record?
4. Which part of the plan needs clarification?
5. Why does the nurse avoid inventing device instructions?

directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.

3. The return time is ___ in the morning.
4. The patient first remembers the wrong ___.
5. The nurse checks the written ___.

Nurse: Would you like a written or spoken explanation? Patient: A spoken explanation, please. Nurse: Your booking says to return this monitor on Thursday at nine in the morning. We will use your own service instructions for any other details. To check that I explained the return clearly, could you tell me the plan? Patient: I should come back on Tuesday at nine. Nurse: Thank you. I may not have made the day clear. Let us check the written booking together: Thursday at nine. Patient: Thursday, not Tuesday. Nurse: Exactly. What else would you like us to clarify?

reading.title: Reading
body: Finding the Correct Room
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

Fictional directory: on the ground floor, reception is immediately inside the main entrance. The waiting area is to the left of reception. The lift is at the end of the corridor. On the first floor, the ECG room is opposite the lift, while the lung-function room is next to the ECG room.

Mr Saidov arrives with an appointment letter for lung-function testing. He tells the student that climbing stairs is difficult for him. The student confirms the destination and offers the lift route. She does not assume that a short distance is manageable for every patient. She asks whether he would like assistance and checks who can provide it in this simulated service.
questions: 1. Where is reception?
2. What is to the left of reception?
3. Where is the ECG room relative to the lift?
4. Which room does Mr Saidov actually need?
5. Why does the student offer a lift route?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.

2. The room is on the ___ floor.
3. The patient should use the ___.
4. The ECG room is ___ the lift.

Patient: Could you help me find the lung-function room? Student: Certainly. Your letter confirms the first floor. Would the lift be more suitable for you? Patient: Yes, I cannot manage the stairs comfortably. Student: Go along this corridor to the lift. On the first floor, the ECG room is opposite the lift. The lung-function room is next to the ECG room. Patient: So I should wait in the ECG room? Student: Not quite. Please go to the lung-function room next door. Would you like me to ask an escort to help you? Patient: Yes, please.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: First conditional; explaining delays and arrangements

Use if + present simple, will + base verb for a possible future arrangement. Do not normally put will in the if-clause. A conditional plan should name an action and a responsible role, not promise an unknown clinical outcome.

reading.title: Reading
body: An Update Without an Empty Promise
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

At a fictional hospital, the lung-function room cannot be used at the scheduled time. The receptionist knows that there is a delay but has not received a new start time. She says, “The clinical team is confirming the arrangement. I will update you when they respond.” She does not promise that the wait will last only five minutes.

Ms Usmonova explains that her transport is due at noon and that she cannot walk a long distance. The student records both constraints and contacts the responsible team. If another room is offered, the team will check that the route is suitable before asking her to move.
questions: 1. What information is initially unconfirmed?
2. Which two practical constraints does Ms Usmonova report?
3. What will happen before she is asked to move?
4. Who confirms the alternative room?
5. Why should the student avoid a five-minute promise?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The appointment has been ___.
2. The new start ___ is not confirmed.
3. Transport is booked for ___.
4. The patient needs a ___-floor room.
5. The student will update the patient after speaking to the ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Receptionist: Your appointment has been delayed. The new start time is not confirmed yet. Patient: My transport is booked for noon, and I need a ground-floor room. Student: Thank you. I will tell the supervisor about both points. If the room changes, we will confirm an accessible route before asking you to move. Patient: Should I go upstairs now? Student: Please remain at reception while I check. I will update you after speaking to the supervisor. Patient: So you are checking the room and the timing, not guaranteeing a particular start? Student: Exactly.

prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.

reading.title: Reading
body: An Admission Record with Honest Gaps
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

During a fictional admission, Mr Sobirov brings an ECG referral and an incomplete medicine list. The student asks him to state the identifying details required by the service, then checks the paperwork. She explains why she is asking questions and uses a private space for personal information.

Mr Sobirov remembers taking a morning tablet but cannot name it. He also reports that an adhesive dressing previously caused a rash. The student records the report and asks what happened, rather than deciding that every adhesive is unsuitable. Medication reconciliation involves checking the current medicine information and resolving discrepancies; missing details should be clarified, not guessed. [R39]
questions: 1. Which two documents does Mr Sobirov bring?
2. Which medicine detail is missing?
3. What reaction does he report?
4. Why should the student not write “no allergies”?
5. Who reviews relevant precautions before the appointment proceeds?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.

2. The medicine is usually taken in the ___.
3. Its ___ is not remembered.
4. An adhesive dressing caused a ___.
5. The student will ask the ___ to review the information.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Student: Have you ever had an ECG? Patient: Yes, once. Student: Which medicines are you currently taking? Patient: One tablet in the morning, but I cannot remember its name. Student: I will record that the name is unverified and ask how we can confirm it. Have you ever had a reaction to a medicine or adhesive? Patient: An adhesive dressing gave me a rash last year. Student: Thank you. I will record your description and ask the supervisor to review the information. I will not make a treatment decision from this brief interview. Patient: Can I bring the labelled packaging? Student: I will confirm the service’s process with you.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language

reading.title: Reading
body: Reported Is Not the Same as Resolved
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

In a fictional admission exercise, the appointment list gives a birth year of 1974, while the referral gives 1976. The patient states 1976. The student notices the difference before linking the diagnostic recording to a record. She tells the patient, “There is a discrepancy in the paperwork. I will ask the responsible colleague to check it.”

The student does not choose a year simply because it appears twice. She reports the conflicting sources and follows the simulated service’s verification process. A structured handover should include uncertainty and a plan for the next action. [R36]
questions: 1. Which two birth years conflict?
2. What year does the patient state?
3. Why does the student avoid deciding by majority?
4. Who makes the documented amendment?
5. What is the difference between reported and resolved?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The discrepancy concerns the date of ___.
2. It appears on the referral and the appointment ___.
3. The referral has been ___, but the mismatch remains.
4. The student will contact the ___.
5. The record has not yet been ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Student: I need to report a discrepancy in the date of birth. The referral and the appointment list do not match. Supervisor: Has the referral been checked? Student: Yes, it has been checked, but the mismatch remains. I have not selected a date by assumption. Supervisor: What will you do next? Student: I will contact the supervisor responsible for verification and explain both sources. Supervisor: Has the record already been corrected? Student: No. The concern has been reported, but the record has not yet been corrected. Patient: Thank you for explaining why the check is needed.

reading.title: Reading
body: Clear Information When Time Matters
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

In a fictional diagnostic waiting area, a man is speaking to reception when he suddenly collapses. A student immediately alerts the responsible clinical team through the local emergency process. She gives the exact location, describes what she witnessed and answers the team’s questions. She does not call the event “just a faint” or continue a routine appointment.

Sudden collapse with failure to recover or other serious features requires urgent help; symptoms such as chest pain can also require emergency assessment. [R40, R41] This English lesson rehearses a call for help, not clinical assessment or resuscitation skills. Actual actions must follow current training, emergency instructions and local protocols.
questions: 1. What was the man doing before he collapsed?
2. What does the student do immediately?
3. Why should she avoid calling it “just a faint”?
4. Which details should a call for help include?
5. How is a witness account different from an assumed explanation?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The event happened outside ECG Room ___.
2. The patient was ___ before he fell.
3. The student is requesting the emergency ___.
4. The ___ is still unknown.
5. The student reports only what she ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Student: I need the emergency team outside ECG Room Two now. An adult was speaking to reception when he fell. I am reporting what I witnessed; the cause is still unknown. Coordinator: Confirm the location. Student: Outside ECG Room Two, on the ground floor beside reception. Coordinator: The team is being contacted. Follow the local emergency instructions and tell the clinical responder what you observed. Student: Understood. I will not label this as a simple faint or delay the call to complete paperwork. Coordinator: Keep the information clear and report any further observation to the responder.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Open questions; past simple and present perfect

Use the past simple for a completed onset event: “It began yesterday.” Use the present perfect for a symptom continuing now: “It has lasted since yesterday.” Use since with a starting point and for with a period. Avoid leading questions.

reading.title: Reading
body: A Pain History, Not a Diagnosis
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

During a simulated diagnostic intake interview, Mr Karimov describes an ache in his right shoulder. It began on Monday after he carried a heavy bag. He has had discomfort for two days, and it becomes worse when he reaches upwards. He rates it as six out of ten. The student diagnostic practitioner asks whether the pain spreads elsewhere rather than assuming that it remains in one place. Mr Karimov says that it does not spread and that he slept poorly last night.

The student records the patient’s own description, the onset, the severity and the effect on sleep. She also asks what he has already tried, but does not select a medicine independently. She alerts the responsible clinician before any routine investigation continues, so the concern can be assessed. Pain assessment should consider the person’s experience and daily functioning, not only a number on a scale. [R1]
questions: 1. Where is the reported pain?
2. What happened before the pain began?
3. Which everyday activity has been affected?
4. Find a present-perfect structure in the text.
5. Why is “The cause has not yet been established” useful?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The pain is in the left ___.
2. It began after a long ___.
3. It has lasted for about ___ hours.
4. The current rating is ___ out of ten.
5. The activity that makes it worse is ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Practitioner: Could you tell me where the pain is? Patient: It is in my left knee. Practitioner: When did it begin? Patient: It began yesterday, after a long journey. It has lasted for about twenty hours. Practitioner: Does it spread anywhere? Patient: No. It stays in my knee. Walking makes it worse. Practitioner: How severe is it now? Patient: Five out of ten. I also slept badly. Practitioner: Thank you. I will record your description and ask my supervisor to assess you. Could you confirm that walking makes it worse? Patient: Yes, that is correct.

speaking.outcome: Communication outcome: Produce a four-sentence pain handover containing one past-simple and one present-perfect structure.
speaking.roleA: Ask about site, onset, duration, severity, spread and daily functioning. You have no diagnosis. Summarise what the patient reports and identify one question for your supervisor.
speaking.roleB: Your lower back began aching two days ago after a long bus journey. You rate it four out of ten; sitting for a long time makes it worse. It does not spread. You want to know why the cause is still uncertain.
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.
Communication outcome: Produce a four-sentence pain handover containing one past-simple and one present-perfect structure.

reading.title: Reading — 10 marks
body: Support Based on the Person, Not the Age
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

Mrs Akhmedova, aged 74 in this fictional case, arrives for a scheduled ECG. She manages her medicines herself and wants staff to speak directly to her. She uses a walking stick and finds long corridors tiring. She also hears more easily when the speaker faces her and background noise is reduced. Her daughter has accompanied her, but Mrs Akhmedova would like to answer the questions first.

The student asks which support would be useful and records these preferences. She checks an accessible route and offers the daughter a role in the conversation only with Mrs Akhmedova’s agreement. She does not infer memory impairment from the patient’s age.
questions: 1. Which investigation is planned?
2. What makes the corridor difficult for Mrs Akhmedova?
3. Which two changes help her hear the explanation?
4. How does she want the interview to begin?
5. Why would it be wrong to infer memory impairment from age alone?

listening.title: Listening — 10 marks
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient usually walks with a ___.
2. He finds long ___ tiring.
3. He would like the nurse to speak more ___.
4. He wants to answer the ___ himself.
5. His ___ may add information with his agreement.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Nurse: What support would make today’s visit easier? Patient: I usually walk with a stick, and long corridors are tiring. Nurse: Would you like us to check a suitable route and offer assistance? Patient: Yes. Could you also speak more slowly? I want to answer the questions myself. Nurse: Of course. Would you like your daughter to add anything afterwards? Patient: Yes, with my agreement. Nurse: Thank you. I will record that you prefer to answer first, that slower speech helps and that you need support with the walking distance. Patient: That is a clear summary.

reading.title: Reading
body: Not Simply “Old Age”
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

During a fictional handover before a diagnostic appointment, a relative says that Mr Ahmedov normally recognises staff and follows conversations. This morning he has become unusually distracted and does not know where he is. The student asks when he was last behaving as usual and whether the change has varied during the day. She records the relative’s account separately from what she has observed.

Dementia is not an inevitable part of ageing. A recent change developing over hours or days, especially with fluctuation, may indicate delirium and needs prompt clinical assessment. [R5, R6] The student does not label the patient as having dementia or decide the cause of the confusion.
questions: 1. What is Mr Ahmedov’s usual functioning according to the relative?
2. When did the new change begin?
3. Which current observation is included in the handover?
4. Why should the student avoid simply writing “old age”?
5. What is the appropriate next step in the case?

4. The family history comes from her ___.

Student: I need to report a new change in Mrs Rasulova’s attention. Supervisor: What is her usual functioning? Student: Her son says that she usually follows a conversation. She spoke clearly last night. Since this morning, she has been distracted and has asked repeatedly where she is. Supervisor: Is this a confirmed diagnosis? Student: No. I am reporting a change from her baseline and requesting prompt assessment. Supervisor: Thank you. Please record when it began and who provided the history. Student: Her son provided the history, and I have also observed difficulty maintaining attention.

body: Progress Can Include Better Function
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

Ms Yuldasheva has been living with recurring back pain for eight months. She wants to attend her daughter’s school meeting but worries about sitting for a long time. At a fictional diagnostic review, the student asks what matters most to her and how pain has been affecting sleep and activity. Ms Yuldasheva has been keeping a diary and wants the team to consider it at her next review.

Chronic pain lasts or recurs for more than three months. A person-centred assessment considers its effects, priorities and wider circumstances. [R1] In this fictional case, the team will discuss an individual plan rather than promise that one intervention will remove every symptom.
questions: 1. How long has Ms Yuldasheva had recurring pain?
2. What activity matters to her?
3. What has she been keeping?
4. Why is the goal functional rather than a promise of cure?

Practitioner: What else should the team know? Patient: My sleep has been disturbed. Practitioner: I will record both concerns. Although we cannot promise immediate relief, we can make sure your priorities are clear. Patient: Please also mention that gardening is important to me.

reading.title: Reading
body: What Does a Longer Life Mean to the Patient?
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

At a fictional preventive-care discussion linked to a diagnostic follow-up, Mr Nurmatov says that a long life matters to him because he wants to remain involved with his family. He is less interested in a “secret remedy” than in being able to visit friends and manage everyday activities. The student asks which routine he would like to discuss with his clinician.

Healthy ageing concerns functional ability and well-being, not only the absence of illness. [R9] Physical activity, sleep and social participation are relevant areas for discussion, but individual needs and circumstances vary. [R10] The student does not promise a particular lifespan or recommend the same screening schedule to everyone.
questions: 1. Why does a long life matter to Mr Nurmatov?
2. What does healthy ageing concern besides illness?
3. How many questions does he prepare?
4. Find an infinitive expressing purpose.
5. Why is one screening schedule not given to everybody?

4. The patient will write down ___.

Patient: I could plan a weekly meeting at a place I can reach. Practitioner: Would you like to discuss activity and preventive care at your next appointment? Patient: Yes. I will write down my questions to remember them. Practitioner: Good. The aim is a realistic plan, not a promise about how long anyone will live. Patient: My first goal is to keep seeing my friends regularly.

notes: Past simple and past perfect; cautious historical interpretation

Use past simple for the main historical sequence and had + past participle for an earlier event. Do not use past perfect merely to make a sentence sound academic. Separate a documented event from a claim about someone’s motives.

formula.label: Structure
formula.text: Example — Meaning / use

formula.label: Past simple
formula.text: The investigators examined the evidence. — Describe a historical event.

formula.label: Past perfect
formula.text: She had worked as a cook before the investigation. — Locate an earlier event.

formula.label: Source attribution
formula.text: The museum account describes her as a carrier. — Identify the source of a historical statement.

practice: Practice A. Complete, choose or rewrite
1. Complete: By the time the interview began, the team had ___ the records. (check / checked)
2. Choose the main event: The investigators (arrived / had arriving) in the morning.
3. Correct: “She had work as a cook.”
4. Combine: “The team collected the samples. Later, the laboratory examined them.” Use after and past perfect.

reading.title: Reading
body: A Historical Case and a Modern Communication Lesson
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

Mary Mallon, often called “Typhoid Mary”, worked as a cook in the New York City area in the early twentieth century. The CDC Museum describes her as a healthy carrier of Salmonella Typhi who spread infection without experiencing the illness herself. [R13] Her story illustrates why the absence of symptoms does not always mean that a person cannot transmit an infection.

Typhoid can spread through food or water contaminated with Salmonella Typhi. Safe water, sanitation and hygiene among food handlers are important in prevention. [R11, R42] These facts do not justify blaming everyone who develops an infection or assuming that a person knew they were infectious.
questions: 1. What work did Mary Mallon do?
2. Which feature made the case important for understanding transmission?
3. Name two prevention measures in the text.
4. Why should students avoid assuming a person’s motives?
5. Which part of the passage is a fictional classroom scenario?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient reports feeling ___.
2. The request concerns a stool ___.
3. The clinician will explain the purpose of the ___.
4. A result must not be ___.
5. The student will record the patient’s ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Patient: I feel well. Why has the team asked me to discuss a stool specimen? Student: I understand your question. In some infections, a person can carry a pathogen without obvious symptoms. That does not tell us your individual result. Patient: Does the request mean that I definitely carry the bacterium? Student: No. The clinician will explain the purpose of the investigation and the relevant instructions. A result must not be assumed. Patient: I would like the explanation before agreeing to the next step. Student: I will record your request and ask the clinician to speak with you.

speaking.outcome: Communication outcome: Explain a general transmission concept while clearly separating it from an unconfirmed individual result.
speaking.roleA: Explain the meaning of asymptomatic carriage in general terms. You have no result for this patient. Ask the clinician to clarify the requested investigation and document the concern.
speaking.roleB: You feel well and believe that a test request must mean a confirmed diagnosis. Ask why the test has been requested and challenge a blaming label.
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.
Communication outcome: Explain a general transmission concept while clearly separating it from an unconfirmed individual result.

practice a: 1. checked. 2. arrived. 3. She had worked as a cook. 4. After the team had collected the samples, the laboratory examined them. 5. “The source records what happened; it does not establish what the person intended.”

culture / revision: “What did the particular historical text say about cleanliness?” “What evidence would support a comparison with modern prevention?” Do not invent a historical claim.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Present simple; relative clauses for structure and function

Use the present simple for general functions and check singular/plural agreement. Relative clauses add identifying information: “cells that carry oxygen”. Use academic terms with a plain-English explanation when speaking to a patient.

formula.text: Example — Meaning / use

formula.label: Relative clause
formula.text: Platelets are fragments that contribute to clotting. — Connect a component and its function.

practice: Practice A. Complete, choose or rewrite
1. Complete: Red blood cells ___ oxygen. (carry / carries)
2. Complete: Plasma ___ dissolved substances. (carry / carries)
3. Complete: Haemoglobin is a protein ___ carries oxygen. (that / who)
4. Correct: “White blood cells helps defend the body.”

reading.title: Reading
body: Explaining a Familiar Word Precisely
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

A student is preparing a fictional patient-information display for a diagnostic department about blood. Her first draft says only, “Blood keeps us alive.” The tutor asks her to explain the components more precisely. She writes that red blood cells carry oxygen with haemoglobin, white blood cells contribute to immune defence, platelets help clot formation and plasma carries cells and dissolved substances. [R16, R29]

The student then checks the language. “Plasma carry” becomes “plasma carries”, while “red cells carries” becomes “red cells carry”. She also decides to introduce “erythrocytes” only after giving the familiar phrase “red blood cells”.
questions: 1. Which protein helps red blood cells carry oxygen?
2. Which component contributes to immune defence?
3. Which component contributes to clot formation?
4. Why does the student give “red blood cells” before “erythrocytes”?
5. Does knowing the functions authorise independent diagnosis from a test?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. Another name for red blood cells is ___.
2. Their oxygen-carrying protein is ___.
3. White cells contribute to immune ___.
4. Platelets help form ___.
5. The liquid part of blood is ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Student: Red blood cells are also called erythrocytes. They carry oxygen using haemoglobin. Patient: And what do white cells do? Student: They contribute to immune defence. Platelets are cell fragments that help blood form clots. Patient: What is plasma? Student: It is the liquid part that carries blood cells and dissolved substances. Patient: Does that explain my blood-test result? Student: It explains the basic terms, but the clinician needs to interpret your particular result. Patient: So this is an explanation of functions, not my diagnosis. Student: Exactly.

speaking.roleA: Student A: Student diagnostic practitioner
speaking.roleB: Student B: Patient
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.

practice a: 1. carry 2. carries 3. that 4. White blood cells help defend the body. 5. Red blood cells carry oxygen.
reading 1–5: 1. Haemoglobin. 2. White blood cells / leucocytes. 3. Platelets. 4. To make the explanation understandable before adding the academic term. 5. No.
mini-quiz 1–6: 1. Red blood cell. 2. Haemoglobin. 3. is 4. White blood cells / leucocytes. 5. Platelets help clot formation. 6. No.
speaking: model: “Red blood cells, or erythrocytes, carry oxygen using haemoglobin. White cells contribute to defence. Platelets help clotting, while plasma is the liquid part. Your clinician will explain how your own results fit your health situation.”
culture / revision: “Which measurable effect is claimed?” “What evidence supports that effect and its safety?” A vague phrase such as “cleans the blood” is not a precise clinical explanation.

Measures intended to reduce troublesome symptoms.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Empathetic language; would like, could and open questions

Use would like to invite preferences and could to offer possibilities. Empathetic statements acknowledge feelings without claiming to know exactly how someone feels. An open question is often more useful than false reassurance.

formula.label: Structure
formula.text: Example — Meaning / use

formula.label: Preference

formula.label: Offer
formula.text: Could I ask the team to explain the comfort plan? — Offer a specific next step.

formula.label: Empathy
formula.text: That sounds difficult. What is worrying you most? — Acknowledge the concern and invite the person’s account.

practice: Practice A. Complete, choose or rewrite
1. Complete: Who would you like to ___? (involve / involving)
2. Correct: “Could I to ask the clinician?”
3. Make respectful: “Your family must hear everything.”
4. Replace false reassurance: “Everything will definitely be fine.”

reading.title: Reading
body: Care Continues When Priorities Change
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

In a fictional conversation, Mr Sobirov asks whether palliative care means that the team has stopped caring for him. The student explains that its purpose is to relieve suffering and support quality of life. Palliative care can address physical, psychological, social and spiritual concerns; it is not limited to the final hours of life. [R18]

Mr Sobirov says that his main worries are discomfort and not knowing whom to ask for information. He would like his sister to attend the next discussion, but he wants questions addressed to him first. The student records these preferences and asks the supervising clinician to explain the current care plan.
questions: 1. What misconception does Mr Sobirov express?
2. What is the main purpose of palliative care in the text?
3. Whom would he like to involve?
4. What does he want concerning how questions are asked?
5. How does the student respond to a request for an exact prognosis?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient is worried about ___.
2. He wants his ___ to understand the plan.
3. He asks staff to speak to him ___.
4. The student will ask the ___ to explain the plan.
5. The student avoids presenting uncertainty as something ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Patient: Does this change mean there is nothing more you can do for me? Practitioner: Your care continues. I would like to understand what matters most to you today. Patient: I am worried about discomfort and about my wife not understanding the plan. Practitioner: Would you like her to join the next discussion? Patient: Yes, but please speak to me directly too. Practitioner: Of course. I will ask the clinician to explain the plan and your questions about comfort. Patient: Can you tell me exactly what will happen? Practitioner: I do not want to give you an uncertain answer as if it were definite. Let us bring that question to the clinician.

speaking.roleA: Student A: Diagnostic student
speaking.roleB: Student B: Patient or professional observer
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.

She acknowledges the question and helps arrange discussion with the responsible clinician without inventing an answer.

speaking: model: “Your care continues, and I would like to understand your priorities. You want help with discomfort and your sister present. I will ask the clinician to explain the plan and address your questions without making promises I cannot support.”
culture / revision: “What reliable evidence supports the claimed benefit and safety?” The label alone is insufficient to recommend a practice or replace the agreed care plan.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Zero and first conditionals; obligation and prohibition

Use the zero conditional for general relationships: if + present, present. Use the first conditional for a possible future situation: if + present, will + base verb. Must expresses an obligation in the given procedure; must not expresses a prohibition.

formula.label: Structure
formula.text: Example — Meaning / use

formula.label: First conditional
formula.text: If supplies are missing, I will report the problem. — Agree a future response.

formula.label: Obligation
formula.text: Staff must follow the relevant hand-hygiene procedure. — State an agreed requirement.

4. Choose: Gloves ___ replace hand hygiene. (do not / always)

reading.title: Reading
body: A Glove Is Not a Complete Hygiene Plan
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

In a fictional sequence between diagnostic appointments, a student removes gloves after a care task and immediately reaches for a shared computer keyboard. Her partner pauses the exercise and asks which step has been missed. They identify hand hygiene after glove removal as the missing action.

Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. Healthcare workers should clean their hands after removing gloves; soap and water are needed when hands are visibly soiled, and the appropriate method also depends on the clinical situation and local precautions. [R20] The class does not reduce every hygiene decision to a single product.
questions: 1. What action is missing after glove removal?
2. Which shared item does the student reach for?
3. Do gloves replace hand hygiene?
4. Which method is needed when hands are visibly soiled?
5. How do the pupils propose responding to an empty dispenser?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. Before touching shared notes, the student must clean the ___.
2. An empty dispenser is a missing ___.
3. The student will follow the approved local ___.
4. Visible soiling requires soap and ___.
5. Feedback should refer to the ___ rather than criticise the person.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Observer: In this scenario, you have removed the gloves. What happens before you touch the shared notes? Student: I need to clean my hands. Observer: What if the dispenser is empty? Student: I will report the missing supply and follow the approved local process for obtaining the appropriate hand-hygiene materials. Observer: Do gloves replace hand hygiene? Student: No. If hands are visibly soiled, soap and water are needed. Observer: How will you mention the lapse to a colleague? Student: I will identify the missing step respectfully and refer to the procedure, rather than criticise the person.

speaking.outcome: Communication outcome: Produce a corrected sequence and a non-blaming incident-prevention message.
speaking.roleA: Review your partner’s fictional task sequence. Identify one hand-hygiene lapse and one missing-supply issue. Give a respectful correction and agree a first-conditional response.
speaking.roleB: Your scenario has two gaps: moving from glove removal to shared paperwork, and an empty dispenser. Ask why gloves are not enough and how to report the supply problem without concealing the lapse.
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.
Communication outcome: Produce a corrected sequence and a non-blaming incident-prevention message.
Peer observation
Culture project: Homeopathy

culture / revision: Hand hygiene remains part of infection prevention. Interest in homeopathy does not justify omitting it, and claims about clinical benefit need reliable evidence.

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Passive voice; sequencing and equipment-status language

Use is/are + past participle for a procedure description and has/have been + past participle for completed status. Sequence words clarify order, but the actual process must come from the applicable instructions. Do not use sterile as a synonym for clean.

practice: Practice A. Complete, choose or rewrite

reading.title: Reading
body: The Label Matters More Than the Appearance
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

In a fictional ECG room, a student finds reusable lead wires beside a packet of electrodes labelled for single use. The room handover does not clearly state whether the lead wires have been processed after the previous appointment. A colleague suggests using them because no dirt is visible. The student pauses and asks the responsible staff member to check the instructions and processing record.

Cleaning, disinfection and sterilisation are not interchangeable terms. Appropriate processing depends on the item, its use and the relevant instructions. [R21] An ECG accessory should not automatically be treated like every other medical device. The language exercise does not supply a chemical concentration or contact time.
questions: 1. Which item is labelled for single use?
2. Which item is reusable?
3. What information is missing?
4. Why is visible cleanliness insufficient in the case?
5. Where must the actual processing requirements come from?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The unclear status concerns the ECG lead ___.
2. The disposable items are the ___.
3. The ___ record must be checked.
4. The student must follow the manufacturer’s ___.
5. The next use should wait for ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Student: These ECG lead wires are reusable, but their processing status is unclear. The electrodes in this packet are labelled for single use. Supervisor: Has the processing record been checked? Student: Not yet. I have not assumed that the wires are ready because they look clean. Supervisor: What should determine the handling process? Student: The manufacturer’s instructions and the approved service procedure. I should not invent a concentration or contact time. Supervisor: Correct. Ask the responsible staff member to verify the status. Student: I will record the uncertainty, and the next use should wait for verification.

speaking.roleB: Student B: Responsible staff member

grammar.title: Grammar and Professional Language
notes: Reflective listening; open questions and gerund patterns

Use an open question, then a reflective statement: “What worries you most?” “It sounds as though the uncertainty is difficult.” Use -ing after avoid, consider and mind: “Would you mind explaining…?” Do not present reassurance as a guarantee.

formula.label: Structure
formula.text: Example — Meaning / use

formula.label: Avoid + -ing
formula.text: Avoid labelling the patient as uncooperative. — Describe a practice to avoid.

formula.label: Consider + -ing
formula.text: We can consider asking for a quieter space. — Discuss a possible action.

formula.label: Would you mind + -ing
formula.text: Would you mind telling me your main concern? — Make a polite request.

practice: Practice A. Complete, choose or rewrite
1. Complete: Avoid ___ a diagnosis from a brief conversation. (guess / guessing)
2. Complete: Would you mind ___ your concern? (explain / explaining)
3. Correct: “Consider to ask for a quieter space.”
4. Write an open question about a patient’s main concern.

reading.title: Reading
body: Distress Before an Investigation
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

In a fictional diagnostic waiting area, Ms Rahimova says that she has been avoiding appointments because unfamiliar procedures make her anxious. She reports poor sleep before today’s visit. The student asks what is most worrying instead of describing her as difficult. Ms Rahimova explains that she does not understand the sequence of the appointment.

Mental health is shaped by a person’s circumstances and support as well as individual experiences. One brief conversation does not establish a psychiatric diagnosis. [R22] The student also avoids assuming that any physical complaint is caused only by anxiety; clinical concerns must reach the appropriate team.
questions: 1. Why has Ms Rahimova been avoiding appointments?
2. Which daily function has been affected before the visit?
3. What is her most specific concern?
4. Name two support requests discussed.
5. Why should the student avoid assuming that all physical complaints are anxiety?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient is worried about not knowing the appointment ___.
2. The patient has been sleeping ___.
3. The student offers to ask for a ___ explanation.
4. A ___ waiting space is requested.
5. The student will record the support ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Student: What is worrying you most about today? Patient: I do not know the appointment sequence, and I have been sleeping badly. Student: It sounds as though uncertainty is making the visit difficult. Have I understood correctly? Patient: Yes. I have considered cancelling. Student: Would you mind telling me what would help you feel better informed? Patient: A clear explanation and a quieter place to wait. Student: I will ask the practitioner for a clear explanation and check whether a quieter waiting space is available. I will record both support requests. Patient: Thank you for asking rather than assuming I do not want care.

speaking.outcome: Communication outcome: Agree two support requests and a clear next contact without using stigmatising language.
speaking.roleA: Ask an open question, use a reflective statement and check understanding. You can request an explanation or a quieter setting but cannot guarantee availability or diagnose the concern.
speaking.roleB: You are anxious because you do not understand a planned investigation. You have considered cancelling and want a plain-English explanation before deciding about the next step.
prompts: Prepare from your own role card. Keep the information gap: do not show it to your partner before the exchange. Ask for clarification, agree a next step, then swap roles.
Communication outcome: Agree two support requests and a clear next contact without using stigmatising language.
Peer observation
Culture project: Sound therapy

culture / revision: “Would you prefer sound or silence while waiting?” is a preference question. It does not establish an effect on a mental-health condition.
