reading.title: Reading — 10 marks
body: A Handover That Separates Facts from Assumptions
Original or adapted teaching text. Cases are fictional; external background is cited separately.

In this fictional summative case, Mr Jalilov is waiting for a diagnostic appointment. He says, “I feel overwhelmed and have slept poorly for a week.” He asks for a quieter space and wants his sister included in the discussion, with his permission. The student observes that he pauses frequently while answering, but does not assign a diagnosis.

She asks what he means by overwhelmed and checks whether there is an immediate safety concern, using the clinical team’s process. A vague expression should be clarified rather than interpreted by assumption. If a person expresses thoughts of suicide or immediate danger, a direct, supportive response and prompt connection with appropriate help are important. [R23] Local emergency procedures, not a foreign telephone number, apply.
questions: 1. How long has poor sleep been reported?
2. Which two support requests does Mr Jalilov make?
3. What does the student directly observe?
4. Why must the handover not say that risk is absent?
5. Who should receive the request for clinical review?

listening.title: Listening — 10 marks
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation, then complete each item with a short answer. The complete script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The reported difficulty is poor ___.
2. It has lasted for one ___.
3. The patient wants his ___ involved with permission.
4. He requests a ___ space.
5. Safety status requires further ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings; do not emphasise only the answers.

Student: I am handing over Mr Jalilov’s concerns before his diagnostic appointment. He reports poor sleep for one week and says that he feels overwhelmed. Supervisor: What support has he requested? Student: He would like his sister involved with his permission and has asked for a quieter space. Supervisor: What have you directly observed? Student: He pauses frequently when answering. I have not assigned a diagnosis. Supervisor: Has immediate safety status been established? Student: No. It requires further clarification through the clinical team’s process. I am requesting your review and confirmation of who will update him. Supervisor: Thank you. Keep the reported facts separate from assumptions.

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Should and must

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: You should to ask the pharmacist.
formula.text: You should ask the pharmacist. — A modal is followed by the base verb.

formula.label: You must guess the missing detail.
formula.text: You must not guess the missing detail. — The negative expresses prohibition.

formula.label: You must not attend; it is optional.
formula.text: You do not have to attend; it is optional. — Optional does not mean prohibited.

practice: 1. Use should + base verb for advice; use must + base verb for a strong obligation in the stated workplace scenario.
2. Must not expresses prohibition. Do not have to means that something is not necessary; these meanings are different.
3. Professional responsibilities vary by setting. State the relevant scenario rule rather than inventing universal legal duties.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. Advice: The team ___ discuss unclear instructions. (should / must not)

reading.title: Reading: The Hospital Team
body: At a simulated morning handover, a nurse notices that a patient’s medicine list differs from the admission record. The pharmacist asks which medicines the patient actually uses, while the prescriber reviews the proposed treatment. Medication reconciliation helps the team identify unintended discrepancies when care changes. [R2] In this exercise, the team must record the uncertainty rather than fill the gap with a guess. A student should ask a supervisor for support when a task exceeds their role. The receptionist helps the patient reach the correct service but does not interpret the prescription. Each team member gives a brief update, identifies an unresolved question and names the person responsible for following it up. The group ends with a read-back: “The pharmacist will clarify the list; the prescriber will review the order.” Clear language makes the next action visible without blaming a colleague.
questions: 1. What discrepancy does the nurse notice?
2. Who reviews the proposed treatment?
3. Find one obligation and one piece of advice.
4. Why is the final read-back useful?
5. Replace “The receptionist must choose the medicine” with a role-appropriate sentence.

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The team must confirm which list is ___.
2. They should compare ___ lists.
3. The student must not change the prescription ___.
4. The supervisor should contact the ___.
5. The record should name the person responsible for ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Pharmacist: Before our meeting, we must confirm which medicine list is current. Nurse: The patient has brought a second list from home. Pharmacist: Thank you. We should compare the two lists and record any discrepancy. Student: May I change the prescription myself? Pharmacist: No. You must not change it independently. Ask your supervisor to contact the prescriber. Nurse: Should I document our discussion? Pharmacist: Yes, please record the unresolved question and the person responsible for follow-up. Student: So I should ask for support rather than guess. Pharmacist: Exactly. That is a useful handover.

speaking.roleA: You have a current admission list, but one medicine name is unclear. Ask the nurse for information, allocate a follow-up action and use one obligation and one recommendation.
speaking.roleB: The patient has a second list at home. A relative can bring it later. Do not invent the missing name. Ask who will clarify the discrepancy and repeat the agreed plan.
prompts: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Admission questions and clarification (supporting language)

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: What medicines you take?
formula.text: What medicines do you take? — Use auxiliary do before the subject.

formula.label: You have no allergies, right?
formula.text: Have you ever had a reaction to a medicine? — Avoid leading the patient towards an answer.

formula.label: The name is probably correct.
formula.text: Could you spell the medicine’s name? — Clarify instead of guessing.

practice: 1. Use do/does for present-simple questions: “Do you take any supplements?”
2. Use what, when and how often to obtain specific information; ask one question at a time.
3. Use clarification and read-back: “Could you spell that?” “Have I understood correctly?” These are supporting functions; the syllabus specifies no separate grammar item.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. Complete: What medicines ___ you take regularly?

reading.title: Reading: Hospital Admission
body: During a simulated admission, a pharmacy student interviews Ms Karimova. She brings two labelled medicine packets and mentions an herbal product whose name she cannot remember. The student records the confirmed names but marks the herbal product as “name not yet confirmed”. A medication history should include relevant prescribed medicines, non-prescription products and supplements. Comparing this history with the proposed hospital list can reveal discrepancies. [R2] The student asks what happened when Ms Karimova previously took an antibiotic. She describes a rash but does not know the medicine’s name. The student records her description without turning it into a new diagnosis. Before finishing, the student checks the spelling of the patient’s name and asks her to repeat the agreed next step. With her permission, a relative will bring the missing packaging. The final summary separates known information from questions that still need professional review.
questions: 1. What does Ms Karimova bring?
2. Which product cannot yet be identified?
3. Why is the phrase “name not yet confirmed” useful?
4. What previous reaction does she describe?
5. What is the agreed next step?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient has brought two medicine ___.
2. Her herbal ___ are at home.
3. The product’s name is recorded as ___.
4. The reported reaction was a ___.
5. The relative can bring the packaging this ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Student: May I check your medicine history, Ms Karimova? Patient: Yes. I have brought two packets, but my herbal drops are at home. Student: Do you know the name of the drops? Patient: No, and I do not want to guess. Student: That is helpful. I will record the name as unconfirmed. Have you had a reaction to a medicine? Patient: An antibiotic caused a rash several years ago. Student: Do you remember its name? Patient: No. Student: I will record your description for the pharmacist to review. Could your relative bring the packaging, with your permission? Patient: Yes, this afternoon.

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Describing people’s appearance

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: She is having short hair.
formula.text: She has short hair. — Use has for a physical feature.

formula.label: He wears a green jacket right now.
formula.text: He is wearing a green jacket. — Present continuous describes clothes worn now.

formula.label: That uniform proves she is the pharmacist.
formula.text: Please check her identification badge. — Appearance helps locate a person, not confirm a role.

practice: 1. Use has for features: “She has short hair.” Use is wearing for clothes being worn now.
2. Use is + adjective for a neutral description: “He is tall.” Avoid unnecessary or judgemental descriptions.
3. Use clear spatial phrases such as opposite, next to and on the first floor; read the location stated in the exercise.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. Complete: The porter ___ wearing a navy jacket.

reading.title: Reading: In and Around the Hospital
body: This fictional hospital has a reception desk beside the main entrance. The pharmacy is opposite reception, and the consultation rooms are on the first floor. A visitor is looking for the pharmacist who arranged an appointment. The receptionist says, “She has short dark hair and is wearing a blue jacket. Please check her badge when you speak to her.” The visitor repeats the route before leaving: “I go past reception, then turn left to the lift.” A porter offers an accessible route because the visitor uses a wheelchair. At the consultation room, the staff member introduces herself and follows the identification process specified for this classroom scenario. A description can help someone find a person, but the task does not treat clothing as proof of identity. Students practise concise directions while protecting privacy and avoiding comments about a person’s attractiveness, ethnicity or presumed medical condition.
questions: 1. Where is the fictional pharmacy?
2. Where are the consultation rooms?
3. Give two details used to describe the pharmacist.
4. Why does the porter offer an accessible route?
5. Why should the visitor check the badge?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The pharmacy is ___ the reception desk.
2. The visitor should take the ___.
3. The appointment is on the ___ floor.
4. The pharmacist is wearing a blue ___.
5. The visitor should check the identification ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Receptionist: Good afternoon. The pharmacy is opposite this desk. Visitor: I have an appointment with a pharmacist upstairs. Receptionist: Please take the lift to the first floor. The consultation room is next to the waiting area. Visitor: How will I recognise the pharmacist? Receptionist: She has short dark hair and is wearing a blue jacket today. Please check her identification badge and introduce yourself. Visitor: First floor, next to the waiting area. Receptionist: Correct. Our porter can show you the wheelchair-accessible route. Visitor: Thank you. Clear directions make this much easier.

speaking.roleB: You are using a wheelchair and need the upstairs pharmacist appointment. You first think the consultation room is on the ground floor. Ask for an accessible route and clarify how to identify the pharmacist.

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: A lot of, much and many

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: How much patients are waiting?
formula.text: How many patients are waiting? — Patients is a plural countable noun.

formula.label: There is many blood on the cloth.
formula.text: There is a lot of blood on the cloth. — Blood is uncountable in this context.

formula.label: We have not many time.
formula.text: We do not have much time. — Time is uncountable here.

practice: 1. Use many with plural countable nouns: many patients, many injuries.
2. Use much with uncountable nouns, especially in questions and negatives: much blood, not much time.
3. A lot of works with both types. Quantifiers do not replace precise information when a reliable measurement is available.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. How ___ patients have arrived? (much / many)

reading.title: Reading: Accidents and Emergencies
body: In a classroom emergency simulation, a visitor falls near the hospital entrance. The student sees a cut on the visitor’s arm and hears that the visitor feels dizzy. The scenario instruction is to alert the supervising clinician immediately, not to diagnose or choose a medicine. The student gives a short report: “One adult has fallen near the main entrance. There is bleeding from the arm, and the person reports dizziness.” The supervisor asks how many people are involved and whether any reliable observations are available. The student replies only with confirmed details. “A lot of blood” describes an impression, whereas an actual measurement would require a reliable method; students must not invent one. The group moves unnecessary questions to a later stage. The language goal is to distinguish observations from assumptions and communicate urgent concerns clearly while trained professionals take responsibility for assessment.
questions: 1. What two observations does the student report?
2. What is the student’s first task under the scenario instruction?
3. Why is “many blood” incorrect?
4. Should the student invent a measurement?
5. Write a one-sentence factual handover.

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The incident involves ___ adult.
2. There are a lot of ___ nearby.
3. The visitor reports feeling ___.
4. The student cannot estimate the blood ___.
5. The patient will be assessed by the trained clinical ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Supervisor: How many people are involved? Student: One adult near the main entrance. There are a lot of visitors nearby, but I have asked a colleague to guide them away from the work area. Supervisor: What have you observed? Student: There is bleeding from the arm. The visitor says they feel dizzy. I cannot estimate how much blood has been lost. Supervisor: Thank you for making that uncertainty clear. We do not have much time for unrelated questions. Student: I will give you the confirmed details and remain available. Supervisor: Good. The trained clinical team will assess the patient.

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Linking words

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: Although she has pain, but she attends class.
formula.text: Although she has pain, she attends class. — Do not add but after although.

formula.label: He stopped because he felt dizzy, therefore.
formula.text: He stopped because he felt dizzy. — Because already introduces the reason.

formula.label: The pain continues however he is resting.
formula.text: The pain continues; however, he is resting. — Separate the contrasting clauses clearly.

practice: 1. Because introduces a reason; so introduces a result between clauses.
2. Although introduces a contrast within a sentence. Do not pair although and but in the same clause structure.
3. However and therefore connect ideas across sentences or after a semicolon; punctuation helps the reader follow the relationship.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. Use because: “She cannot sleep. The pain wakes her.”

reading.title: Reading: Pain
body: Pain is a personal experience, and its impact cannot be judged from appearance alone. [R3] In a simulated pharmacy consultation, Mr Salimov says his shoulder discomfort began four days ago. He can attend work, although reaching for objects is difficult. Because the discomfort interrupts sleep, he feels tired during the day. The student asks about onset, location, intensity and activities that make the symptom better or worse. The student also checks which products he has already used, without recommending a new dose. Mr Salimov explains that he has tried an unnamed tablet; therefore, the medicine history remains incomplete. The student records the uncertainty and asks the supervising pharmacist to review it. The summary uses contrast carefully: “He continues working; however, the discomfort affects reaching and sleep.” The aim is not to identify a diagnosis from one conversation, but to provide a coherent account that supports further professional assessment.
questions: 1. When did the discomfort begin?
2. Name two activities affected by the discomfort.
3. Find the linker that introduces a reason.
4. Why does the medicine history remain incomplete?
5. Write one accurate contrast from the case using however.

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The discomfort began ___ days ago.
2. Reaching a high ___ is difficult.
3. The patient feels tired because sleep is ___.
4. The medicine history is ___.
5. The supervising ___ will review the information.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Student: When did the discomfort begin? Patient: Four days ago. I can still work, although reaching a high shelf is difficult. Student: How does it affect your routine? Patient: I feel tired because it interrupts my sleep. I took a tablet yesterday, but I do not know its name. Student: Thank you. The medicine history is incomplete; therefore, I will ask the supervising pharmacist to review it. Patient: I look fine, but it is still uncomfortable. Student: I understand. Your description matters. I will record the effect on sleep and reaching, so the pharmacist has a clear account.

speaking.roleA: Ask about onset, location, intensity, aggravating factors and functional impact. Summarise the answers using because, although and however. Refer unknown medicine details to your supervisor.
speaking.roleB: Your shoulder discomfort began four days ago. Reaching makes it worse; you can still work but sleep is interrupted. You used an unnamed tablet. Do not invent a score or medicine name when asked.

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Polite requests

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: Would you mind to repeat that?
formula.text: Would you mind repeating that? — Mind is followed by -ing.

formula.label: Could you showing me the list?
formula.text: Could you show me the list? — Could takes the base verb.

formula.label: Your daughter can answer for you.
formula.text: Would you like your daughter to join the discussion? — Ask about the patient’s preference.

practice: 1. Could you / Would you + base verb makes a polite request: “Could you repeat that?”
2. Would you mind + -ing: “Would you mind sitting here?” A polite yes/no response depends on whether the person objects.
3. Ask permission before involving another person: “Would you like your caregiver to join us?” Give time to respond.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. Complete: Could you ___ your medicine list? (show / showing)

reading.title: Reading: Old Age and Brain
body: An older adult who occasionally forgets a name does not automatically have dementia; dementia is not an inevitable part of normal ageing. [R4] In a fictional consultation, Ms Akramova explains that she has gradually become less confident about her medicine routine. The student faces her, speaks clearly and asks, “Could you show me the list you use at home?” With her permission, her daughter joins the discussion. The student asks about Ms Akramova’s usual routine rather than treating the daughter as the only source of information. This planned conversation is different from a sudden change in attention or awareness. Sudden confusion needs immediate medical assessment, not a long classroom-style interview. [R5] The group practises two communication goals: supporting autonomy during a routine review and recognising the need to escalate an acute change. Polite requests are useful when they make an action clear, give the person time and avoid unnecessary pressure.
questions: 1. Does the text describe dementia as inevitable in ageing?
2. What concern does Ms Akramova describe?
3. Why can her daughter join the discussion?
4. Which change requires immediate medical assessment?
5. Find a polite request in the text.

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient wants the questions explained to ___ first.
2. The student asks to see the medicine ___.
3. The change in confidence has been ___.
4. The medicine packets are kept in a labelled ___.
5. The patient asks the student to speak more ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Student: Good morning, Ms Akramova. Would you like your daughter to join us? Patient: Yes, but please explain the questions to me first. Student: Of course. Could you show me your medicine list? Patient: Here it is. I have gradually become less sure about my routine. Student: Would you mind telling me how you organise the packets? Patient: I keep them in a labelled box. Student: Thank you. I will ask the pharmacist to review the routine with you. Patient: Could you speak a little more slowly? Student: Certainly. Please stop me whenever you need more time.

speaking.roleA: Conduct a routine, non-urgent medicine discussion. Ask permission to involve the caregiver, use three polite requests and allow a read-back. If your partner introduces sudden confusion, stop the routine interview and request urgent professional assessment.
speaking.roleB: You have gradually become less confident organising labelled packets. You want to answer for yourself, with a relative present. Ask the student to slow down. This is a fictional role; you do not need to disclose personal health information.

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Applying for a job

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: I apply job of pharmacy trainee.
formula.text: I am writing to apply for the pharmacy trainee position. — State the position and purpose clearly.

formula.label: I have experience in record findings.
formula.text: I have experience in recording findings. — Use -ing after in.

formula.label: I can diagnose all tongue problems.
formula.text: I can document observations and seek appropriate supervision. — State realistic competence rather than an unsupported claim.

practice: 1. Use “I am writing to apply for ...” to state the purpose of a covering letter.
2. Use experience in + -ing and responsible for + -ing to describe relevant skills.
3. Use “I would welcome the opportunity to ...” for a formal, courteous closing. Do not exaggerate qualifications.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. Complete: I am writing ___ apply for the position.

reading.title: Reading: Tongue Diagnosis
body: Dear Recruitment Team, I am writing to apply for the pharmacy trainee position at your training centre. During simulated consultations, I have practised taking patient histories, documenting oral concerns and explaining why a referral may be needed. In one fictional case, a patient reported an ulcer that had lasted four weeks. An oral ulcer lasting more than three weeks should be assessed by a dentist or doctor. [R6] I recorded the duration and location without presenting the appearance as a confirmed diagnosis. I understand that a trainee must work within the supervision arrangements of the role. I have experience in communicating uncertainty and checking that a patient understands the next step. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how these skills could support your team. Yours faithfully, A. Rahimova. This model application illustrates professional language; the applicant, employer and clinical case are fictional. The syllabus title “Tongue diagnosis” is retained, but tongue appearance alone is not used to establish a systemic diagnosis.
questions: 1. Which job is the applicant seeking?
2. How long had the fictional ulcer lasted?
3. What does the applicant record rather than claim?
4. Find one phrase suitable for a formal application closing.
5. Why is the original exaggerated claim unsuitable?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The applicant wants to develop skills under ___.
2. The applicant would document ___.
3. Tongue ___ alone is not used for a systemic diagnosis.
4. The fictional ulcer has lasted four ___.
5. The applicant values clear ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Interviewer: Why are you applying for this trainee role? Applicant: I would like to develop my pharmacy communication skills under supervision. Interviewer: How would you discuss a tongue concern? Applicant: I would ask about the symptom, duration and relevant history, then document observations. I would not diagnose a systemic illness from tongue colour alone. Interviewer: What if a patient reports an ulcer lasting four weeks? Applicant: I would explain that it needs assessment by a dentist or doctor and follow the supervisor’s referral process. Interviewer: What strength would you bring? Applicant: Clear documentation and honest communication about the limits of my competence.

speaking.roleA: You are recruiting a supervised pharmacy trainee. Ask about relevant communication experience and a fictional four-week oral ulcer. Look for accurate limits of competence, not impressive-sounding diagnoses.
speaking.roleB: Explain experience in recording findings, asking about symptoms and checking understanding. Use two application phrases. State that a persistent oral ulcer needs professional assessment, without naming a diagnosis.
prompts: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Present perfect

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: She has change her routine.
formula.text: She has changed her routine. — Use the past participle.

formula.label: I have changed it yesterday.
formula.text: I changed it yesterday. — A finished time takes the past simple here.

formula.label: He has followed the plan since two weeks.
formula.text: He has followed the plan for two weeks. — For introduces duration.

practice: 1. Form the present perfect with have/has + past participle: “She has changed her routine.”
2. Use for with a duration and since with a starting point; use already, yet and recently appropriately.
3. Use the past simple with a finished time such as yesterday. Ask permission before discussing weight; grammar practice must not become blame.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. Complete: She has ___ her breakfast routine. (change)

reading.title: Reading: Nutrition and Obesity
body: Obesity is a complex condition, not a reliable measure of a person’s motivation or character. [R7] In a fictional follow-up, a pharmacist first asks whether the patient is comfortable discussing food routines. The patient agrees and says, “I have kept a food diary for two weeks, but I have not changed everything.” The pharmacist asks what has been manageable rather than demanding rapid weight loss. The patient has recently replaced one sugary drink and has spoken with a dietitian about portion sizes. A varied dietary pattern can support health, but individual plans need to account for circumstances and clinical needs. [R20] The discussion focuses on practical barriers, including work hours and food availability. The student notices that “I have spoken with a dietitian” connects a past event with the current discussion, while “I spoke with the dietitian on Monday” gives a finished time. Progress is described accurately without claiming that one change guarantees a particular outcome.
questions: 1. How long has the patient kept a diary?
2. What permission does the pharmacist request?
3. Name two changes or actions mentioned.
4. Why is “on Monday” used with the past simple in the example?
5. Does the reading promise a particular outcome?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient has kept a diary for two ___.
2. Late ___ make regular meals difficult.
3. The patient has spoken with a ___.
4. Evening meals have not been planned ___.
5. Portion sizes were discussed on ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Pharmacist: Would you be comfortable discussing your food routine? Patient: Yes. I have kept a diary for two weeks. Pharmacist: What have you found useful? Patient: I have noticed that late shifts make regular meals difficult. I have already spoken with the dietitian, but I have not planned my evening meals yet. Pharmacist: Have you made any manageable changes? Patient: I have replaced one sugary drink. I discussed portion sizes with the dietitian on Monday. Pharmacist: Thank you. Let us focus on what fits your circumstances rather than judging your progress by appearance.

speaking.outcome: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.
speaking.roleA: Ask permission to discuss routines. Use present-perfect questions to explore recent changes. Summarise one achievement and one barrier without making weight-based assumptions or prescribing a diet.
speaking.roleB: You have kept a food diary for two weeks and replaced one sugary drink. You spoke with a dietitian on Monday. Late shifts remain a barrier. You do not want a strict plan or comments about your appearance.
prompts: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.
Peer observation

practice a: 1. changed 2. spoken 3. for 4. since 5. I discussed it yesterday.
reading 1–5: 1. For two weeks. 2. Permission to discuss food routines. 3. Replacing one sugary drink and speaking with a dietitian. 4. It identifies a finished past time. 5. No; it describes progress without guarantees.
mini-quiz 1–6: 1. kept 2. for 3. since 4. They have spoken to the dietitian. 5. Negative judgement or discrimination based on body weight. 6. “Would you be comfortable discussing your food routine?”

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Present perfect: interrogative form

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: You have tried the plan?
formula.text: Have you tried the plan? — Invert have and the subject.

formula.label: What she has changed?
formula.text: What has she changed? — Place has before the subject.

formula.label: How long have you use the diary?
formula.text: How long have you used the diary? — Use the past participle.

practice: 1. Yes/no question: Have/Has + subject + past participle? “Have you tried an activity diary?”
2. Wh-question: question word + have/has + subject + past participle? “What have you found helpful?”
3. How long asks about duration continuing to the present. Use ever for experience and yet for an expected action up to now.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. Reorder: you / ever / have / tried / an activity diary / ?

reading.title: Reading: The Place of Doing Exercises in a Healthy Lifestyle
body: Physical activity includes more than organised sport; movement during travel, work and leisure can also count. Activity can benefit physical and mental health, and appropriate opportunities differ between people. [R8] In a fictional review, a student asks, “Have you ever used an activity diary?” The patient says that a short diary has helped identify long periods of sitting. The student follows with “What have you found enjoyable?” rather than assuming that everyone wants to join a gym. The patient has tried short walks with a neighbour and has discussed activity limits with a clinician. “How long have you followed this routine?” asks about a period that continues to the present. The class records the patient’s preferences, barriers and agreed follow-up. The task does not set exercise intensity or ignore symptoms; it practises questions that help a qualified professional understand the person’s experience and develop an individualised plan.
questions: 1. Name two settings for activity other than organised sport.
2. What has the diary helped identify?
3. What activity has the patient tried?
4. Which question asks about an ongoing duration?
5. Why does the student avoid assuming the patient wants a gym?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The diary has been used for ___ days.
2. The patient sits for long periods at ___.
3. The patient walks with a ___.
4. The activity limits were reviewed last ___.
5. The current routine has lasted one ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Student: Have you ever kept an activity diary? Patient: Yes, I have used one for ten days. Student: What have you found helpful? Patient: I have noticed how long I sit during work. Student: Have you tried an activity you enjoy? Patient: I have taken short walks with my neighbour. Student: Have you discussed your activity limits with your clinician yet? Patient: Yes, we reviewed them last week. Student: How long have you followed the current routine? Patient: For one week. Student: Thank you. I will record your preferences and the points for your next review.

speaking.outcome: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.
speaking.roleA: Ask one question with ever, one with yet, one with how long and two other present-perfect questions. Identify a preferred activity, a barrier and what the clinician has already discussed.
speaking.roleB: You have used a diary for ten days, walked with a neighbour and reviewed your activity limits last week. Your current routine is one week old. You prefer company to a gym. Ask for a question to be repeated.
prompts: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.
Peer observation

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: There is many contaminated water.

reading.title: Reading: Formative Assessment: Contamination of Water
body: Unsafe drinking-water can transmit infection, and safe water and sanitation are important public-health protections. [R9] The following assessment case is fictional. At 09:00, staff at Riverside Training Clinic notice a leaking pipe near a drinking-water tap. Two people say that the water looks cloudy. No sample has yet been tested, and no illness has been linked to the supply. The supervisor asks staff not to use that tap while the concern is being reviewed, and arranges an alternative drinking-water supply. A student is asked to draft a letter to the responsible water service. The letter should give the location and time, describe the observations and request inspection and advice. It must not claim that cloudy water proves a particular infection. A contact person, Ms Yunusova, is available at the clinic reception. Students should distinguish a suspected problem from a confirmed laboratory finding throughout their response.
questions: 1. Where is the concern located?
2. When do staff notice the leak?
3. Has a laboratory result confirmed contamination?
4. What temporary arrangement does the supervisor make?
5. What should the letter request?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The leak was noticed at ___ o’clock.
2. ___ people reported cloudy water.
3. The cause is ___.
4. An alternative drinking-water ___ has been arranged.
5. The contact person works at ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Supervisor: Please record a water-supply concern at Riverside Training Clinic. The leak was noticed at nine o’clock this morning, beside the drinking-water tap. Student: Has the water been tested? Supervisor: Not yet. Two people have reported cloudy water, but the cause is unconfirmed. Please do not describe a confirmed infection. Student: What action has been arranged? Supervisor: An alternative drinking-water supply. The affected tap is not being used while the concern is reviewed. Student: Who should the water service contact? Supervisor: Ms Yunusova at reception. Please request an inspection and written advice about the next steps.

speaking.roleA: Student A: Clinic representative
speaking.roleB: Student B: Water-service officer
prompts: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.
Peer observation
Assessment reflection — after collection
After the assessed work has been collected, compare a confirmed observation with an unsupported conclusion. Identify one sentence you would revise in a future public-health letter.

practice a: 1. report 2. How much 3. noticed 4. We are requesting advice because the supply may be affected. 5. Have you tested the water?
reading 1–5: 1. At a drinking-water tap near a leaking pipe at Riverside Training Clinic. 2. At 09:00. 3. No; no sample has yet been tested. 4. An alternative drinking-water supply and non-use of the affected tap during review. 5. Inspection and advice on the next steps.
mini-quiz 1–6: 1. How many. 2. reported 3. An organism or agent capable of causing disease. 4. Could you send us advice, please? 5. No. 6. The cause is unconfirmed.

writing: model response: Dear Water Service Team, I am writing to report a water-supply concern at Riverside Training Clinic. At 09:00 today, staff noticed a leaking pipe beside the drinking-water tap. Two people have reported cloudy water, but no sample has been tested and the cause is unconfirmed. The supervisor has arranged an alternative supply while the affected tap is not being used. Could you inspect the area and provide written advice on the next steps? Please contact Ms Yunusova at reception. Yours faithfully, Clinic Representative.

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Take and get

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: Please get a break.
formula.text: Please take a break. — Take a break is the usual collocation.

formula.label: His symptoms took worse.
formula.text: His symptoms got worse. — Get worse describes a change in condition.

formula.label: We have took action.
formula.text: We have taken action. — Taken is the past participle of take.

practice: 1. Take combines with action, a break, precautions and a medicine: “Take the medicine as directed.”
2. Get combines with worse, better, help and information: “Get help if the concern is urgent.”
3. Choose the tense from context: take–took–taken; get–got–got in the British-English forms used here.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. Complete: The clinic will ___ action. (take / get)

reading.title: Reading: Air Pollution and Its Role in Human Health
body: Air pollution can affect respiratory and cardiovascular health; fine particulate matter is an important component of that risk. [R10] In a fictional clinic, staff receive an air-quality alert and prepare a short information message. The message asks people to get reliable local information and follow relevant clinical advice rather than assume that one response suits everyone. A patient says that breathing symptoms have become worse during the week. The student does not claim that air pollution is the only possible explanation. Instead, the student records the concern and asks a clinician to review it. The class notices useful combinations: the clinic can take action, people can get information, and symptoms can get worse. The communication task is to distinguish a general environmental risk from a personal diagnosis. Advice should be understandable, linked to the actual alert and appropriate to the person’s situation rather than based on an unsupported promise.
questions: 1. Which two areas of health can air pollution affect?
2. What prompts the clinic’s information message?
3. Why does the student avoid naming a single cause for the symptoms?
4. Find two collocations with get.
5. Who is asked to review the patient’s concern?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient has seen an air-quality ___.
2. The patient asks where to get reliable ___.
3. The symptoms got worse ___.
4. The student takes the concern to a ___.

reading.title: Reading: Secrets of Long Life
body: Healthy ageing concerns the abilities and opportunities that allow people to do what they value; it is not simply a promise to avoid every illness. [R11] In a fictional review, Mr Hasanov says, “I want to remain independent enough to visit my friends.” The student asks what would help him work towards that goal. He plans to discuss his routine with his clinician and hopes to make changes that fit his circumstances. The conversation includes purpose: “I keep notes to remember the questions I want to ask.” It also includes realistic limits. No supplement or single habit is presented as a guaranteed secret of longevity. [R18] The student summarises a shared aim instead of imposing a universal plan: “It is useful to choose a step you can maintain.” The class compares grammatical intention with certainty. “I hope to improve my routine” describes a goal; it does not prove that a specific health outcome will occur.

reading.title: Reading: Typhoid Mary
body: Mary Mallon, widely known as “Typhoid Mary”, was a cook whose history became associated with the recognition and management of asymptomatic typhoid carriage. Her case also raises questions about communication, stigma and the relationship between individual freedom and public protection. [R13] Typhoid can spread through food or water contaminated by an infected person or carrier, including someone without symptoms. [R12] For the language task, students consider a fictional modern interview, not a recreation of Mallon’s words. A food handler says, “Feeling well makes it difficult to understand why testing matters.” The health worker responds by explaining the purpose of the assessment and checking understanding. The class practises avoiding blame, asking neutral questions and discussing the relevant guidance. Gerunds help organise these ideas: “Explaining the reason matters”; “Avoid making assumptions”; “Before returning to food handling, follow professional advice.” The lesson does not ask students to determine work restrictions or a medical diagnosis independently.

Food handler: Explaining the reason helps. Health worker: Could you repeat the plan in your own words? Food handler: I will ask the health team for guidance before returning to food handling.

reading.title: Reading: Function of Blood
body: Red blood cells transport oxygen, white blood cells contribute to immune defence, and platelets help blood clot. Plasma carries blood cells and dissolved substances. [R14] In a fictional teaching laboratory, the tutor explains these broad functions before practising a handover. No numerical results are supplied, so students are not asked to diagnose anaemia or interpret a patient’s blood count. The nurse says, “I have checked the label.” The student reports that the nurse had checked the label. Later, the clinician says, “I will review the report,” and the student records that the clinician would review it. The group distinguishes a report of someone’s words from proof that a clinical conclusion is correct. They also notice that a general fact can stay in the present tense: “The tutor explained that platelets help blood to clot.” The final handover identifies the specimen, the confirmed action and the person responsible for the next step, without inventing a result.

2. Respond to a fictional end-of-life discussion with empathy and without predicting an unsupported timeline.
3. Summarise shared and differing preferences accurately.

stages.label: WARM-UP
stages.detail: Use a neutral fictional example: two relatives ask for a quieter room; three team members attend a meeting. Describe the groups with both and all. Personal bereavement disclosure is not required.

stages.label: VISUAL MEDICAL VOCABULARY
stages.detail: Use Handout 1. Model pronunciation for entries 1–6; pairs explain them in their own words. Keep entries 7–12 available as extension support. Each pupil writes an original sentence for three terms.

stages.label: GRAMMAR DISCOVERY
stages.detail: Use Handout 2. Pairs explain the changes in the example table, formulate the rule and complete Practice A. Check difficult points through a brief comparison of answers.

stages.label: READING
stages.detail: Use Handout 3. Pupils read for the main message, then answer the five questions. Ask partners to identify the sentence supporting an answer and distinguish facts from unknown details.

stages.label: LISTENING
stages.detail: Read the teacher script twice, first for gist and then for detail. Pupils complete Handout 4, compare briefly and listen for any detail they need to confirm.

stages.label: SPEAKING AND CULTURE
stages.detail: Use Handout 5: two minutes to prepare, four minutes per role, three minutes for peer feedback and two minutes with a neighbouring pair for the culture task. Aim for three medical terms and two target structures.

stages.label: MINI-QUIZ AND HOMEWORK
stages.detail: Pupils complete Handout 6 individually. Check the key, give one focused correction and assign the 100–120-word writing task. Writing itself is completed after class.

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Both, neither and all

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: Both of the three colleagues are present.
formula.text: All three colleagues are present. — Both is used for two, not three.

formula.label: Neither option are clear.
formula.text: Neither option is clear. — Use a singular verb with neither option.

formula.label: Both relatives want this, so the patient wants it.
formula.text: Both relatives want this; we should also ask the patient. — Do not substitute relatives’ preferences for the patient’s.

practice: 1. Both refers to two and normally takes a plural verb: “Both relatives are present.”
2. Neither refers to not one of two. For the formal practice here, use “Neither option is ...” and “Neither of the two options is ...”.
3. All refers to the whole group: “All three colleagues agree.” A family’s preference must not be assumed to be the patient’s preference.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. Two relatives are present. Complete: ___ relatives are present.

reading.title: Reading: Death and Dying
body: Palliative care addresses suffering and quality of life, including physical, psychological, social and spiritual concerns. It is not limited to a conversation about the final hours of life. [R15] In a fictional family meeting, Ms Sobirova asks for a calm explanation of her care plan. Both of her chosen relatives are present, and all three professionals introduce their roles. The pharmacist explains that medicine-related questions can be reviewed with the prescribing team. Neither relative wants staff to guess how much time remains. The student practises acknowledging uncertainty: “The clinician is best placed to discuss what is known and what remains uncertain.” The group also asks Ms Sobirova what matters to her. Her own preferences are recorded rather than inferred from the relatives’ comments. The language task is to express agreement and difference accurately, offer space for questions and avoid reassurance that makes a promise the team cannot support.
questions: 1. What is the broad purpose of palliative care?
2. How many chosen relatives are present?
3. How many professionals introduce themselves?
4. What do neither of the relatives want staff to do?
5. Whose preferences must be asked about directly?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient wants ___ relatives to stay.
2. Neither relative wants staff to ___.
3. There are ___ team members.
4. The patient’s main priority is ___.
5. The patient asks about the next ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Student: Thank you for meeting with us, Ms Sobirova. Would you like both relatives to stay? Patient: Yes, please. Relative: We both want a clear explanation, but neither of us wants anyone to guess. Student: I understand. All three members of the team will explain their roles. Patient: My main priority is comfort and being able to ask questions. Pharmacist: We can discuss your medicine-related concerns with the prescribing team. Student: Could you tell us which question matters most today? Patient: I want to understand the next review. Student: We will make sure that question is recorded and passed to the clinician.

speaking.roleB: Student B: Patient or chosen relative

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Conditionals

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: If the dispenser will be empty, I will report it.
formula.text: If the dispenser is empty, I will report it. — Use present simple after if in this first conditional.

formula.label: If staff remove gloves, they never clean their hands.
formula.text: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene; hands are cleaned after removal. — A correct grammatical pattern cannot make unsafe content correct.

formula.label: If a step is unclear, staff checked the procedure.
formula.text: If a step is unclear, staff check the procedure. — Use consistent present forms for the stated routine.

practice: 1. Zero conditional: if + present simple, present simple; use it for a general relationship or a stated routine.
2. First conditional: if + present simple, will + base verb; use it for a possible future situation and response.
3. The grammar pattern does not prove a medical claim. Use the evidence-based statement or the explicit classroom procedure provided.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. General routine: If a label is unclear, the team ___ it. (check)

reading.title: Reading: Hygiene
body: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene, and hands should be cleaned after gloves are removed. [R16] In a fictional training ward, pupils review a written hygiene procedure. The procedure says, “If a dispenser is empty, staff report it to the supervisor.” This is a routine expressed with the zero conditional. A student then offers a future response: “If I notice an empty dispenser this afternoon, I will report it.” The class compares the grammar without confusing it with proof of effectiveness. A separate task asks pupils to give a respectful reminder to a colleague: “Could we check the hand-hygiene step before continuing?” The aim is not to shame the colleague, but to clarify the next action. Students use classroom props rather than clinical materials and identify one missing piece of information that would require checking the local procedure. They do not improvise cleaning chemicals or replace professional infection-prevention guidance with a culture-project claim.
questions: 1. Do gloves replace hand hygiene?
2. What does the fictional routine require when a dispenser is empty?
3. Which sentence gives a possible future response?
4. Why should a reminder avoid shaming the colleague?
5. What should pupils check when a procedure detail is missing?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The dispenser is ___.
2. The problem should be reported to the ___.
3. Gloves do not replace hand ___.
4. Another missing ___ will also be reported.
5. The students aim to record the problem without ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Student A: The hand-rub dispenser is empty. Student B: What does our training procedure say? Student A: If a dispenser is empty, staff report it to the supervisor. Student B: I will do that now. Student A: Also, could we check the hand-hygiene step before continuing? Student B: I thought gloves replaced that step. Student A: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. Let us ask the supervisor if any detail is unclear. Student B: Agreed. If I notice another missing supply, I will report it rather than improvise. Student A: Good. We can record the problem without blaming anyone.

speaking.outcome: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.
speaking.roleA: Identify an empty dispenser in the fictional ward. State the routine using a zero conditional and offer a future action using a first conditional. Give one respectful hand-hygiene reminder.
speaking.roleB: Ask which procedure applies. Initially confuse gloves with hand hygiene, then clarify the rule. Agree who will report the supply issue and repeat the next action.
prompts: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Zero conditional

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: If the label is unclear, staff guesses.
formula.text: If the label is unclear, staff ask for clarification. — Use correct agreement and a safe stated routine.

formula.label: If an item are damaged, we report it.
formula.text: If an item is damaged, we report it. — Item is singular.

formula.label: Every disinfectant works immediately.
formula.text: Staff follow the product’s specified contact time. — The required time is product-specific.

practice: 1. Zero conditional pattern: if + present simple, present simple. It can describe a general procedure: “If a label is missing, staff ask for clarification.”
2. Use singular/plural agreement accurately: “If an item is damaged, the team removes it from use.”
3. When the if-clause comes first, use a comma. Do not invent a universal contact time; it depends on the product instructions.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. Complete: If an item is damaged, the team ___ it. (report)

reading.title: Reading: Hygiene Equipment
body: Cleaning, disinfection and sterilisation have different purposes and are not interchangeable labels. Appropriate equipment processing depends on the item and the relevant instructions. A disinfectant needs its specified contact time rather than an assumed instant effect. [R17] In a fictional classroom inventory, pupils inspect unused picture cards labelled “single use”, “reusable” and “damaged”. The local simulation rule states: “If an item is damaged, the team removes it from the practice set and reports it.” Another rule says, “If processing instructions are missing, students ask the supervisor.” Pupils explain these routines with zero conditionals and identify which facts are known. They are not asked to mix chemicals, sterilise instruments or practise with real sharps. A partner checks the distinction between an observation and an instruction: “The label is missing” describes a finding; “We ask the supervisor” describes the agreed response. The final task is to make the routine clear without adding technical details that the exercise does not supply.
questions: 1. Are cleaning, disinfection and sterilisation interchangeable terms?
2. Where should a disinfectant’s contact time come from?
3. What happens to a damaged practice item?
4. What should students do when processing instructions are missing?
5. Why are pupils not given a chemical-mixing task?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The first item is labelled ___.
2. Its processing instructions are ___.
3. The second card shows a damaged ___.
4. Contact time is specified for the ___.
5. The cards practise communication, not chemical ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Supervisor: Please check the picture-card inventory. Student: One card shows a reusable item, but its processing instructions are missing. Supervisor: If instructions are missing, students ask the supervisor. Student: Another card shows a damaged packet. Supervisor: If an item is damaged, the team removes it from the practice set and reports it. Student: Does every disinfectant have the same contact time? Supervisor: No. Staff follow the time specified for the product. Student: So if the label is unclear, we request clarification rather than guess. Supervisor: Correct. These cards practise communication, not chemical preparation.

speaking.outcome: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.
speaking.roleA: You have three imaginary cards: a reusable item with missing instructions, a damaged packet and a clearly labelled single-use item. Explain each finding and the stated response using zero conditionals.
speaking.roleB: Ask what is actually written on each card. Confirm that missing instructions require clarification and damaged items are removed from the practice set. Ask your partner to distinguish cleaning from disinfection.
prompts: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: First and second conditionals

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: If the packet will be unlabelled, I will ask.
formula.text: If the packet is unlabelled, I will ask. — Use present simple in the first-conditional if-clause.

formula.label: If I would manage the service, I would improve it.
formula.text: If I managed the service, I would improve it. — Use past simple in the second-conditional if-clause.

formula.label: If I were you, I will ask for help.
formula.text: If I were you, I would ask for help. — Use would for the imagined situation.

practice: 1. First conditional: if + present simple, will + base verb for a possible future situation.
2. Second conditional: if + past simple, would + base verb for an imagined or less likely situation.
3. Use “If I were ...” in formal hypothetical advice. Do not normally put would in the if-clause of these patterns.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. First conditional: If stock is unavailable, I ___ the pharmacist. (tell)

reading.title: Reading: First and Second Conditionals
body: A fictional pharmacy training exercise presents two problems: a missing stock item and a packet with an unreadable label. The student says, “If the item is unavailable, I will tell the pharmacist.” This first conditional describes a possible next action. The student does not choose a replacement independently. A second discussion imagines responsibility for the service: “If I managed the stock system, I would make the records easier to check.” This second conditional explores a hypothetical improvement, not a claim that the student already has that authority. A colleague then suggests replacing the prescribed product with a homeopathic one. The class distinguishes cultural discussion from clinical substitution: homeopathy has little supporting evidence for treating specific conditions and should not replace established care. [R19] Students practise explaining the uncertainty, identifying the responsible professional and agreeing a communication step. No medicine brand, dose or storage temperature is invented when the information is absent.
questions: 1. What two problems are presented?
2. Who should be told about the unavailable item?
3. Which sentence imagines responsibility for the service?
4. Should the student independently replace the medicine with a homeopathic product?
5. Name one technical detail the case does not provide.

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The student will report the unavailable item to the ___.
2. The student needs ___.
3. The imagined improvement concerns clearer ___.
4. The packet’s label is ___.
5. The concern will follow the agreed escalation ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Student: If this item is unavailable, I will tell the pharmacist. Colleague: Could you choose another product yourself? Student: No. I need supervision. If I were responsible for the stock system, I would make the records easier to read. Colleague: This packet also has an unreadable label. Student: If the label is unclear, I will ask for clarification. Colleague: What about replacing it with a homeopathic product? Student: We should not treat that as an equivalent substitute. The pharmacist needs to review the request. Colleague: Understood. We will record the concern and follow the agreed escalation pathway.

speaking.outcome: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.
speaking.roleA: An item is unavailable and another packet has an unreadable label. Use two first conditionals to state your next actions and one second conditional to suggest a hypothetical system improvement.
speaking.roleB: Ask whether the trainee can choose a substitute and what they would improve if they managed the service. Request clarification about who has authority to make the clinical decision.
prompts: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.
Peer observation

culture.title: Homeopathy
notes: Use a first conditional to explain that a request about homeopathy will be referred to the pharmacist. Use a second conditional to discuss how you would respond to a claim that it can replace any prescribed treatment. Do not present that claim as established evidence. [R19]
Two-minute group exchange: join another pair, give a short response and invite one question. Separate a cultural description, a personal account and a claim requiring evidence.

practice a: 1. will tell 2. would improve 3. were 4. If the name is unclear, I will check it. 5. If I worked here, I would ...
reading 1–5: 1. A missing stock item and a packet with an unreadable label. 2. The pharmacist. 3. “If I managed the stock system, I would make the records easier to check.” 4. No. 5. A medicine brand, dose or storage temperature.
mini-quiz 1–6: 1. will tell 2. would review 3. were 4. An error or unsafe situation identified before reaching the patient or causing harm. 5. If I worked here, I would check it. 6. No.
speaking: model response: “If the item is unavailable, I will tell the pharmacist. If the label is unreadable, I will request clarification. If I managed the stock system, I would make the records easier to check.”
culture / reflection: suggested response: “If a patient asks about homeopathy, I will refer the question to the pharmacist. If I heard a universal replacement claim, I would ask for evidence.”

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Defining relative clauses

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: The pharmacist which checks the list ...
formula.text: The pharmacist who checks the list ... — Use who for a person.

formula.label: The room which patients ask questions ...
formula.text: The room where patients ask questions ... — Where introduces what happens in the place.

formula.label: The patient who label is missing ...
formula.text: The patient whose label is missing ... — Whose shows possession.

practice: 1. Use who for people and which/that for things in defining relative clauses.
2. Use where for a place followed by a clause about what happens there: “the room where patients ask questions”.
3. Use whose for possession. Defining clauses identify the person or thing and are not separated by commas.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. Complete: The pharmacist ___ checks the record is upstairs.

reading.title: Reading: Relative Pronouns: Describing Things and Places
body: In a fictional pharmacy orientation, the tutor labels three areas: the dispensing bench, the consultation booth and the storage area. Pupils receive descriptions rather than a map of a real pharmacy. “The booth is the place where patients can ask private questions.” “The leaflet is the document that explains the medicine.” A new trainee meets the pharmacist who supervises the exercise and checks which items are being discussed. The task also includes a patient whose packet has an unreadable label. The trainee does not identify the medicine by the tablet’s appearance; the missing information is referred to the supervisor. Students practise precise definitions rather than instructions for clinical use. An oral syringe is described as a device for measuring or giving oral liquid medicine, but no dose is supplied. Each pair ends by selecting the correct item from the glossary and explaining which part of the relative clause made the meaning clear.
questions: 1. Which three areas are named?
2. Which relative word introduces what happens in the booth?
3. Who supervises the exercise?
4. What is wrong with the patient’s packet label?
5. Is the exercise asking students to calculate an oral-medicine dose?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The booth is a place for ___ questions.
2. The leaflet is a ___ that explains a medicine.
3. The ___ checks the students’ work.
4. The patient’s label is ___.
5. Students should not ___ the medicine from its appearance.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Tutor: Describe the consultation booth without naming it. Student: It is the place where patients can discuss private questions. Tutor: Good. Now describe the leaflet. Student: It is the document that explains a medicine. Tutor: Which person supervises this exercise? Student: The pharmacist who checks our work. Tutor: A patient has arrived with an unreadable label. Student: The patient whose label is unreadable needs help confirming the information. Tutor: Should you guess the medicine from its appearance? Student: No. I should ask the supervisor to clarify the details. Tutor: Exactly. Precise descriptions should reduce uncertainty, not hide it.

speaking.outcome: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.
speaking.roleA: Choose three glossary entries without telling your partner their names. Define one person with who, one object with which/that and one place with where. Add a fictional ownership sentence with whose.
speaking.roleB: Identify the objects or places from the definitions. Ask a clarification question when a description fits more than one item. Explain which clause helped you decide, then swap roles.
prompts: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.
Peer observation

culture.title: Mineral therapy
notes: An imaginary display is called “Mineral therapy”. Write a defining clause describing the display, not a medical benefit: “This is the display that ...”. Then ask which mineral, product or practice is actually meant before evaluating any health claim.
Two-minute group exchange: join another pair, give a short response and invite one question. Separate a cultural description, a personal account and a claim requiring evidence.

practice a: 1. who 2. which 3. where 4. whose 5. This is a device that/which measures a liquid amount.
reading 1–5: 1. The dispensing bench, consultation booth and storage area. 2. Where. 3. The pharmacist. 4. It is unreadable. 5. No; no dose is supplied.
mini-quiz 1–6: 1. who 2. that/which 3. where 4. whose 5. No. 6. A medicine cabinet is a cupboard that/which stores medicines under the required conditions.
speaking: model response: “An oral syringe is a device that measures or gives oral liquid medicine. The booth is the place where patients ask private questions. The pharmacist who supervises us will clarify the label.”
culture / reflection: suggested response: “This is the display that discusses historical uses of minerals.” Ask which substance or product is intended before evaluating a claim.

grammar.title: Grammar Focus: Relative clauses: adding and clarifying information

formula.label: Less accurate wording / prompt
formula.text: Improved wording — Reason

formula.label: Ms Aliyeva, that is our pharmacist, will help.
formula.text: Ms Aliyeva, who is our pharmacist, will help. — Use who, not that, in a non-defining clause about a person.

formula.label: This leaflet which is large-print is for you. (extra information)
formula.text: This leaflet, which is large-print, is for you. — Mark the extra information with commas.

formula.label: The patient, who packet is damaged, has a question.
formula.text: The patient, whose packet is damaged, has a question. — Whose expresses possession.

practice: 1. A non-defining relative clause adds information about an already identified person or thing and is separated by commas.
2. Use who, which or whose in these non-defining clauses; do not use that.
3. Place the relative clause near the noun it describes. Clear grammar should make the referent identifiable, not leave the reader guessing.
Practice A. Complete or rewrite the sentences
1. Complete: Ms Aliyeva, ___ is the supervising pharmacist, will explain.

reading.title: Reading: Relative Pronouns: Describing Things and Places
body: This fictional consultation focuses on whether written information is usable. Ms Saidova says that the print on her leaflet is too small. The trainee asks which format would help and speaks to Ms Aliyeva, who is the supervising pharmacist. A large-print version is available in the simulation. The trainee says, “This leaflet, which has larger text, is for you.” The additional clause describes a leaflet that has already been identified. A second example changes the meaning: “Choose the leaflet that has larger text” identifies one leaflet from several. The pharmacist asks Ms Saidova to explain the agreed next step in her own words. In this task, teach-back checks how clearly the information was explained; it is not a test of the patient’s intelligence. No product strength or storage instruction is invented. If a required detail is missing, the trainee identifies the gap and asks the pharmacist rather than making the sentence sound certain.
questions: 1. What communication barrier does Ms Saidova describe?
2. Who is Ms Aliyeva?
3. What does the clause “which has larger text” add in the example?
4. How does “the leaflet that has larger text” differ?
5. What does teach-back check in this task?

listening.title: Listening
directions: Listen twice. First identify the situation; then complete each item with the missing detail. Use short answers. The full script is in the teacher section, not on this handout.
questions: 1. The patient finds the print too ___.
2. Ms Aliyeva is the supervising ___.
3. The new leaflet has ___ text.
4. The patient will bring the damaged ___.
5. The team will confirm information rather than ___.
script: Read the complete script twice at a natural pace. Keep the wording stable between readings.

Patient: The print on this leaflet is too small for me. Trainee: Thank you for telling me. Ms Aliyeva, who is our supervising pharmacist, can help us check another format. Pharmacist: This leaflet, which has larger text, may be easier for you to read. Patient: Yes, that helps. Trainee: Could you tell me the next step in your own words so I can check that I explained it clearly? Patient: I will bring the damaged packet to you before we discuss its details. Pharmacist: Correct. We will confirm the information rather than guess the product strength or storage requirements.

speaking.outcome: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.
speaking.roleA: Explain that Ms Aliyeva is the supervisor and offer a fictional large-print leaflet. Use two non-defining relative clauses and one defining clause. Ask for teach-back to check your explanation.
speaking.roleB: You cannot easily read small print and have a damaged packet. Ask which leaflet is meant when the description is ambiguous. Explain the agreed next step in your own words without inventing medicine details.
prompts: Prepare with your own role card. Do not show it to your partner during the first exchange. Listen, ask for clarification and agree on a clear next step; then swap roles.
Peer observation

culture.title: Sound therapy
notes: A fictional patient enjoys calming sounds and calls this “sound therapy”. Practise asking what activity is meant and what the patient expects. Use a non-defining clause without turning enjoyment into a claim that the activity treats a disease.
Two-minute group exchange: join another pair, give a short response and invite one question. Separate a cultural description, a personal account and a claim requiring evidence.

practice a: 1. who 2. which 3. This leaflet, which has large print, is for Ms Saidova. 4. whose 5. The leaflet, which explains storage, is on the desk.
reading 1–5: 1. The print is too small. 2. The supervising pharmacist. 3. Extra information about an already identified leaflet. 4. It identifies one leaflet from several. 5. How clearly the information was explained and understood, not the patient’s intelligence.
mini-quiz 1–6: 1. who 2. which 3. Yes. 4. whose 5. Asking a person to explain information in their own words to check clarity. 6. No.
speaking: model response: “Ms Aliyeva, who supervises the exercise, will help. This leaflet, which has larger text, is for you. Please bring the packet that is damaged. Could you explain the next step in your own words?”
culture / reflection: suggested response: “The patient, who enjoys calming sounds, wants to explain the activity.” Enjoyment alone does not establish treatment effectiveness.
